Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verses 1–6:

Surat al-Qasas, which has eighty-eight verses, is Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Sin-Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ ﴿We recite to you some of the news of Musa and Fir'awn in truth, for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Fir'awn exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them: slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was among the corrupters.﴾ ﴿And We wished to show favour to those who were oppressed in the land, to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors.﴾ ﴿And to establish them in the land, and to show Fir'awn and Haman and their hosts what they feared from them.﴾

This surah is entirely Meccan; this was said by al-Hasan, Ata' and Ikrimah. Muqatil said: among it is something Medinan, ﴿those to whom We gave the Book before it﴾ [al-Qasas: 52] up to His words ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qasas: 55]. It was also said: it was revealed between Makkah and al-Juhfah. Ibn Abbas said: at al-Juhfah, during his (ﷺ) departure for the Hijrah. Ibn Salam said: ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained the Qur'an for you will surely return you to a place of return﴾ [al-Qasas: 85] was revealed at al-Juhfah, at the time of the Hijrah to Madinah. The connection between the beginning of this surah and the end of the surah before it is that He, the Exalted, commanded him to praise Him, then said: ﴿He will show you His signs﴾ [al-Naml: 93].

Among what He explained as His signs are the miracles of the Messenger, and He attributed them to Himself, since he was the one who reported them on His behalf, so He said: ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾, since the Book is the greatest of miracles and the greatest of the clear signs. The apparent meaning is that the Book is the Qur'an; it was also said: the Preserved Tablet. (We recite) means: we read to you with the recitation of Jibril, or we narrate. The object of "natlu" is "min naba'" (some of the news), meaning some part of the news. "Bil-haqq" (in truth) is connected to "natlu", meaning justly, or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from "naba'", meaning accompanied by truth. He specified the believers because they are the ones who benefit from the recitation.

﴿Exalted in the land﴾ means he acted arrogantly and proudly until he claimed lordship and divinity. "Al-ard" (the land) is the land of Egypt, and "al-shiya'" means factions. He ruled the Copts and enslaved the Children of Israel. That is, they follow him as he wishes, or some of them incite others to obey him, or some are made to build and some to dig, and other crafts that are humiliating. Whoever he did not employ, he imposed the jizyah on him, or he set some of them against others so that they would be more obedient to him. The oppressed group were the Children of Israel. Apparently, ﴿yastad'if﴾ (he oppressed) is a resumptive clause explaining the condition of some of the factions; it may be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "wa-ja'ala", and it may be a descriptive clause for "shiya'an". "Yudhabbih" (he slaughters) is an explanation of the oppression, and an interpretation, or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yastad'if", or in the position of a descriptive clause for "ta'ifah". The majority read "yudhabbih" with doubled dhal; Abu Haywah and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a fatha on the ya' and sukun on the dhal.

﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾ is the cause of his arrogance and of the slaughter of the sons, since there is in that nothing but mere corruption.

"Wa-nurid" (And We wish) is the narration of a past state, and the clause is conjoined to His words ﴿Indeed, Fir'awn﴾, since both are explanations of the building. It is weak for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yastad'if", because it requires supposing a subject, meaning "and we wish", and that is weak. If it is a circumstantial clause, how can the oppression by Fir'awn coexist with the wish for favour from Allah, when they cannot be concurrent? It was said: since the favour of their deliverance from Fir'awn was a certain outcome, the wish for its occurrence was treated as if it were concurrent with their oppression. "An namunna" means: by delivering them from Fir'awn and drowning him.

﴿And to make them leaders﴾ means: those who are followed in religion and in worldly affairs. Mujahid said: callers to good. Qatadah said: rulers, as in their saying ﴿and made you kings﴾. Al-Dahhak said: prophets.

﴿And to make them the inheritors﴾ means: they inherit Fir'awn and his people, (p-105) their kingdom and what belonged to them. From Ali: the inheritors are Yusuf and his offspring. Also from Qatadah: they inherited the land of Egypt and al-Sham. The majority read "wa-numakkina" conjoined to "namunna". Al-A'mash read "wa-li-numakkina" with the lam of purpose, meaning: we willed that in order that We establish them, or: we did that in order to establish them. "Al-tamkin" means settling in the land, namely the land of Egypt and al-Sham, such that their command is executed and they dominate over others. The majority read "wa-nura" as the imperfect of "arayna", with the following noun in the accusative. Abdullah, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-yara", the imperfect of "ra'a", with the following noun in the nominative.

﴿And Haman﴾ was the vizier of Fir'awn and one of his men, and he was mentioned for his prominence among his people and his standing in disbelief. Do you not see his saying to him: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower﴾ [Ghafir: 36]? "Yahdharun" means fear of the loss of their kingdom and their destruction at the hands of a boy from the Children of Israel.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verses 7–9:**

﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: "Suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear nor grieve. We will surely return him to you and make him one of the messengers."﴾ ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief. Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners.﴾ ﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said: "A delight of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son," while they did not perceive.﴾.

The revelation (*iyhaa'*) of God to the mother of Moses is an inspiration and a casting into the heart (*ilham* and *qadhf*), as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. Or it is a dream, as said by a group of people. Or it is the sending of an angel, as said by Qutrub and a group. This last is the apparent meaning, because of His saying: ﴿We will surely return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾. They agreed that she was not a prophetess. If the revelation was by the sending of an angel, as is the apparent meaning, then it is like the sending of an angel to the leper, the bald man and the blind man, and like what is reported of the angels speaking to people. The apparent meaning is that this revelation was after the birth, so there is an omitted clause in the text, meaning: "Moses' mother gave birth to him at the time of the slaughter of the sons, and she feared for him."

In ﴿And We revealed﴾, the *'an* is either explanatory (*tafsiriyyah*, "that," introducing an explanation of the revelation) or verbal (*masdariyyah*, "that" forming a verbal noun clause). It has also been said that the revelation was before the birth. 'Amr ibn 'Abd al-Wahid and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz read: "انِ ارْضِعِيهِ" ("an irdi'iihi"), with a kasra on the nun after the hamza was dropped, contrary to analogy. The analogical form would be to transfer the vowel of the hamza, which is a fatha, onto the nun, as in the reading of Warsh.

﴿When you fear for him﴾ means from the spies of Pharaoh and his agents, who kill the sons. ﴿Then cast him into the river﴾. Al-Junayd said: "If you fear for his safety through an intermediary, then hand him over to Us by casting him into the sea, and cut off your compassion and your management of him." The period of his suckling is three months, or four, or eight, according to different opinions. The *yamm* (river) here is the Nile of Egypt.

﴿And do not fear﴾, that is, of his drowning and loss, and of his being picked up so that he is killed. ﴿And do not grieve﴾ at your separation from him. ﴿We will surely return him to you﴾ is a true promise that calms her heart and gives her good news of his life and of his being made a messenger. A part of the story of the chest, its being thrown into the river and the manner of his being picked up, has already been mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha, so it is not repeated here. Al-Asma'i tested the eloquence of an Arab woman who recited poetry. He said: "Is this eloquence, after His saying: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses﴾ up to the verse?" For it combines two commands, two prohibitions, two reports and two good tidings.

In ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾ there is an omission in the speech. Its estimate is: "So she did what she was commanded regarding suckling him and casting him into the river." The *lam* in ﴿that he might become﴾ is the *lam* of metaphorical causation (*lam al-ta'lil al-majazi*), since the outcome of their picking him up and raising him was that he would become an enemy to them and ﴿a grief﴾, even though they did not pick him up except to adopt him, and that he would become beloved to them. This *lam* is called the *lam* of consequence (*lam al-'aqibah*) and the *lam* of becoming (*lam al-sayrurah*). The majority read "وحَزَنًا" ("wa hazanan") with a fatha on the ha' and the zay, which is the dialect of Quraysh. Ibn Thabbab, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn Sa'dan read it with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the zay.

The *khati'* (sinner) is one who intends the error, while the *mukhti'* (one who errs) is one who does not intend it. It is possible that there is an omission in the speech, and this is the apparent meaning, namely: "So he became for them an enemy and a grief," because they were sinners, who did not return to his religion and deliberately committed crimes and disbelief in God. Al-Mubarrad said: "They were sinners against themselves by picking him up." It has been said: "by killing the sons of the Children of Israel." It has also been said: "by raising their enemy."

The word "soldiers" (*jund*) is attributed here and in what precedes to Pharaoh and Haman, although Haman has no soldiers. This is because the affairs of soldiers are not orderly except by the king and the vizier, since through the vizier wealth is collected, and through the king and his power it is reached, and the maintenance of soldiers is only by wealth. It was read: "خاطِيِينَ" ("khatiyiin"), without a hamza. It is possible that its original form had a hamza which was dropped, and this is the apparent meaning. It has also been said that it comes from *khata yakhtu*, meaning "those who stray from the right course."

When they picked him up, they intended to kill him, fearing that he was the newborn whom they feared would bring about the end of their rule at his hands. But God put His love into the heart of Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh. It is related that she saw a light in the chest, and that its opening became easy for her after it had been difficult for others to open. It is also related that Pharaoh's daughter loved him too, because she was cured of her ailment, which was leprosy (*baras*), by the report of one who informed them that it would be cured only by the saliva of a human being found in a chest in the sea.

"*Qurrah*" (a delight) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is a delight." It is far-fetched that it should be a subject whose predicate is ﴿Do not kill him﴾. The explanation of "*qurrah*" has already been given at the end of Surah al-Furqan. It is mentioned that when she said to Pharaoh: ﴿A delight of the eye for me and for you﴾, he said: "For you, not for me." It is also reported that she said to him: "Perhaps he is from another people, not from the Children of Israel." She followed the prohibition against killing him with her hope that he would benefit them, because of the signs of good that appeared in him, from the light she had seen and from the healing of the leprosy, or that they might take him as a son, for he was fit for that.

﴿While they did not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), meaning: they did not perceive that he was the one whose rule would be ruined at his hands. This was said by Qatada. Or that he was an enemy to them, as said by Mujahid. Or that I do what I will, not what they will, as said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq. The apparent meaning is that this is part of the speech of God, the Exalted. It has also been said that it is part of the speech of the wife of Pharaoh, meaning that she said this to Pharaoh, and that those who had recommended killing him did not perceive her speech to him or her appeal to his heart concerning him, lest they incite him to kill him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The estimate of the speech is: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾, and ﴿the wife of Pharaoh said﴾ thus, and ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that they were in a great error in picking him up, hoping for benefit from him, and adopting him. His saying: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh﴾ and the verse that follows is a parenthetical clause placed between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, confirming the meaning of their error. End of quotation. Whenever it is possible to take the speech in its apparent meaning without a break, that is better.

It has also been said that it comes from *khata yakhtu*, meaning "those who stray from the right course."

When they picked him up, they intended to kill him, fearing that he was the newborn whom they feared would bring about the end of their rule at his hands. But God put His love into the heart of Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh. It is related that she saw a light in the chest, and that its opening became easy for her after it had been difficult for others to open. It is also related that Pharaoh's daughter loved him too, because she was cured of her ailment, which was leprosy (*baras*), by the report of one who informed them that it would be cured only by the saliva of a human being found in a chest in the sea.

"*Qurrah*" (a delight) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is a delight." It is far-fetched that it should be a subject whose predicate is ﴿Do not kill him﴾. The explanation of "*qurrah*" has already been given at the end of Surah al-Furqan. It is mentioned that when she said to Pharaoh: ﴿A delight of the eye for me and for you﴾, he said: "For you, not for me." It is also reported that she said to him: "Perhaps he is from another people, not from the Children of Israel." She followed the prohibition against killing him with her hope that he would benefit them, because of the signs of good that appeared in him, from the light she had seen and from the healing of the leprosy, or that they might take him as a son, for he was fit for that.

﴿While they did not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), meaning: they did not perceive that he was the one whose rule would be ruined at his hands. This was said by Qatada. Or that he was an enemy to them, as said by Mujahid. Or that I do what I will, not what they will, as said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq. The apparent meaning is that this is part of the speech of God, the Exalted. It has also been said that it is part of the speech of the wife of Pharaoh, meaning that she said this to Pharaoh, and that those who had recommended killing him did not perceive her speech to him or her appeal to his heart concerning him, lest they incite him to kill him.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The estimate of the speech is: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾, and ﴿the wife of Pharaoh said﴾ thus, and ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that they were in a great error in picking him up, hoping for benefit from him, and adopting him. His saying: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh﴾ and the verse that follows is a parenthetical clause placed between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, confirming the meaning of their error. End of quotation. Whenever it is possible to take the speech in its apparent meaning without a break, that is better.

**[Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit, on Surah 28, verses 10–14]**

﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became empty. She was about to disclose him, had We not bound her heart so that she would be among the believers.﴾ ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him up," so she watched him from a distance while they were unaware.﴾ ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses from before, so she said, "Shall I direct you to a household who will raise him for you, and who will be sincere toward him?"﴾ ﴿So We returned him to his mother that her eye might be comforted, and she would not grieve, and she would know that the promise of God is true, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿And when he reached his full strength and became mature, We gave him judgment and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good-doers.﴾

﴿وأصْبَحَ﴾ means it became (صار) empty of reason. This happened when she learned that he had fallen into the hands of Pharaoh. An event of this magnitude overwhelmed her, and reason cannot remain intact under it, especially the reason of a woman who feared for her son so much that she cast him into the river, hoping he would be saved from slaughter. This was despite the revelation to her that God would return him to her and make him a messenger. Nevertheless, her mind was disturbed and she was overcome by what overcomes humans when confronted with a great calamity. Afterwards she grew calm and submitted to God's promise.

Ahmad ibn Musa, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﻓﻮﺍﺩ (fu'ad) with a waw. Ibn 'Abbas said: empty of everything except the remembrance of Moses. Malik said: it means the loss of reason. A group said: empty of patience. Ibn Zayd said: empty of God's promise and His revelation to her, (p. 107) having forgotten it because of distress. Abu 'Ubayda said: empty of grief, since he did not drown. This view is weak, and the irregular readings (al-qira'at al-shadhdha, readings not transmitted through the standard channels) of the word weaken it.

Fadala ibn 'Ubayd, al-Hasan, Yazid ibn Qutayb, and Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir read ﻓﺰﻋﺎ (fazi'an), with zay and the unpointed ʿayn, from fazaʿ, meaning fear and anxiety. Ibn 'Abbas read ﻗﺮﻋﺎ (qari'an), with qaf and a kasra or sukun on the ra, from qara'a ra'suhu, meaning his hair receded, as if she had been emptied of everything except the remembrance of Moses. It is also said: ﻗﺮﻋﺎ (qar'an), with sukun, as a verbal noun, meaning she is struck with a blow from al-qari'a, which is a great distress. Some Companions read ﻓِﺰﻏﺎ (fizgha), with a kasra on the fa, sukun on the zay, and the dotted ghayn, meaning going to waste, lost, destroyed by distress and grief. From this is the verse of Tulayha al-Asadi about his brother Hibal:

*If their souls have been struck among the slain, yet you shall not go in vain (fizgha) for the killing of Hibal.*

That is: for the killing of Hibal, in vain, meaning unavenged and without retribution. Khalil ibn Ahmad read ﻓُﺮُﻏﺎ (furuga), with a damma on the fa and the ra.

﴿إنْ كادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾: the ﺇﻥ here is the lightened form of the heavy particle (ان المخففة من الثقيلة), and the lam is the distinguishing lam (اللام الفارقة). It is also said that ﺇﻥ is a negative particle and the lam means "except" (إلا). This is a Kufan view. The verb ﺍﻹﺑﺪﺍﺀ (ibda', disclosing) means making a thing manifest. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﺑِﻪ refers to Moses, peace be upon him. It is said that the ba' is superfluous, meaning "she would reveal him." It is also said the object of ﺗُﺒْﺪِﻱ is omitted, meaning she would reveal the matter concerning him, that he was her son. It is also said that the pronoun in ﺑِﻪ refers to the revelation, meaning she would disclose the revelation. Ibn 'Abbas said: she nearly cried out "Woe, my son!" when she cast him into the sea. It is also said: when she saw the waves striking him. ﴿لَوْلا أنْ رَبَطْنا عَلى قَلْبِها﴾: Qatada said: with faith. Al-Suddi said: with protection (al-'isma). Al-Sadiq said: with certainty. Ibn 'Ata said: with revelation. ﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: We did this, meaning, that she might be among those who affirm God's promise and that it will certainly come to pass. Binding upon the heart is a metaphor for its steadiness and tranquility, likened to something tied for fear that it might slip loose.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible to read: "And her heart became empty of distress when she heard that Pharaoh had shown affection for him and adopted him."

﴿إنْ كادَتْ لَتُبْدِي﴾ [that she was about to reveal] that he was her son, because she could not control herself out of joy and delight at what she had heard. Had We not reassured her heart and calmed the agitation that arose in it from the intensity of joy and elation.

﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [among the believers]: those who trust in God's promise, not in Pharaoh's adoption and affection. End of quotation. What al-Zamakhshari said, permitting that she was empty of distress and so on, contradicts what the exegetes understood from the verse. The answer to ﻟﻮﻻ (lawla) is omitted, its estimate being: "she would have nearly disclosed him," and what indicates it is His saying ﴿إنْ كادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾. This is comparable to His saying: ﴿And she desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ [Yusuf 12:24].

﴿وقالَتْ لِأُخْتِهِ﴾ [And she said to his sister]: hoping to learn about his condition.

﴿قُصِّيهِ﴾ [Follow him up]: follow his trace and pursue his news. It is related that she went out in the streets of the city in secret, and saw him with people from the entourage of Pharaoh's wife, who were looking for a woman to nurse him, since he would not accept the wet-nurses. The name of his sister is Maryam; it is said Kalthama, and it is said Kulthum. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: she followed his trace.

﴿فَبَصُرَتْ بِهِ﴾: she saw him. ﴿عَنْ جُنُبٍ﴾: from a distance. ﴿وهم لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾: they were unaware of her searching for him or of her watching. It is also said that the meaning of ﴿عَنْ جُنُبٍ﴾ is "from longing for him." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala related this and said: it is the dialect of Judham, who say: "I longed (janabtu) toward you," meaning "I yearned." Al-Kirmani said: "junubin" is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "from a remote place (makan junubin)," meaning "far away." It is also said: "from the side," because she was walking along the bank, and they did not perceive that she was tracking him. It is also said: they did not perceive that she was his sister. It is also said: they did not perceive that he was their enemy; this was said by Mujahid.

The majority read ﻋَﻦْ ﺟُﻨُﺐٍ (ʿan junub) with two dammas. Qatada read ﻓَﺒَﺼَﺮَﺕْ (fabasarat) with a fatha on the ṣad. 'Isa read it with a kasra. Qatada, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﺟَﻨْﺐٍ (janb), with a fatha on the jim and sukun on the nun. From Qatada: with fatha on both. From al-Hasan: with damma on the jim and sukun on the nun. Al-Nu'man ibn Salim read ﻋَﻦْ ﺟَﺎﻧِﺐٍ (ʿan janib). Al-janb, al-janib, al-janaba, and al-janab have one meaning. Qatada said: the meaning of "from junub" is that she looked at him as if she did not want him.

Prohibition here means restraint: We prevented him from suckling the breast of any woman. The word ﺍﻟﻤﺮﺍﺿﻊ (al-maradi') is the plural of mursi'a, the woman who nurses, or the plural of marda', the place of nursing, meaning the breast, or the act of nursing.

﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ [from before]: from the beginning of his affair. It is also said: before her following his trace and her coming upon those who had him.

﴿فَقالَتْ هَلْ أدُلُّكُمْ﴾ [So she said, "Shall I direct you?"]: I guide you to ﴿أهْلِ بَيْتٍ يَكْفُلُونَهُ لَكم وهم لَهُ ناصِحُونَ﴾ [a household who will raise him for you, and who will be sincere toward him], because they have compassion and mercy for the one they raise and good upbringing. His saying ﴿وحَرَّمْنا عَلَيْهِ المَراضِعَ﴾ [We had forbidden him the wet-nurses] indicates that a number of nursing women were presented to him. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﻟَﻪُ (lahu) refers to Moses. It is said it may refer to the king, whom the child was, in outward appearance, among. Ibn Jurayj said: the people interpreted the pronoun as referring to the child, so they said to her: "You know him, so tell us who he is." She said: I only intended that they are sincere toward the king. Thus she escaped from them with this interpretation. There is an ellipsis in the speech, estimated as: she passed by them to his mother, and they spoke to her about nursing him; or she brought his mother to them, and they spoke to her about his matter, and she nursed him, and he took her breast. It is related that Pharaoh said to her: "What is the reason that this child accepts your breast, when he has refused every breast?" She said: "I am a woman of good scent and good milk; no child is brought to me without accepting me." So he gave him to her, and she took him to her house, and he gave her a dinar every day. It was permissible for her to take it, because it was the property of a combatant (harbi), and so it is lawful; and that was not a wage for nursing.

﴿فَرَدَدْناهُ إلى أُمِّهِ﴾ [So We returned him to his mother], as He said, ﴿We will return him to you﴾ [al-Qasas 28:7]. The tears of joy are cool, while the eye of the grieving is hot and scalding. Abu Tammam said:

*As for the eyes of lovers, they are heated; as for the eyes of the gloaters, they are cooled.*

When He, exalted is He, fulfilled His promise in the return, it became established for her that he would be a prophet and messenger.

﴿ولِتَعْلَمَ أنَّ وعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقٌّ﴾ [and she would know that the promise of God is true]: We did this. ﴿ولا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [but they do not know], meaning that God's promise is true, so they were doubtful about it; or they did not know that the return was only because of her knowledge of the truthfulness of God's promise. "But most people do not know" that the return was for this reason. In His saying ﴿ولِتَعْلَمَ أنَّ وعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقٌّ﴾ there is evidence against those who held that the inspiration to her was inspiration (ilham) or a dream, because it would be unlikely to call that a promise. His saying "and she would know" refers to the occurrence of that, so it is knowledge by witnessing, since she already knew that it would happen. "Most of them" are the Copts, and they do not know the secret of the divine decree. Al-Dahhak said: they do not know their own interests and the goodness of their outcomes. Al-Dahhak also said, as did Muqatil: they do not know that God had promised to return him to her.

The exegesis of ﴿ولَمّا بَلَغَ أشُدَّهُ﴾ [And when he reached his full strength] through ﴿المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ [the good-doers] has already been given in Surah Yusuf, peace be upon him.

Ahmad ibn Musa, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read ﻓﻮﺍﺩ (fu'ad) with a waw. Ibn 'Abbas said: empty of everything except the remembrance of Moses. Malik said: it means the loss of reason. A group said: empty of patience. Ibn Zayd said: empty of God's promise and His revelation to her, (p. 107) having forgotten it because of distress. Abu 'Ubayda said: empty of grief, since he did not drown. This view is weak, and the irregular readings (al-qira'at al-shadhdha, readings not transmitted through the standard channels) of the word weaken it.

Fadala ibn 'Ubayd, al-Hasan, Yazid ibn Qutayb, and Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir read ﻓﺰﻋﺎ (fazi'an), with zay and the unpointed ʿayn, from fazaʿ, meaning fear and anxiety. Ibn 'Abbas read ﻗﺮﻋﺎ (qari'an), with qaf and a kasra or sukun on the ra, from qara'a ra'suhu, meaning his hair receded, as if she had been emptied of everything except the remembrance of Moses. It is also said: ﻗﺮﻋﺎ (qar'an), with sukun, as a verbal noun, meaning she is struck with a blow from al-qari'a, which is a great distress. Some Companions read ﻓِﺰﻏﺎ (fizgha), with a kasra on the fa, sukun on the zay, and the dotted ghayn, meaning going to waste, lost, destroyed by distress and grief. From this is the verse of Tulayha al-Asadi about his brother Hibal:

*If their souls have been struck among the slain, yet you shall not go in vain (fizgha) for the killing of Hibal.*

That is: for the killing of Hibal, in vain, meaning unavenged and without retribution. Khalil ibn Ahmad read ﻓُﺮُﻏﺎ (furuga), with a damma on the fa and the ra.

﴿إنْ كادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾: the ﺇﻥ here is the lightened form of the heavy particle (ان المخففة من الثقيلة), and the lam is the distinguishing lam (اللام الفارقة). It is also said that ﺇﻥ is a negative particle and the lam means "except" (إلا). This is a Kufan view. The verb ﺍﻹﺑﺪﺍﺀ (ibda', disclosing) means making a thing manifest. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﺑِﻪ refers to Moses, peace be upon him. It is said that the ba' is superfluous, meaning "she would reveal him." It is also said the object of ﺗُﺒْﺪِﻱ is omitted, meaning she would reveal the matter concerning him, that he was her son. It is also said that the pronoun in ﺑِﻪ refers to the revelation, meaning she would disclose the revelation. Ibn 'Abbas said: she nearly cried out "Woe, my son!" when she cast him into the sea. It is also said: when she saw the waves striking him. ﴿لَوْلا أنْ رَبَطْنا عَلى قَلْبِها﴾: Qatada said: with faith. Al-Suddi said: with protection (al-'isma). Al-Sadiq said: with certainty. Ibn 'Ata said: with revelation. ﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: We did this, meaning, that she might be among those who affirm God's promise and that it will certainly come to pass. Binding upon the heart is a metaphor for its steadiness and tranquility, likened to something tied for fear that it might slip loose.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible to read: "And her heart became empty of distress when she heard that Pharaoh had shown affection for him and adopted him."

﴿إنْ كادَتْ لَتُبْدِي﴾ [that she was about to reveal] that he was her son, because she could not control herself out of joy and delight at what she had heard. Had We not reassured her heart and calmed the agitation that arose in it from the intensity of joy and elation.

﴿لِتَكُونَ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [among the believers]: those who trust in God's promise, not in Pharaoh's adoption and affection. End of quotation. What al-Zamakhshari said, permitting that she was empty of distress and so on, contradicts what the exegetes understood from the verse. The answer to ﻟﻮﻻ (lawla) is omitted, its estimate being: "she would have nearly disclosed him," and what indicates it is His saying ﴿إنْ كادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾. This is comparable to His saying: ﴿And she desired him, and he would have desired her had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾ [Yusuf 12:24].

﴿وقالَتْ لِأُخْتِهِ﴾ [And she said to his sister]: hoping to learn about his condition.

﴿قُصِّيهِ﴾ [Follow him up]: follow his trace and pursue his news. It is related that she went out in the streets of the city in secret, and saw him with people from the entourage of Pharaoh's wife, who were looking for a woman to nurse him, since he would not accept the wet-nurses. The name of his sister is Maryam; it is said Kalthama, and it is said Kulthum. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: she followed his trace.

﴿فَبَصُرَتْ بِهِ﴾: she saw him. ﴿عَنْ جُنُبٍ﴾: from a distance. ﴿وهم لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾: they were unaware of her searching for him or of her watching. It is also said that the meaning of ﴿عَنْ جُنُبٍ﴾ is "from longing for him." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala related this and said: it is the dialect of Judham, who say: "I longed (janabtu) toward you," meaning "I yearned." Al-Kirmani said: "junubin" is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "from a remote place (makan junubin)," meaning "far away." It is also said: "from the side," because she was walking along the bank, and they did not perceive that she was tracking him. It is also said: they did not perceive that she was his sister. It is also said: they did not perceive that he was their enemy; this was said by Mujahid.

The majority read ﻋَﻦْ ﺟُﻨُﺐٍ (ʿan junub) with two dammas. Qatada read ﻓَﺒَﺼَﺮَﺕْ (fabasarat) with a fatha on the ṣad. 'Isa read it with a kasra. Qatada, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read ﺟَﻨْﺐٍ (janb), with a fatha on the jim and sukun on the nun. From Qatada: with fatha on both. From al-Hasan: with damma on the jim and sukun on the nun. Al-Nu'man ibn Salim read ﻋَﻦْ ﺟَﺎﻧِﺐٍ (ʿan janib). Al-janb, al-janib, al-janaba, and al-janab have one meaning. Qatada said: the meaning of "from junub" is that she looked at him as if she did not want him.

Prohibition here means restraint: We prevented him from suckling the breast of any woman. The word ﺍﻟﻤﺮﺍﺿﻊ (al-maradi') is the plural of mursi'a, the woman who nurses, or the plural of marda', the place of nursing, meaning the breast, or the act of nursing.

﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ [from before]: from the beginning of his affair. It is also said: before her following his trace and her coming upon those who had him.

﴿فَقالَتْ هَلْ أدُلُّكُمْ﴾ [So she said, "Shall I direct you?"]: I guide you to ﴿أهْلِ بَيْتٍ يَكْفُلُونَهُ لَكم وهم لَهُ ناصِحُونَ﴾ [a household who will raise him for you, and who will be sincere toward him], because they have compassion and mercy for the one they raise and good upbringing. His saying ﴿وحَرَّمْنا عَلَيْهِ المَراضِعَ﴾ [We had forbidden him the wet-nurses] indicates that a number of nursing women were presented to him. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﻟَﻪُ (lahu) refers to Moses. It is said it may refer to the king, whom the child was, in outward appearance, among. Ibn Jurayj said: the people interpreted the pronoun as referring to the child, so they said to her: "You know him, so tell us who he is." She said: I only intended that they are sincere toward the king. Thus she escaped from them with this interpretation. There is an ellipsis in the speech, estimated as: she passed by them to his mother, and they spoke to her about nursing him; or she brought his mother to them, and they spoke to her about his matter, and she nursed him, and he took her breast. It is related that Pharaoh said to her: "What is the reason that this child accepts your breast, when he has refused every breast?" She said: "I am a woman of good scent and good milk; no child is brought to me without accepting me." So he gave him to her, and she took him to her house, and he gave her a dinar every day. It was permissible for her to take it, because it was the property of a combatant (harbi), and so it is lawful; and that was not a wage for nursing.

﴿فَرَدَدْناهُ إلى أُمِّهِ﴾ [So We returned him to his mother], as He said, ﴿We will return him to you﴾ [al-Qasas 28:7]. The tears of joy are cool, while the eye of the grieving is hot and scalding. Abu Tammam said:

*As for the eyes of lovers, they are heated; as for the eyes of the gloaters, they are cooled.*

When He, exalted is He, fulfilled His promise in the return, it became established for her that he would be a prophet and messenger.

﴿ولِتَعْلَمَ أنَّ وعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقٌّ﴾ [and she would know that the promise of God is true]: We did this. ﴿ولا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [but they do not know], meaning that God's promise is true, so they were doubtful about it; or they did not know that the return was only because of her knowledge of the truthfulness of God's promise. "But most people do not know" that the return was for this reason. In His saying ﴿ولِتَعْلَمَ أنَّ وعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقٌّ﴾ there is evidence against those who held that the inspiration to her was inspiration (ilham) or a dream, because it would be unlikely to call that a promise. His saying "and she would know" refers to the occurrence of that, so it is knowledge by witnessing, since she already knew that it would happen. "Most of them" are the Copts, and they do not know the secret of the divine decree. Al-Dahhak said: they do not know their own interests and the goodness of their outcomes. Al-Dahhak also said, as did Muqatil: they do not know that God had promised to return him to her.

The exegesis of ﴿ولَمّا بَلَغَ أشُدَّهُ﴾ [And when he reached his full strength] through ﴿المُحْسِنِينَ﴾ [the good-doers] has already been given in Surah Yusuf, peace be upon him.

[p. 109] (the city): Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is Memphis (Manf). Pharaoh once rode out and headed toward it. Moses (peace be upon him) learned of his ride, so he entered that city at the time of the midday rest (al-qāʾilah). It is also reported from him that it was between the evening (al-ʿishāʾ) and the late night (al-ʿatamah). Ibn Ishaq said: the city is Egypt itself. Moses had openly shown opposition to Pharaoh and his people in ways they disliked, so he went into hiding and feared them. He entered the city disguised, cautious, and taking people unawares. Ibn Zayd said: Pharaoh had expelled him from the city, so he stayed away for years, and [Pharaoh] forgot him. He came while the people were heedless, because they had forgotten him and a long time had passed since they knew him. It was said: it was a feast day and they were busy with their amusements. It was said: he left Pharaoh's palace and entered Egypt. It was said: the city is ʿAyn Shams. It was said: it is a village two farsakhs from Egypt called Ḥābīn. It was said: it is Alexandria.

Abu Ṭalib al-Qari recited ﴿ʿalā ḥīna﴾ with a fatḥah on the nūn of ḥīna (ḥīn). The reasoning (wajh) for this is that he treated the verbal noun as if it were a verb, as though he had said "when its people had become heedless," and so he made it indeclinable, as it is made indeclinable when it is annexed to a clause that begins with a past-tense verb, as in the poet's words:

"At the time when I reproached grey hair for my youth"

This is an anomalous (shādh) reading.

Nuʿaym ibn Maysarah recited ﴿yaqattilān﴾ by assimilating the first tāʾ into the second and transferring its fatḥah to the qāf. It was said: they were fighting over religion, since one of them was an Israelite believer and the other a Copt. It was also said: they were fighting because the Copt had been assigned to carry firewood to Pharaoh's kitchen on the back of the Israelite. In this view, ﴿yaqtatilān﴾ is a descriptive clause (ṣifah) qualifying ﴿rajulayn﴾ (two men). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: ﴿yaqtatilān﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The end of his words. A ḥāl from an indefinite noun was permitted by Sibawayh without condition.

﴿This one is of his party﴾: that is, of those who supported him in his religion, namely the Israelite. It was said: he was Sāmirī. ﴿And this one is of his enemy﴾: that is, of the Copts. It was said: his name was Fātūn. The phrase is a narration of a present state (ḥikāyat ḥāl), since both were present at the time Moses found them. Or, for the narration of the state, the past absent one is referred to with the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah), which is designated for what is present. Al-Mubarrad said: the Arabs use this demonstrative to refer to the absent. Jarir said:

"This is my paternal cousin in Damascus, a caliph; if I wished, he would drive your herds to me."

The majority recited ﴿fa-istaghāthahu﴾, meaning he asked him for help and support against the Copt. Sibawayh, Ibn Miqsam, and al-Zaʿfarani recited it with ʿayn (ʿ) and nūn in place of the thāʾ, meaning he asked him for assistance against the Copt. Abu al-Qasim Yusuf ibn ʿAli ibn Jubarah said: the preferred reading is that of Ibn Miqsam, because assistance (al-iʿānah) is more fitting in this matter. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: al-Akhfash mentioned it, and it is a scribal error (taṣḥīf), not a recognized reading. The end of his words. But it is not a scribal error, since Ibn Khalawayh transmitted it from Sibawayh, and Ibn Jubarah transmitted it from Ibn Miqsam and al-Zaʿfarani.

It is narrated that when the dispute between them grew intense, the Copt said to Moses: "I was about to load him onto you," meaning the firewood. Moses's anger intensified, for he had been given strength. ﴿So he struck him﴾ and he died. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) recited ﴿falakazahu﴾ with a lām, and it is also reported from him as ﴿fa-nakazahu﴾ with a nūn. Qatadah said: he struck him with his staff. Others said: with the closed fist. The apparent meaning is that the subject of ﴿fa-qaḍā﴾ (and he decreed) is a pronoun referring to Moses. It was also said that it refers to God, meaning God decreed death upon him. It may also refer to the verbal noun implied by ﴿wakazahu﴾ (he struck him), meaning the blow decreed upon him. Moses had not intended to kill him, but his blow coincided with the appointed term, so Moses regretted it. It is narrated that he buried him in the sand and said: ﴿This is of the work of Satan﴾, meaning the anger that befell him, which led to the blow that decreed the Copt's death. He attributed it to the work of Satan and called it wrongdoing against himself, and he sought forgiveness for it, because it led to the killing of a person whom he had not been authorized to kill. It is reported from Ibn Jurayj: it is not for a prophet to kill what he has not been commanded to kill. Kaʿb said: Moses was then twelve years old, and the killing was accidental, since a blow usually does not kill. Al-Naqqash said: this occurred before prophethood, and Moses (peace be upon him) followed the path of Adam (peace be upon him) when he said: ﴿We have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:23].

The bāʾ in ﴿bi-mā anʿamta﴾ is for an oath, and the sense is: "I swear by what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness," and the answer is omitted, meaning "I will surely repent," ﴿so I will never be﴾. Or it is connected to an omitted element whose sense is: "Protect me by the right of what You have bestowed upon me of [p. 110] forgiveness," ﴿so I will never be﴾ if You protect me, ﴿a supporter of the criminals﴾. It was also said: ﴿so I will never be﴾ is a supplication, not a statement, and that lan here means lā in supplication. The correct view is that lan does not occur in supplication. It has been argued that lan can occur in supplication from this verse and from the poet's words:

"You will not cease thus, and you will remain for them everlasting like the eternity of the mountains."

Being a supporter may be either by keeping company with Pharaoh and being counted among his circle and increasing his numbers, since he used to ride with him like a child with a parent, and he was called "Pharaoh's son." Or the support led to the killing that happened at his hand. It was also said: by what You have bestowed upon me of prophethood, so I will use it only to support Your allies, and I will not allow a Copt to overcome an Israelite. The scholars cited this verse as evidence for prohibiting assisting the people of injustice and serving them; ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah and others stated this explicitly. A man said to ʿAṭāʾ: "My brother strikes with his knowledge, and it does not exceed his livelihood." He said: "Then who is the head?" meaning who writes for him. He said: "Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Qasri." He said: "Then where is the statement of Moses?" And he recited the verse.

﴿So he became in the city, fearful﴾ of being seized for the killing of the Copt, ﴿watching for [what might happen]﴾, anticipating the occurrence of something hateful to him, or news about whether they had discovered what he had done. It was said: fearful, watching for forgiveness. It was said: fearful, watching for the help of his Lord, or watching for the guidance of his people, or waiting for his people to hand him over.

﴿Then suddenly the one who had sought his help the day before﴾: that is, the Israelite on whose behalf he had killed the Copt. The ﴿idhā﴾ here is for sudden occurrence (lil-mufājaʾah). ﴿Yesterday﴾ means the day before the day of the call for help. It is declinable (muʿrab), so the vowel on its sīn is an inflectional vowel (ḥarakat iʿrāb), because the definite article ʾal has entered it. This differs from its state when it is stripped of ʾal: the Ḥijāzīs build it when it is definite, while the Tamīm prevent it from taking nunation only in the nominative case, and some prevent it from nunation absolutely. It may also be built with ʾal occasionally, by rarity. The poet said:

"I thought today and yesterday before it until the night, until the sun almost set."

﴿He cried out to him﴾: he shouted to him seeking help against another Copt. The poet said:

"Whenever a frightened crier came to us, his shout was the striking of tent-ropes."

Moses said to him: the apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿lahu﴾ refers to the one ﴿you are clearly a misguided one﴾, because he was the cause of the Copt's killing the day before. He said this to him in the manner of rebuke and reproach. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿lahu﴾ and the address are to the Copt, indicated by ﴿yastaṣrikhuhu﴾, and the Israelite did not realize that the address was to the Copt.

﴿So when he intended to strike﴾: the apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿arāda﴾ and ﴿yabṭisha﴾ refers to Moses.

﴿The one who was an enemy to both of them﴾: that is, to the one seeking help and to Moses. The Copt gave the Israelite the impression that his words ﴿you are clearly a misguided one﴾ were meant to harm him, and he thought Moses would attack him. The Israelite said: ﴿O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?﴾, to repel what he thought was Moses's attack against him. The identity of the Copt killer had been hidden from the people, so it spread through the city that the killer of the Copt was Moses. This news reached Pharaoh, and he ordered Moses to be killed. It was also said: the pronouns in ﴿arāda﴾ and ﴿yabṭisha﴾ refer at that moment to the Israelite, who wanted to attack Moses and addressed him with what was ugly. It was also said that after ﴿lammā﴾ its extra use (ziyādah) is regular. It was also said that ﴿law﴾ (if) is used when preceded by an oath, as in the poet's words:

"So I swear that if we met, and you, there would be for you a dark day of evil."

The majority recited ﴿yabṭisha﴾ with a kasrah on the ṭāʾ. Al-Ḥasan and Abu Jaʿfar recited it with a ḍammah.

﴿You intend only to be a tyrant in the land﴾. The characteristic of a tyrant (jabbār) is to kill without right. Al-Shaʿbi said: whoever kills two men is a tyrant, meaning without right. When he attributed tyranny (al-jabarūtiyyah) to him, he denied him righteousness.

﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city﴾. It was said: he was the believer from Pharaoh's household, and he was a cousin of Pharaoh. Al-Kalbi said: his name was Jibril ibn Shamʿun. Al-Ḍaḥḥak said: Shamʿun ibn Isḥaq. It was also said: he was not the believer from Pharaoh's household.

﴿Running﴾: hurrying in his walk. When Pharaoh ordered his killing, the police (al-jalawiz) went out along the main road to seek him, so this man took a shorter path to Moses. The phrases ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾ and ﴿running﴾ are two descriptions, and ﴿running﴾ may be a circumstantial clause. The phrase ﴿from the farthest part﴾ may be connected to ﴿came﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: if you make ﴿from the farthest part﴾ a circumstantial clause for ﴿came﴾, then ﴿running﴾ can only be a description. The end of his words. That is, a rajul (man) is indefinite and is not described, so a circumstantial clause cannot come from it. Sibawayh permitted that in his book without a description. He said: ﴿Indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you﴾, and the chiefs are the notables of Pharaoh's government, ﴿to kill you﴾. ﴿They are conspiring﴾: they are consulting. The poet al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"I see that people have invented a custom, and in every event one is consulted."

Ibn Qutaybah said: one tells another by his words, from the Exalted's saying: ﴿and confer among yourselves in kindness﴾ [al-Ṭalāq 65:6].

﴿So leave; indeed I am to you among the advisors﴾. ﴿Lakā﴾ (to you) is connected either to an omitted element, meaning "a sincere advisor to you among the advisors," or to an omitted element by way of explanation, meaning "to you I mean," or to ﴿al-nāṣiḥīn﴾ (the advisors), though it is within the relative clause of ʾal, because adverbials and prepositional phrases are treated more leniently than other elements. These are three views among the grammarians on such constructions. Moses complied with what that man ordered him, knowing his truthfulness and sincerity, and he left, while his pursuers had missed him and could not find him. Moses did not know that road and had not accompanied anyone, so he went into an unknown route, trusting in God the Exalted, calling upon and turning eagerly to his Lord to save him from the wrongdoers.

[p. 109] (the city): Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is Memphis (Manf). Pharaoh once rode out and headed toward it. Moses (peace be upon him) learned of his ride, so he entered that city at the time of the midday rest (al-qāʾilah). It is also reported from him that it was between the evening (al-ʿishāʾ) and the late night (al-ʿatamah). Ibn Ishaq said: the city is Egypt itself. Moses had openly shown opposition to Pharaoh and his people in ways they disliked, so he went into hiding and feared them. He entered the city disguised, cautious, and taking people unawares. Ibn Zayd said: Pharaoh had expelled him from the city, so he stayed away for years, and [Pharaoh] forgot him. He came while the people were heedless, because they had forgotten him and a long time had passed since they knew him. It was said: it was a feast day and they were busy with their amusements. It was said: he left Pharaoh's palace and entered Egypt. It was said: the city is ʿAyn Shams. It was said: it is a village two farsakhs from Egypt called Ḥābīn. It was said: it is Alexandria.

Abu Ṭalib al-Qari recited ﴿ʿalā ḥīna﴾ with a fatḥah on the nūn of ḥīna (ḥīn). The reasoning (wajh) for this is that he treated the verbal noun as if it were a verb, as though he had said "when its people had become heedless," and so he made it indeclinable, as it is made indeclinable when it is annexed to a clause that begins with a past-tense verb, as in the poet's words:

"At the time when I reproached grey hair for my youth"

This is an anomalous (shādh) reading.

Nuʿaym ibn Maysarah recited ﴿yaqattilān﴾ by assimilating the first tāʾ into the second and transferring its fatḥah to the qāf. It was said: they were fighting over religion, since one of them was an Israelite believer and the other a Copt. It was also said: they were fighting because the Copt had been assigned to carry firewood to Pharaoh's kitchen on the back of the Israelite. In this view, ﴿yaqtatilān﴾ is a descriptive clause (ṣifah) qualifying ﴿rajulayn﴾ (two men). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: ﴿yaqtatilān﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The end of his words. A ḥāl from an indefinite noun was permitted by Sibawayh without condition.

﴿This one is of his party﴾: that is, of those who supported him in his religion, namely the Israelite. It was said: he was Sāmirī. ﴿And this one is of his enemy﴾: that is, of the Copts. It was said: his name was Fātūn. The phrase is a narration of a present state (ḥikāyat ḥāl), since both were present at the time Moses found them. Or, for the narration of the state, the past absent one is referred to with the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah), which is designated for what is present. Al-Mubarrad said: the Arabs use this demonstrative to refer to the absent. Jarir said:

"This is my paternal cousin in Damascus, a caliph; if I wished, he would drive your herds to me."

The majority recited ﴿fa-istaghāthahu﴾, meaning he asked him for help and support against the Copt. The scholars cited this verse as evidence for prohibiting assisting the people of injustice and serving them; ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah and others stated this explicitly. A man said to ʿAṭāʾ: "My brother strikes with his knowledge, and it does not exceed his livelihood." He said: "Then who is the head?" meaning who writes for him. He said: "Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Qasri." He said: "Then where is the statement of Moses?" And he recited the verse.

﴿So he became in the city, fearful﴾ of being seized for the killing of the Copt, ﴿watching for [what might happen]﴾, anticipating the occurrence of something hateful to him, or news about whether they had discovered what he had done. It was said: fearful, watching for forgiveness. It was said: fearful, watching for the help of his Lord, or watching for the guidance of his people, or waiting for his people to hand him over.

﴿Then suddenly the one who had sought his help the day before﴾: that is, the Israelite on whose behalf he had killed the Copt. The ﴿idhā﴾ here is for sudden occurrence (lil-mufājaʾah). ﴿Yesterday﴾ means the day before the day of the call for help. It is declinable (muʿrab), so the vowel on its sīn is an inflectional vowel (ḥarakat iʿrāb), because the definite article ʾal has entered it. This differs from its state when it is stripped of ʾal: the Ḥijāzīs build it when it is definite, while the Tamīm prevent it from taking nunation only in the nominative case, and some prevent it from nunation absolutely. It may also be built with ʾal occasionally, by rarity. The poet said:

"I thought today and yesterday before it until the night, until the sun almost set."

﴿He cried out to him﴾: he shouted to him seeking help against another Copt. The poet said:

"Whenever a frightened crier came to us, his shout was the striking of tent-ropes."

Moses said to him: the apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿lahu﴾ refers to the one ﴿you are clearly a misguided one﴾, because he was the cause of the Copt's killing the day before. He said this to him in the manner of rebuke and reproach. It was also said: the pronoun in ﴿lahu﴾ and the address are to the Copt, indicated by ﴿yastaṣrikhuhu﴾, and the Israelite did not realize that the address was to the Copt.

﴿So when he intended to strike﴾: the apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿arāda﴾ and ﴿yabṭisha﴾ refers to Moses.

﴿The one who was an enemy to both of them﴾: that is, to the one seeking help and to Moses. The Copt gave the Israelite the impression that his words ﴿you are clearly a misguided one﴾ were meant to harm him, and he thought Moses would attack him. The Israelite said: ﴿O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?﴾, to repel what he thought was Moses's attack against him. The identity of the Copt killer had been hidden from the people, so it spread through the city that the killer of the Copt was Moses. This news reached Pharaoh, and he ordered Moses to be killed. It was also said: the pronouns in ﴿arāda﴾ and ﴿yabṭisha﴾ refer at that moment to the Israelite, who wanted to attack Moses and addressed him with what was ugly. It was also said that after ﴿lammā﴾ its extra use (ziyādah) is regular. It was also said that ﴿law﴾ (if) is used when preceded by an oath, as in the poet's words:

"So I swear that if we met, and you, there would be for you a dark day of evil."

The majority recited ﴿yabṭisha﴾ with a kasrah on the ṭāʾ. Al-Ḥasan and Abu Jaʿfar recited it with a ḍammah.

﴿You intend only to be a tyrant in the land﴾. The characteristic of a tyrant (jabbār) is to kill without right. Al-Shaʿbi said: whoever kills two men is a tyrant, meaning without right. When he attributed tyranny (al-jabarūtiyyah) to him, he denied him righteousness.

﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city﴾. It was said: he was the believer from Pharaoh's household, and he was a cousin of Pharaoh. Al-Kalbi said: his name was Jibril ibn Shamʿun. Al-Ḍaḥḥak said: Shamʿun ibn Isḥaq. It was also said: he was not the believer from Pharaoh's household.

﴿Running﴾: hurrying in his walk. When Pharaoh ordered his killing, the police (al-jalawiz) went out along the main road to seek him, so this man took a shorter path to Moses. The phrases ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾ and ﴿running﴾ are two descriptions, and ﴿running﴾ may be a circumstantial clause. The phrase ﴿from the farthest part﴾ may be connected to ﴿came﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: if you make ﴿from the farthest part﴾ a circumstantial clause for ﴿came﴾, then ﴿running﴾ can only be a description. The end of his words. That is, a rajul (man) is indefinite and is not described, so a circumstantial clause cannot come from it. Sibawayh permitted that in his book without a description. He said: ﴿Indeed the chiefs are conspiring against you﴾, and the chiefs are the notables of Pharaoh's government, ﴿to kill you﴾. ﴿They are conspiring﴾: they are consulting. The poet al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"I see that people have invented a custom, and in every event one is consulted."

Ibn Qutaybah said: one tells another by his words, from the Exalted's saying: ﴿and confer among yourselves in kindness﴾ [al-Ṭalāq 65:6].

﴿So leave; indeed I am to you among the advisors﴾. ﴿Lakā﴾ (to you) is connected either to an omitted element, meaning "a sincere advisor to you among the advisors," or to an omitted element by way of explanation, meaning "to you I mean," or to ﴿al-nāṣiḥīn﴾ (the advisors), though it is within the relative clause of ʾal, because adverbials and prepositional phrases are treated more leniently than other elements. These are three views among the grammarians on such constructions. Moses complied with what that man ordered him, knowing his truthfulness and sincerity, and he left, while his pursuers had missed him and could not find him. Moses did not know that road and had not accompanied anyone, so he went into an unknown route, trusting in God the Exalted, calling upon and turning eagerly to his Lord to save him from the wrongdoers.

[p. 109] (the city): Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is Memphis (Manf). Pharaoh once rode out and headed toward it. Moses (peace be upon him) learned of his ride, so he entered that city at the time of the midday rest (al-qāʾilah). It is also reported from him that it was between the evening (al-ʿishāʾ) and the late night (al-ʿatamah). Ibn Ishaq said: the city is Egypt itself. Moses had openly shown opposition to Pharaoh and his people in ways they disliked, so he went into hiding and feared them. He entered the city disguised, cautious, and taking people unawares. Ibn Zayd said: Pharaoh had expelled him from the city, so he stayed away for years, and [Pharaoh] forgot him. He came while the people were heedless, because they had forgotten him and a long time had passed since they knew him. It was said: it was a feast day and they were busy with their amusements. It was said: he left Pharaoh's palace and entered Egypt. It was said: the city is ʿAyn Shams. It was said: it is a village two farsakhs from Egypt called Ḥābīn. It was said: it is Alexandria.

Abu Ṭalib al-Qari recited ﴿ʿalā ḥīna﴾ with a fatḥah on the nūn of ḥīna (ḥīn). The reasoning (wajh) for this is that he treated the verbal noun as if it were a verb, as though he had said "when its people had become heedless," and so he made it indeclinable, as it is made indeclinable when it is annexed to a clause that begins with a past-tense verb, as in the poet's words:

"At the time when I reproached grey hair for my youth"

This is an anomalous (shādh) reading.

Nuʿaym ibn Maysarah recited ﴿yaqattilān﴾ by assimilating the first tāʾ into the second and transferring its fatḥah to the qāf. It was said: they were fighting over religion, since one of them was an Israelite believer and the other a Copt. It was also said: they were fighting because the Copt had been assigned to carry firewood to Pharaoh's kitchen on the back of the Israelite. In this view, ﴿yaqtatilān﴾ is a descriptive clause (ṣifah) qualifying ﴿rajulayn﴾ (two men). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: ﴿yaqtatilān﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The end of his words. A ḥāl from an indefinite noun was permitted by Sibawayh without condition.

﴿This one is of his party﴾: that is, of those who supported him in his religion, namely the Israelite. It was said: he was Sāmirī. ﴿And this one is of his enemy﴾: that is, of the Copts. It was said: his name was Fātūn. The phrase is a narration of a present state (ḥikāyat ḥāl), since both were present at the time Moses found them. Or, for the narration of the state, the past absent one is referred to with the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah), which is designated for what is present. Al-Mubarrad said: the Arabs use this demonstrative to refer to the absent. Jarir said:

"This is my paternal cousin in Damascus, a caliph; if I wished, he would drive your herds to me."

The majority recited ﴿fa-istaghāthahu﴾, meaning he asked him for help and support against the Copt. Sibawayh, Ibn Miqsam, and al-Zaʿfarani recited it with ʿayn (ʿ) and nūn in place of the thāʾ, meaning he asked him for assistance against the Copt. Abu al-Qasim Yusuf ibn ʿAli ibn Jubarah said: the preferred reading is that of Ibn Miqsam, because assistance (al-iʿānah) is more fitting in this matter. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: al-Akhfash mentioned it, and it is a scribal error (taṣḥīf), not a recognized reading. The end of his words. But it is not a scribal error, since Ibn Khalawayh transmitted it from Sibawayh, and Ibn Jubarah transmitted it from Ibn Miqsam and al-Zaʿfarani.

It is narrated that when the dispute between them grew intense, the Copt said to Moses: "I was about to load him onto you," meaning the firewood. Moses's anger intensified, for he had been given strength. ﴿So he struck him﴾ and he died. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) recited ﴿falakazahu﴾ with a lām, and it is also reported from him as ﴿fa-nakazahu﴾ with a nūn. Qatadah said: he struck him with his staff. Others said: with the closed fist. The apparent meaning is that the subject of ﴿fa-qaḍā﴾ (and he decreed) is a pronoun referring to Moses. It was also said that it refers to God, meaning God decreed death upon him. It may also refer to the verbal noun implied by ﴿wakazahu﴾ (he struck him), meaning the blow decreed upon him. Moses had not intended to kill him, but his blow coincided with the appointed term, so Moses regretted it. It is narrated that he buried him in the sand and said: ﴿This is of the work of Satan﴾, meaning the anger that befell him, which led to the blow that decreed the Copt's death. He attributed it to the work of Satan and called it wrongdoing against himself, and he sought forgiveness for it, because it led to the killing of a person whom he had not been authorized to kill. It is reported from Ibn Jurayj: it is not for a prophet to kill what he has not been commanded to kill. Kaʿb said: Moses was then twelve years old, and the killing was accidental, since a blow usually does not kill. Al-Naqqash said: this occurred before prophethood, and Moses (peace be upon him) followed the path of Adam (peace be upon him) when he said: ﴿We have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:23].

The bāʾ in ﴿bi-mā anʿamta﴾ is for an oath, and the sense is: "I swear by what You have bestowed upon me of forgiveness," and the answer is omitted, meaning "I will surely repent," ﴿so I will never be﴾. Or it is connected to an omitted element whose sense is: "Protect me by the right of what You have bestowed upon me of [p. 110] forgiveness," ﴿so I will never be﴾ if You protect me, ﴿a supporter of the criminals﴾. It was also said: ﴿so I will never be﴾ is a supplication, not a statement, and that lan here means lā in supplication. The correct view is that lan does not occur in supplication. It has been argued that lan can occur in supplication from this verse and from the poet's words:

"You will not cease thus, and you will remain for them everlasting like the eternity of the mountains."

Being a supporter may be either by keeping company with Pharaoh and being counted among his circle and increasing his numbers, since he used to ride with him like a child with a parent, and he was called "Pharaoh's son." Or the support led to the killing that happened at his hand. It was also said: by what You have bestowed upon me of prophethood, so I will use it only to support Your allies, and I will not allow a Copt to overcome an Israelite. The scholars cited this verse as evidence for prohibiting assisting the people of injustice and serving them; ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah and others stated this explicitly. A man said to ʿAṭāʾ: "My brother strikes with his knowledge, and it does not exceed his livelihood." He said: "Then who is the head?" meaning who writes for him. He said: "Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Qasri." He said: "Then where is the statement of Moses?" And he recited the verse.

﴿So he became in the city, fearful﴾ of being seized for the killing of the Copt, ﴿watching for [what might happen]﴾, anticipating the occurrence of something hateful to him, or news about whether they had discovered what he had done. It was said: fearful, watching for forgiveness. It was said: fearful, watching for the help of his Lord, or watching for the guidance of his people, or waiting for his people to hand him over.

﴿Then suddenly the one who had sought his help the day before﴾: that is, the Israelite on whose behalf he had killed the Copt. The ﴿idhā﴾ here is for sudden occurrence (lil-mufājaʾah). ﴿Yesterday﴾ means the day before the day of the call for help.
