(I answer): its meaning is: just as, if I were pressed for an addition beyond the ten, that would be transgression beyond doubt, so likewise if I were pressed for an addition beyond the eight. He intended by this to affirm the option, and that it is firm and settled, and that the two terms are equal, either this or that, without difference between them in fulfilment. As for completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish I will do it, and otherwise I shall not be compelled to it. It has been said: its meaning is: then I shall not be a transgressor, and it is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying: no sin is upon me and no consequence. End. His first answer contains some verbosity.

﴿And God is witness to what we say﴾, that is, to what we have covenanted and pledged. ﴿Trustee (wakil)﴾, that is, witness. Qatada said: guardian (hafiz). Ibn Shajara said: watchful (raqib). The wakil is one to whom a matter is entrusted; when the meaning of witness or the like was implied, it took "'ala" after it.

﴿Then when Musa had fulfilled the term﴾: it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he fulfilled the longer of the two terms, which is the ten. From Mujahid: he fulfilled ten, or ten and then more; but this is weak.

﴿And he journeyed with his family﴾, that is, toward Egypt, his land and the land of his people. There is disagreement about whom he married, the elder or the younger, and likewise about her name. The manner of his journey and his sighting of the fire has been mentioned in Surat Ta-Ha and elsewhere. The majority read "jidhwatin" (جِذْوَةٍ) with a kasra on the jim; al-A'mash, Talha, Abu Haywa, and Hamza read it with a damma; 'Asim, except al-Ju'fi, read it with a fatha.

﴿That perhaps you may warm yourselves﴾, that is, that you may be warmed by it, since it was a cold night, and they had lost the way.

[p. 112]

﴿Tawajjaha﴾ means he turned his face. ﴿Tilqā'a﴾ has already been discussed under Yunus, meaning "toward the direction of his face." The verbal noun is used as an adverb of place. There were three roads, and Musa took the middle one, while those who pursued him took the other two, saying: "The one who is guilty does not take the main roads, and he travels only the side paths." He remained on the road for eight nights [p. 113] barefoot, eating nothing but the leaves of trees. The apparent meaning of his words, ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way﴾, is that he did not know the road, so he asked his Lord to guide him to the most direct road, so that he would not go astray, because if he took a road that did not lead him to his destination, he would be lost. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he set out for Madyan and began walking without knowing the way, and God brought him to Madyan. It was also said that Gabriel guided him to Madyan, and it was said that it was another angel. It was also said that he took a road where he would be safe, and it happened that his journey led to Madyan. The apparent meaning of "the right way" is the middle of the road that he followed to the place where he would be safe. Mujahid said: "the right way" means the road to Madyan. Al-Hasan said: it is the way of guidance, so Musa, peace be upon him, walked until he reached Madyan, and he was not under the obedience of Pharaoh.

﴿When he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾, meaning he reached it. Warid (arrival) means reaching a thing and also means entering it. It was said that this water was a well. Ummah means a large group, and ʿalayhi means at its edge and border.

﴿Drawing water﴾ means their livestock.

﴿And he found beside them﴾, meaning from the direction he came from before he reached the group. They were "beside them" in relation to him, as Ibn ʿAtiyyah said. Al-Zamakhshari said: in a place lower than their place.

﴿Holding back﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: they were holding back their flock from the water, fearing the strong drawers of water. Qatadah said: they were holding back people from their flock. Al-Zajjaj said: it seems they disliked crowding at the water. It was also said: so that their flock would not mix with their sheep. It was also said: they were shielding their faces from the gaze of onlookers to conceal themselves. Al-Farra' said: they were keeping them from scattering. The name of the younger is ʿIbra, and the name of the elder is Sabura.

When Musa, peace be upon him, saw them standing and not moving forward to water, he asked them, saying: ﴿What is your matter?﴾ Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: asking about a matter (khatb) is only when someone is afflicted, oppressed, pitied, or does something unusual. Al-Zamakhshari said: its literal meaning is "What is your matter to be sought?" That is, what do you seek by holding back? The object of the matter is called khatb, just as affairs are called sha'n, as in your saying: "What is your sha'n?" It is said: "I attended to his sha'n," meaning I aimed at his aim. End of quotation. In his question, peace be upon him, there is evidence for the permissibility of speaking with a non-related woman about what is needed. Their father had no hired worker, so they were driving the flock to the water, and they did not have the strength to draw water. The shepherds used to draw water from the well and water their livestock, and when they left, if some water remained in the trough, the two women watered their flock. Musa, peace be upon him, came on that day while they were holding their flock back from the water, so he took pity on them and said: ﴿What is your matter?﴾ Shimr recited it with a kasra on the kha', meaning: who is your husband, and why does he not water (the flock) himself? This is an irregular and rare reading.

﴿They said: We do not water﴾. Ibn Musarrif read it as lā nusqī, with a damma on the nun. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and the two Arab readers read yaṣdura with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the dal, meaning they (the shepherds) return with their sheep. The rest of the seven, al-A'raj, Talhah, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and ʿIsa read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the dal, meaning they send their sheep back. The majority read al-ri'ā' with a kasra on the ra', as a broken plural. Al-Zamakhshari said: as for al-ri'ā' with a kasra, it is analogical, like ṣiyām and qiyām. End of quotation. This is not analogical, because it is the plural of rā'in (shepherd), and the analogical plural of an active participle describing a rational being is fu'ala, like qāḍin and quḍāh (judges). Anything other than this plural is not analogical. It was also read al-ru'ā' with a damma on the ra', which is a collective noun, like al-rijāl and al-thanā'. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: ʿAyyash recited from Abu ʿAmr al-ra'ā' with a fatha on the ra', which is a verbal noun put in place of an adjective, so the singular and plural forms are the same in it, and it is also possible that a noun in construct was omitted from it.

﴿And our father is a very old man﴾: an excuse to Musa for their doing the watering themselves, and an indication that their father cannot water because of his old age and infirmity, and an appeal to Musa to help them.

﴿So he watered for them﴾, meaning he watered their flock for their sake. It is reported that the shepherds used to place on the mouth of the well a stone that only a number of men could lift. The reports differ on the number: the least they said was seven, and the most was a hundred. He lifted it alone. It was also said that they had a bucket that only forty men could draw with, and he drew with it alone. It is also reported that he pushed among them for the water until he watered for the two women, all of this out of desire for reward, despite the hardship of travel and his great hunger, so that green of herbs could be seen in his stomach [p. 114] from the vegetables he had eaten. It was also said that he walked until the soles of his feet were worn through, and yet he helped them and relieved them of the task of watering. Their answer matches his question. He asked them about the reason for holding back, and they answered him: "We are two weak women in seclusion, we cannot compete with men, so we delay watering until they are finished." Their doing this is not forbidden, and the custom of the Arabs and desert people in this is different from the custom of town dwellers and non-Arabs, especially when necessity calls for it.

﴿Then he withdrew to the shade﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: the shade of a tree. It was said: it was a sumrah tree. It was also said: the shade of a wall with no roof. It was also said: he put his back to what was facing his face of the sun.

﴿He said: My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾. The commentators said: he hinted at what he would eat, because of the hunger he had suffered, but did not state the request directly. Here "You sent down" means "You send down." Al-Zamakhshari said: it was transitive with lām. "Faqīr" (in need) because it was implicitly meant as "one who asks and seeks." It is possible that he meant: in need of worldly things for the sake of the good of religion that You sent down to me, which is deliverance from the wrongdoers, because he had been with Pharaoh in rule and wealth. He said this in contentment with the noble exchange, joyfully, and thankfully to Him. Al-Hasan said: he asked for more knowledge and wisdom.

﴿Then one of the two came to him walking bashfully﴾. The speech contains an omission, and the implied meaning is: they went back to their father without delay in watering, and they told him about the man who had watered for them, so he told one of them to call him.

﴿One of the two came to him﴾. Ibn Muhaysin read fa-jā'athu iḥdāhumā, dropping the hamza for lightness without analogy, like wayla ummihi for wayla ummihi and yābā Fulān. The analogical form would be to make it between the two (between hamza and vowel). "Iḥdāhumā" is indefinite. It was said: she was the elder. It was said: they were twins, and the first was born half a day before the other. "Bashfully" is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning bashful and cautious. Umar ibn al-Khattab said: she had covered her face with the sleeve of her garment. The majority hold that the one calling them was their father Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and they were his daughters. Al-Hasan said: he was the son of Shu'ayb's brother, named Marwan. Abu ʿUbaydah said: Harun. It was said: he was a righteous man not related to Shu'ayb by lineage. It was also said: he was their paternal uncle, the owner of the flock, and he was the one who gave her in marriage, and she referred to him as father because he held that position.

﴿So that he may reward you for the wage of what you watered for us﴾. This reflects the generosity and reciprocity of Shu'ayb toward one who did work for him, even if the worker did not intend reward.

﴿When he came to him﴾, meaning he went with them to their father. In this there is evidence for relying on the report of a woman, as Musa went with her, just as her reports are relied upon in matters of narration.

﴿And he related to him the story﴾, meaning what happened to him regarding his departure from Egypt and the reason for it.

﴿He said: Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning God accepted your supplication in your saying: ﴿My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Qasas: 21], or he informed him of his deliverance from them. He comforted him with his saying: ﴿Do not fear﴾, and he brought him food close. Musa said to him: "We are a family that does not sell our religion for the filling of the earth with gold." Shu'ayb said to him: "This is not the payment for the watering, but my custom and the custom of my fathers is hospitality to guests and feeding food." Then Musa, peace be upon him, ate.

﴿One of them said﴾: she is left unspecified, and she is the one who went, the one who spoke, and the one who was later married. ﴿O my father, hire him﴾, meaning to herd and water the sheep. She described him as strong, because he lifted the stone from the well alone, drew with that bucket, and pushed among them until he overpowered them at the water. And she described him as trustworthy, because when he walked behind her, the wind blew and pressed her clothes against her body, and she described her shape, so he said: "Walk behind me and guide me to the road." Her statement is a wise and comprehensive saying, because when sufficiency and trustworthiness combine in the one entrusted with a matter, the purpose is complete. It is a saying that became a proverb (mathal), passed among people. This was a reason for hiring him. It is as if she said: hire him for his trustworthiness and strength, and these two qualities serve as indications of him. A parallel to this construction is the saying of the poet:

Indeed, the best of people, living or dead,
Is the captive of Thaqif among them in chains.

He placed ﴿the best one you hire﴾ as the subject, to emphasize it, and judged him by strength and trustworthiness. When she described him with these two qualities, her father said to her: "How do you know this?" She mentioned his lifting the stone alone, and his modesty in not looking at her when the wind blew her clothes. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and others. It was also said: Musa spoke to her first, saying: "Walk behind me, for I am a man who does not look at the backs of women; guide me on the road, right or left." Ibn Mas'ud said: the three most perceptive people are the daughter of Shu'ayb, the companion of Yusuf in his saying ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾ [Yusuf], and Abu Bakr in his choosing of Umar. In her saying ﴿hire him﴾ there is evidence for the legitimacy of hiring (ijara) according to them, and it was so in every religious community; it is a necessity of people and a benefit of association. This differs from the view of Ibn ʿUlayyah and al-Asamm, who did not permit it. This is something on which there is ijma' (scholarly consensus), and their disagreement is a breach of it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verses 22–29 (part 2 of 2):

﴿He said: "I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾ Shu'ayb desired this in-law relationship (musahara) because of what she had described of him, and because he saw in him his detachment from worldly things, his attachment to God, and his flight from the disbelievers. Warsh, Ahmad ibn Musa, and (from Abu 'Amr) read: "unkihaka ihda" (أُنْكِحَكَ احْدى), with the hamza elided. The apparent sense of His words ﴿that I marry you﴾ is that the giving of a woman in marriage (inkah) belongs to the guardian (wali), and the woman has no right in it, contrary to Abu Hanifa in some of its cases, namely where she is an adult, knowledgeable of her own interests, for then she concludes the contract herself in the presence of witnesses. In it there is evidence for the guardian offering his guardianship to the husband, and 'Umar did this; and it is evidence for giving one's virgin daughter in marriage without seeking her permission, which is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: when a virgin reaches maturity, she is not married except with her consent. It has been said: in it there is evidence for the view of those who say that the contract is not valid except with the wording of tazwij or inkah; this was the view of Rabi'a, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubayd, and Dawud. "Ihda ibnatayya" (إحْدى ابْنَتَيَّ) is indefinite, and this is an offer (ard), not a contract. Do you not see His words: ﴿I want﴾? At the time of the contract he would specify whichever of the two he wished. Likewise he did not set the first limit of the term of hire. The apparent meaning of the verse permits marriage in exchange for service (ijara), and this was the view of al-Shafi'i, his companions, and Ibn Habib. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿these two﴾ indicates that he had other daughters besides them. End. There is no proof in that, for these two were the ones he had seen driving (the flocks), and one of them came to him, so he pointed to them, and pointing to them does not indicate that he had others.

﴿On condition that you serve me﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in "unkihaka", either the subject or the object. "Ta'jurani" is from ajartuhu: I became his hired servant (ajir), like your saying abawtuhu: I became his father. The second object of "ta'jurani" is omitted, its estimated form being "nafsaka" (yourself). ﴿Eight years﴾ (thamaniya hijajin) is an adverbial of time, as Abu al-Baqa' said. Al-Zamakhshari said: "hijaj" is an object, meaning: his pasturing (the flock) for eight years.

﴿But if you complete ten, it is from you﴾, that is, it is a voluntary favour and bounty, not a stipulation.

﴿And I do not wish to burden you﴾ by imposing upon you either of the two terms, nor in companionship and dispute over observing times, nor in imposing upon you the tasks of shepherding and services outside the condition.

﴿You will find me, God willing, among the righteous﴾: a true promise, conditioned by God's will. "Among the righteous" refers to good dealing and gentleness of character, or "among the righteous" in general, so that good dealing falls within it.

When Shu'ayb had finished what he discussed with Musa, Musa said: ﴿That is between me and you﴾, by way of affirming and making firm that the condition was made only for eight years. "Dhalika" (that) is the subject, and its predicate is "bayni wa baynaka" (between me and you), referring to what he covenanted with him, that is: that which you have pledged and stipulated with me stands between us all, and we shall not depart from it. Then he said: ﴿Whichever of the two terms﴾, that is, the eight or the ten? ﴿Then there is no enmity against me﴾, that is, no transgression shall be against me in seeking an addition. "Ayyu" is a conditional particle and "ma" is superfluous. Al-Hasan and al-'Abbas, from Abu 'Amr, read: "ayyama", with the second ya' elided, as the poet said:

"They awaited Nasr and the two Simaks; whichever (ayyama) of them the rain-clouds poured upon me..."

'Abd Allah read: "ayya al-ajalayni ma qadaytu" (أَيَّ الأجَلَيْنِ ما قَضَيْتُ), with ma added between the two terms and "qadaytu". Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): what is the difference between the placement of the superfluous "ma" in the two readings? (I answer): In the widely transmitted reading it stands emphasizing the indefiniteness, that is, increasing its generality; and in the irregular reading it is an emphasis on the decision, as if he said: whichever of the two terms I have resolved to fulfil and devoted my determination to? Abu Haywa and Ibn Qutayb read: "fala 'idwana" (فَلا عِدْوانَ), with a kasra on the 'ayn. Al-Mubarrad said: he knew that there would be no transgression against him in completing the longer of them, but he combined them so that the first would be like the complete one in fulfilment. Al-Zamakhshari said: the conception of transgression applies only to the shorter of the two terms, which is the demand for completing the ten; so what is the meaning of tying transgression to both of them together? (I answer): its meaning is: just as, if I were pressed for an addition beyond the ten, that would be transgression beyond doubt, so likewise if I were pressed for an addition beyond the eight. He intended by this to affirm the option, and that it is firm and settled, and that the two terms are equal, either this or that, without difference between them in fulfilment. As for completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish I will do it, and otherwise I shall not be compelled to it. It has been said: its meaning is: then I shall not be a transgressor, and it is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying: no sin is upon me and no consequence. End. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was transitive with lām. "Faqīr" (in need) because it was implicitly meant as "one who asks and seeks." It is possible that he meant: in need of worldly things for the sake of the good of religion that You sent down to me, which is deliverance from the wrongdoers, because he had been with Pharaoh in rule and wealth. He said this in contentment with the noble exchange, joyfully, and thankfully to Him. Al-Hasan said: he asked for more knowledge and wisdom.

﴿Then one of the two came to him walking bashfully﴾. The speech contains an omission, and the implied meaning is: they went back to their father without delay in watering, and they told him about the man who had watered for them, so he told one of them to call him.

﴿One of the two came to him﴾. Ibn Muhaysin read fa-jā'athu iḥdāhumā, dropping the hamza for lightness without analogy, like wayla ummihi for wayla ummihi and yābā Fulān. The analogical form would be to make it between the two (between hamza and vowel). "Iḥdāhumā" is indefinite. It was said: she was the elder. It was said: they were twins, and the first was born half a day before the other. "Bashfully" is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning bashful and cautious. Umar ibn al-Khattab said: she had covered her face with the sleeve of her garment. The majority hold that the one calling them was their father Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and they were his daughters. Al-Hasan said: he was the son of Shu'ayb's brother, named Marwan. Abu ʿUbaydah said: Harun. It was said: he was a righteous man not related to Shu'ayb by lineage. It was also said: he was their paternal uncle, the owner of the flock, and he was the one who gave her in marriage, and she referred to him as father because he held that position.

﴿So that he may reward you for the wage of what you watered for us﴾. This reflects the generosity and reciprocity of Shu'ayb toward one who did work for him, even if the worker did not intend reward.

﴿When he came to him﴾, meaning he went with them to their father. In this there is evidence for relying on the report of a woman, as Musa went with her, just as her reports are relied upon in matters of narration.

﴿And he related to him the story﴾, meaning what happened to him regarding his departure from Egypt and the reason for it.

﴿He said: Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning God accepted your supplication in your saying: ﴿My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Qasas: 21], or he informed him of his deliverance from them. He comforted him with his saying: ﴿Do not fear﴾, and he brought him food close. Musa said to him: "We are a family that does not sell our religion for the filling of the earth with gold." Shu'ayb said to him: "This is not the payment for the watering, but my custom and the custom of my fathers is hospitality to guests and feeding food." Then Musa, peace be upon him, ate.

﴿One of them said﴾: she is left unspecified, and she is the one who went, the one who spoke, and the one who was later married. ﴿O my father, hire him﴾, meaning to herd and water the sheep. She described him as strong, because he lifted the stone from the well alone, drew with that bucket, and pushed among them until he overpowered them at the water. And she described him as trustworthy, because when he walked behind her, the wind blew and pressed her clothes against her body, and she described her shape, so he said: "Walk behind me and guide me to the road." Her statement is a wise and comprehensive saying, because when sufficiency and trustworthiness combine in the one entrusted with a matter, the purpose is complete. It is a saying that became a proverb (mathal), passed among people. This was a reason for hiring him. It is as if she said: hire him for his trustworthiness and strength, and these two qualities serve as indications of him. A parallel to this construction is the saying of the poet:

Indeed, the best of people, living or dead,
Is the captive of Thaqif among them in chains.

He placed ﴿the best one you hire﴾ as the subject, to emphasize it, and judged him by strength and trustworthiness. When she described him with these two qualities, her father said to her: "How do you know this?" She mentioned his lifting the stone alone, and his modesty in not looking at her when the wind blew her clothes. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and others. It was also said: Musa spoke to her first, saying: "Walk behind me, for I am a man who does not look at the backs of women; guide me on the road, right or left." Ibn Mas'ud said: the three most perceptive people are the daughter of Shu'ayb, the companion of Yusuf in his saying ﴿perhaps he will benefit us﴾ [Yusuf], and Abu Bakr in his choosing of Umar. In her saying ﴿hire him﴾ there is evidence for the legitimacy of hiring (ijara) according to them, and it was so in every religious community; it is a necessity of people and a benefit of association. This differs from the view of Ibn ʿUlayyah and al-Asamm, who did not permit it. This is something on which there is ijma' (scholarly consensus), and their disagreement is a breach of it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verses 22–29 (part 2 of 2):

﴿He said: "I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine"﴾ Shu'ayb desired this in-law relationship (musahara) because of what she had described of him, and because he saw in him his detachment from worldly things, his attachment to God, and his flight from the disbelievers. Warsh, Ahmad ibn Musa, and (from Abu 'Amr) read: "unkihaka ihda" (أُنْكِحَكَ احْدى), with the hamza elided. The apparent sense of His words ﴿that I marry you﴾ is that the giving of a woman in marriage (inkah) belongs to the guardian (wali), and the woman has no right in it, contrary to Abu Hanifa in some of its cases, namely where she is an adult, knowledgeable of her own interests, for then she concludes the contract herself in the presence of witnesses. In it there is evidence for the guardian offering his guardianship to the husband, and 'Umar did this; and it is evidence for giving one's virgin daughter in marriage without seeking her permission, which is the view of Malik and al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa said: when a virgin reaches maturity, she is not married except with her consent. It has been said: in it there is evidence for the view of those who say that the contract is not valid except with the wording of tazwij or inkah; this was the view of Rabi'a, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubayd, and Dawud. "Ihda ibnatayya" (إحْدى ابْنَتَيَّ) is indefinite, and this is an offer (ard), not a contract. Do you not see His words: ﴿I want﴾? At the time of the contract he would specify whichever of the two he wished. Likewise he did not set the first limit of the term of hire. The apparent meaning of the verse permits marriage in exchange for service (ijara), and this was the view of al-Shafi'i, his companions, and Ibn Habib. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿these two﴾ indicates that he had other daughters besides them. End. There is no proof in that, for these two were the ones he had seen driving (the flocks), and one of them came to him, so he pointed to them, and pointing to them does not indicate that he had others.

﴿On condition that you serve me﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in "unkihaka", either the subject or the object. "Ta'jurani" is from ajartuhu: I became his hired servant (ajir), like your saying abawtuhu: I became his father. The second object of "ta'jurani" is omitted, its estimated form being "nafsaka" (yourself). ﴿Eight years﴾ (thamaniya hijajin) is an adverbial of time, as Abu al-Baqa' said. Al-Zamakhshari said: "hijaj" is an object, meaning: his pasturing (the flock) for eight years.

﴿But if you complete ten, it is from you﴾, that is, it is a voluntary favour and bounty, not a stipulation.

﴿And I do not wish to burden you﴾ by imposing upon you either of the two terms, nor in companionship and dispute over observing times, nor in imposing upon you the tasks of shepherding and services outside the condition.

﴿You will find me, God willing, among the righteous﴾: a true promise, conditioned by God's will. "Among the righteous" refers to good dealing and gentleness of character, or "among the righteous" in general, so that good dealing falls within it.

When Shu'ayb had finished what he discussed with Musa, Musa said: ﴿That is between me and you﴾, by way of affirming and making firm that the condition was made only for eight years. "Dhalika" (that) is the subject, and its predicate is "bayni wa baynaka" (between me and you), referring to what he covenanted with him, that is: that which you have pledged and stipulated with me stands between us all, and we shall not depart from it. Then he said: ﴿Whichever of the two terms﴾, that is, the eight or the ten? ﴿Then there is no enmity against me﴾, that is, no transgression shall be against me in seeking an addition. "Ayyu" is a conditional particle and "ma" is superfluous. Al-Hasan and al-'Abbas, from Abu 'Amr, read: "ayyama", with the second ya' elided, as the poet said:

"They awaited Nasr and the two Simaks; whichever (ayyama) of them the rain-clouds poured upon me..."

'Abd Allah read: "ayya al-ajalayni ma qadaytu" (أَيَّ الأجَلَيْنِ ما قَضَيْتُ), with ma added between the two terms and "qadaytu". Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): what is the difference between the placement of the superfluous "ma" in the two readings? (I answer): In the widely transmitted reading it stands emphasizing the indefiniteness, that is, increasing its generality; and in the irregular reading it is an emphasis on the decision, as if he said: whichever of the two terms I have resolved to fulfil and devoted my determination to? Abu Haywa and Ibn Qutayb read: "fala 'idwana" (فَلا عِدْوانَ), with a kasra on the 'ayn. Al-Mubarrad said: he knew that there would be no transgression against him in completing the longer of them, but he combined them so that the first would be like the complete one in fulfilment. Al-Zamakhshari said: the conception of transgression applies only to the shorter of the two terms, which is the demand for completing the ten; so what is the meaning of tying transgression to both of them together? (I answer): its meaning is: just as, if I were pressed for an addition beyond the ten, that would be transgression beyond doubt, so likewise if I were pressed for an addition beyond the eight. He intended by this to affirm the option, and that it is firm and settled, and that the two terms are equal, either this or that, without difference between them in fulfilment. As for completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish I will do it, and otherwise I shall not be compelled to it. It has been said: its meaning is: then I shall not be a transgressor, and it is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying: no sin is upon me and no consequence. End. His first answer contains some verbosity.

﴿And God is witness to what we say﴾, that is, to what we have covenanted and pledged. ﴿Trustee (wakil)﴾, that is, witness. Qatada said: guardian (hafiz). Ibn Shajara said: watchful (raqib). The wakil is one to whom a matter is entrusted; when the meaning of witness or the like was implied, it took "'ala" after it.

﴿Then when Musa had fulfilled the term﴾: it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he fulfilled the longer of the two terms, which is the ten. From Mujahid: he fulfilled ten, or ten and then more; but this is weak.

﴿And he journeyed with his family﴾, that is, toward Egypt, his land and the land of his people. There is disagreement about whom he married, the elder or the younger, and likewise about her name. The manner of his journey and his sighting of the fire has been mentioned in Surat Ta-Ha and elsewhere. The majority read "jidhwatin" (جِذْوَةٍ) with a kasra on the jim; al-A'mash, Talha, Abu Haywa, and Hamza read it with a damma; 'Asim, except al-Ju'fi, read it with a fatha.

﴿That perhaps you may warm yourselves﴾, that is, that you may be warmed by it, since it was a cold night, and they had lost the way.

[p. 112]

﴿Tawajjaha﴾ means he turned his face. ﴿Tilqā'a﴾ has already been discussed under Yunus, meaning "toward the direction of his face." The verbal noun is used as an adverb of place. There were three roads, and Musa took the middle one, while those who pursued him took the other two, saying: "The one who is guilty does not take the main roads, and he travels only the side paths." He remained on the road for eight nights [p. 113] barefoot, eating nothing but the leaves of trees. The apparent meaning of his words, ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way﴾, is that he did not know the road, so he asked his Lord to guide him to the most direct road, so that he would not go astray, because if he took a road that did not lead him to his destination, he would be lost. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he set out for Madyan and began walking without knowing the way, and God brought him to Madyan. It was also said that Gabriel guided him to Madyan, and it was said that it was another angel. It was also said that he took a road where he would be safe, and it happened that his journey led to Madyan. The apparent meaning of "the right way" is the middle of the road that he followed to the place where he would be safe. Mujahid said: "the right way" means the road to Madyan. Al-Hasan said: it is the way of guidance, so Musa, peace be upon him, walked until he reached Madyan, and he was not under the obedience of Pharaoh.

﴿When he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾, meaning he reached it. Warid (arrival) means reaching a thing and also means entering it. It was said that this water was a well. Ummah means a large group, and ʿalayhi means at its edge and border.

﴿Drawing water﴾ means their livestock.

﴿And he found beside them﴾, meaning from the direction he came from before he reached the group. They were "beside them" in relation to him, as Ibn ʿAtiyyah said. Al-Zamakhshari said: in a place lower than their place.

﴿Holding back﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: they were holding back their flock from the water, fearing the strong drawers of water. Qatadah said: they were holding back people from their flock. Al-Zajjaj said: it seems they disliked crowding at the water. It was also said: so that their flock would not mix with their sheep. It was also said: they were shielding their faces from the gaze of onlookers to conceal themselves. Al-Farra' said: they were keeping them from scattering. The name of the younger is ʿIbra, and the name of the elder is Sabura.

When Musa, peace be upon him, saw them standing and not moving forward to water, he asked them, saying: ﴿What is your matter?﴾ Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: asking about a matter (khatb) is only when someone is afflicted, oppressed, pitied, or does something unusual. Al-Zamakhshari said: its literal meaning is "What is your matter to be sought?" That is, what do you seek by holding back? The object of the matter is called khatb, just as affairs are called sha'n, as in your saying: "What is your sha'n?" It is said: "I attended to his sha'n," meaning I aimed at his aim. End of quotation. In his question, peace be upon him, there is evidence for the permissibility of speaking with a non-related woman about what is needed. Their father had no hired worker, so they were driving the flock to the water, and they did not have the strength to draw water. The shepherds used to draw water from the well and water their livestock, and when they left, if some water remained in the trough, the two women watered their flock. Musa, peace be upon him, came on that day while they were holding their flock back from the water, so he took pity on them and said: ﴿What is your matter?﴾ Shimr recited it with a kasra on the kha', meaning: who is your husband, and why does he not water (the flock) himself? This is an irregular and rare reading.

﴿They said: We do not water﴾. Ibn Musarrif read it as lā nusqī, with a damma on the nun. Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and the two Arab readers read yaṣdura with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the dal, meaning they (the shepherds) return with their sheep. The rest of the seven, al-A'raj, Talhah, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and ʿIsa read it with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the dal, meaning they send their sheep back. The majority read al-ri'ā' with a kasra on the ra', as a broken plural. Al-Zamakhshari said: as for al-ri'ā' with a kasra, it is analogical, like ṣiyām and qiyām. End of quotation. This is not analogical, because it is the plural of rā'in (shepherd), and the analogical plural of an active participle describing a rational being is fu'ala, like qāḍin and quḍāh (judges). Anything other than this plural is not analogical. It was also read al-ru'ā' with a damma on the ra', which is a collective noun, like al-rijāl and al-thanā'. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: ʿAyyash recited from Abu ʿAmr al-ra'ā' with a fatha on the ra', which is a verbal noun put in place of an adjective, so the singular and plural forms are the same in it, and it is also possible that a noun in construct was omitted from it.

﴿And our father is a very old man﴾: an excuse to Musa for their doing the watering themselves, and an indication that their father cannot water because of his old age and infirmity, and an appeal to Musa to help them.

﴿So he watered for them﴾, meaning he watered their flock for their sake. It is reported that the shepherds used to place on the mouth of the well a stone that only a number of men could lift. The reports differ on the number: the least they said was seven, and the most was a hundred. He lifted it alone. It was also said that they had a bucket that only forty men could draw with, and he drew with it alone. It is also reported that he pushed among them for the water until he watered for the two women, all of this out of desire for reward, despite the hardship of travel and his great hunger, so that green of herbs could be seen in his stomach [p. 114] from the vegetables he had eaten. It was also said that he walked until the soles of his feet were worn through, and yet he helped them and relieved them of the task of watering. Their answer matches his question. He asked them about the reason for holding back, and they answered him: "We are two weak women in seclusion, we cannot compete with men, so we delay watering until they are finished." Their doing this is not forbidden, and the custom of the Arabs and desert people in this is different from the custom of town dwellers and non-Arabs, especially when necessity calls for it.

﴿Then he withdrew to the shade﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: the shade of a tree. It was said: it was a sumrah tree. It was also said: the shade of a wall with no roof. It was also said: he put his back to what was facing his face of the sun.

﴿He said: My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾. The commentators said: he hinted at what he would eat, because of the hunger he had suffered, but did not state the request directly. Here "You sent down" means "You send down." Al-Zamakhshari said: it was transitive with lām. "Faqīr" (in need) because it was implicitly meant as "one who asks and seeks." It is possible that he meant: in need of worldly things for the sake of the good of religion that You sent down to me, which is deliverance from the wrongdoers, because he had been with Pharaoh in rule and wealth. He said this in contentment with the noble exchange, joyfully, and thankfully to Him. Al-Hasan said: he asked for more knowledge and wisdom.

﴿Then one of the two came to him walking bashfully﴾. The speech contains an omission, and the implied meaning is: they went back to their father without delay in watering, and they told him about the man who had watered for them, so he told one of them to call him.

﴿One of the two came to him﴾. Ibn Muhaysin read fa-jā'athu iḥdāhumā, dropping the hamza for lightness without analogy, like wayla ummihi for wayla ummihi and yābā Fulān. The analogical form would be to make it between the two (between hamza and vowel). "Iḥdāhumā" is indefinite. It was said: she was the elder. It was said: they were twins, and the first was born half a day before the other. "Bashfully" is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning bashful and cautious. Umar ibn al-Khattab said: she had covered her face with the sleeve of her garment. The majority hold that the one calling them was their father Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, and they were his daughters. Al-Hasan said: he was the son of Shu'ayb's brother, named Marwan. Abu ʿUbaydah said: Harun. It was said: he was a righteous man not related to Shu'ayb by lineage. It was also said: he was their paternal uncle, the owner of the flock, and he was the one who gave her in marriage, and she referred to him as father because he held that position.

﴿So that he may reward you for the wage of what you watered for us﴾. This reflects the generosity and reciprocity of Shu'ayb toward one who did work for him, even if the worker did not intend reward.

﴿When he came to him﴾, meaning he went with them to their father. In this there is evidence for relying on the report of a woman, as Musa went with her, just as her reports are relied upon in matters of narration.

﴿And he related to him the story﴾, meaning what happened to him regarding his departure from Egypt and the reason for it.

﴿He said: Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning God accepted your supplication in your saying: ﴿My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Qasas: 21], or he informed him of his deliverance from them. He comforted him with his saying: ﴿Do not fear﴾, and he brought him food close. Musa said to him: "We are a family that does not sell our religion for the filling of the earth with gold." Shu'ayb said to him: "This is not the payment for the watering, but my custom and the custom of my fathers is hospitality to guests and feeding food." Then Musa, peace be upon him, ate.

﴿One of them said﴾: she is left unspecified, and she is the one who went, the one who spoke, and the one who was later married. ﴿O my father, hire him﴾, meaning to herd and water the sheep. She described him as strong, because he lifted the stone from the well alone, drew with that bucket, and pushed among them until he overpowered them at the water. 'Abd Allah read: "ayya al-ajalayni ma qadaytu" (أَيَّ الأجَلَيْنِ ما قَضَيْتُ), with ma added between the two terms and "qadaytu". Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): what is the difference between the placement of the superfluous "ma" in the two readings? (I answer): In the widely transmitted reading it stands emphasizing the indefiniteness, that is, increasing its generality; and in the irregular reading it is an emphasis on the decision, as if he said: whichever of the two terms I have resolved to fulfil and devoted my determination to? Abu Haywa and Ibn Qutayb read: "fala 'idwana" (فَلا عِدْوانَ), with a kasra on the 'ayn. Al-Mubarrad said: he knew that there would be no transgression against him in completing the longer of them, but he combined them so that the first would be like the complete one in fulfilment. Al-Zamakhshari said: the conception of transgression applies only to the shorter of the two terms, which is the demand for completing the ten; so what is the meaning of tying transgression to both of them together? (I answer): its meaning is: just as, if I were pressed for an addition beyond the ten, that would be transgression beyond doubt, so likewise if I were pressed for an addition beyond the eight. He intended by this to affirm the option, and that it is firm and settled, and that the two terms are equal, either this or that, without difference between them in fulfilment. As for completion, it is left to my judgement: if I wish I will do it, and otherwise I shall not be compelled to it. It has been said: its meaning is: then I shall not be a transgressor, and it is in negating transgression from himself, like your saying: no sin is upon me and no consequence. End. His first answer contains some verbosity.

﴿And God is witness to what we say﴾, that is, to what we have covenanted and pledged. ﴿Trustee (wakil)﴾, that is, witness. Qatada said: guardian (hafiz). Ibn Shajara said: watchful (raqib). The wakil is one to whom a matter is entrusted; when the meaning of witness or the like was implied, it took "'ala" after it.

﴿Then when Musa had fulfilled the term﴾: it is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he fulfilled the longer of the two terms, which is the ten. From Mujahid: he fulfilled ten, or ten and then more; but this is weak.

﴿And he journeyed with his family﴾, that is, toward Egypt, his land and the land of his people. There is disagreement about whom he married, the elder or the younger, and likewise about her name. The manner of his journey and his sighting of the fire has been mentioned in Surat Ta-Ha and elsewhere. The majority read "jidhwatin" (جِذْوَةٍ) with a kasra on the jim; al-A'mash, Talha, Abu Haywa, and Hamza read it with a damma; 'Asim, except al-Ju'fi, read it with a fatha.

﴿That perhaps you may warm yourselves﴾, that is, that you may be warmed by it, since it was a cold night, and they had lost the way.

﴿So when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿And cast down your staff." But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in flight and did not return. "O Moses, come forward and do not fear; indeed you are among the secure.﴾ ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without harm. And draw your arm close to your side against fear. These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs; indeed they have been a defiantly disobedient people."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I killed a soul from among them, so I fear that they will kill me.﴾ ﴿And my brother Aaron, he is more eloquent in speech than I, so send him with me as a helper, to confirm me. Indeed I fear that they will deny me."﴾ ﴿He said, "We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will give you both authority, so they will not reach you. By Our signs, you and whoever follows you will be the victors."﴾.

The "min" in "min shati'" is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), and "min al-shajara" is likewise, since it is a substitute (badal) for the first, meaning "from the direction of the tree." As for "al-ayman," it may be an attribute of both the shore and the valley, in the sense of blessing and good fortune, or "al-ayman" may mean what is opposite the left limb, in which case it is relative to Moses and not to the shore or the valley, meaning the right of Moses as he faces it, until he descends into the valley; or the reverse of that. All these opinions regarding "al-ayman" have been related. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and Maslama read "fi al-buq'a" with a fatha on the ba'. Abu Zayd said: "I heard from the Arabs: 'hadhihi buq'a tayyiba' (this is a good spot), with a fatha on the ba'." The spot is described as blessed because of the signs of Allah and His lights that it was singled out with, and His speaking to Moses, peace be upon him, or because of the provisions and good fruits it contained. "Fi al-buq'a" is connected to "nuwdiya," or it may be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "shati'." "Al-shajara" is a jujube tree (unnab), or a... (in the reports) a thorny bush ('ulayq), or an acacia (samura), or a thorny shrub ('awsaj), these being the opinions. "An" may be an explanatory particle (harf tafsir), and it may be a lightened form of the heavy "anna." (p-117) A group read "anni ana" with a fatha on the hamza. In its i'rab there is a difficulty: if "inna" is explanatory, then "inni" should be with a kasra; and if it is verbal (masdariyya), it is equivalent to a single noun, and a single noun cannot be the predicate of the dummy pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). So the parsing of this reading is that "inna" is explanatory, and "inni" is governed by a hidden element whose estimate is: "inni, O Moses, I know that I am Allah."

It came in Ta-Ha: ﴿O Moses, I am your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 11], and in al-Naml: ﴿Called out: blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾ [al-Naml: 8], and here: ﴿was called from the shore﴾. There is no contradiction, since each surah relates some of what that call included. The majority hold that He spoke to him in this station without an intermediary. Al-Hasan said: He called him with the call of revelation (wahy), not the call of speech. The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿and cast down your staff. But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in flight and did not return﴾ has already preceded. Then He commanded him, saying: ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket﴾, and the "jayb" is the opening of the robe from where the head comes out, and the sleeve of the robe was extremely tight. The discussion of ﴿it will come out white without harm﴾ has already preceded. "Al-janah" (wing) here has been interpreted as the hand, as the upper arm (adud), as the side (i'taf), and as what lies below the upper arm down to the wrist, and as the collar of his tunic. "Al-rahb" means fear, and the readings concerning it will come. It has been said that with a fatha on the ra' and ha', it means "the sleeve," in the dialect of Banu Hanifa and Himyar, and al-Asma'i heard a speaker say: "Give me what is in your rahb," meaning in your sleeve. The apparent meaning of ﴿draw your janah close to you from the rahb﴾ is to be taken literally.

al-Thawri said: Moses feared that some harm had befallen him, so Allah commanded him to return his hand to his pocket so that it would return to its original state, and Moses would know that it was not harm but a sign from Allah. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: He commanded him to press his upper arm and forearm, which is the wing, to his side, so that his fright would be lightened by that. It is the nature of a person that when he does this at the time of his fright, his heart becomes strong. It has been said: When the staff turned into a snake, Moses was frightened and trembled, and he protected himself with his hand, as the one who fears something does; so it was said to him: "Put your hand under your upper arm in place of your protecting yourself with it," then he brought it out white so that another miracle would appear. This opinion was expounded by al-Zamakhshari, because it is like a repetition of His saying: ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket﴾. He himself said: "The janah here is the hand." He said: "Because the two hands of a person are like the two wings of a bird, and when he puts his right hand under his left upper arm, he has drawn his wing to himself." It has been said: The meaning is that when a matter terrifies you because of the glare of its light, draw it to yourself and you will be calm. A group said: It is a figurative usage (majaz); He commanded him to resolve upon what He commanded him, as the Arabs say: "shidda hayazimaka wa-rbut jash'aka" (gird your loins and steady your heart), meaning: "exert yourself in your affair and leave off fear." This is because his fear and fright had multiplied in more than one place. This was said by Abu 'Ali, and it is as if the fright made him fly, and the instrument of flying is the wing. So it was said to him: "Be still and do not fear, and fold the spread of your wing to yourself out of fear." Al-Zamakhshari also mentioned this opinion, and he said: "The second is that by drawing his wing to himself is meant his steadfastness, his self-restraint and his firmness at the transformation of the staff into a snake, so that he would not tremble or be afraid, as a metaphor (isti'ara) borrowed from the action of a bird, because when it fears it spreads its wings and lowers them; otherwise its wings are folded to it and tucked up." The meaning of ﴿from the rahb﴾ is "because of the rahb," that is: if fear afflicts you at the sight of the snake, then draw your wing to yourself. He made the fear that used to befall him the cause and reason for what he was commanded regarding folding his wing to himself. The meaning of ﴿and draw your janah close to you﴾ and His saying ﴿insert your hand into your pocket﴾ is one and the same according to one of the two explanations, but the two expressions were varied, and the one meaning was repeated because the purposes differ: the purpose in one is the hand coming out white, and in the second is the concealing of fear. (If you say): The janah, which is the hand, has been made in one of the two places folded, and in the other folded to something; that is His saying ﴿and draw your janah close to you﴾ and ﴿and draw your hand to your janah﴾ [Ta-Ha: 22]. So how is the reconciliation between them? (I say): By the folded janah is meant the right hand, and by that to which it is folded is the left hand, and each of the right and left of both hands is a janah. Among the strange interpretations is that "al-rahb" is the sleeve, in the dialect of Himyar, and that they say: "give me what is in your rahb"; I wish I knew how this is sound in the language, and whether it has been heard from the trustworthy authorities whose Arabic is accepted? Then I wish I knew: how is its position in the verse, and how does the separation (fasl) give it, like the rest of the words of the revelation? Moreover, Moses, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, on the night of the intimate conversation was wearing nothing but a woolen tunic, with no sleeves to it. End. As for his saying "and has it been heard from the authorities?", this is related from al-Asma'i, and he is trustworthy and reliable. As for his saying "how is its position in the verse?", they said: its meaning is: bring your hand out of your sleeve, and he had been holding the staff by the sleeve. The two Harams and Abu 'Amr read "min al-rahab" with a fatha on the ra' and ha'; Hafs: with a fatha on the ra' and sukun on the ha'; and the rest of the seven: with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the ha'. Qatada, al-Hasan, 'Isa and al-Jahdari read with a damma on both.

﴿Fa-dhanika﴾ refers to the staff and the hand, and both are feminine, but they were made masculine for the masculinity of the predicate, just as the masculine may be made feminine for the femininity of the predicate, like the reading of one who read: "thumma lam takun fitnatuhum illa an qalu" (then their trial was only that they said), with the ya' in "takun." 

﴿Burhanani﴾: two shining proofs. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "fa-dhannika" with a shadda on the nun; the rest of the seven with a lightened nun. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Isa, Abu Nawfal, Ibn Hurmuz and Shibl read "fa-dhaniyka," with a ya' after the kasra nun, which is the dialect of Hudhayl. It has been said: rather it is the dialect of Tamim, and Shibl related it from Ibn Kathir; and also from him: "fa-dhanayka," with a fatha on the nun before the ya', according to the dialect of one who puts a fatha on the nun of the dual, like his saying:

"Over two swift [horses], in which they set out one evening."

Ibn Mas'ud read with a shadda on the nun with a kasra and a ya' after it. It has been said: this is the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-Mahdawi said: rather their dialect is the lightening of it. And "ila Fir'awn" is connected to an omitted element indicated by the meaning; its estimate: "go to Pharaoh."

﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I killed a soul from among them"﴾: he is the Copt whom he struck and who died. So he asked his Lord for what would increase him in strength, and he mentioned his brother and the reason for which there would be additional help in conveying the message. "Afsah" (more eloquent) indicates that there is eloquence in him, but his brother is more eloquent.

﴿So send him with me as a helper﴾, that is, an assistant who confirms me. The meaning is not that he says to me, "You have spoken the truth," since the same statement is made by the stammerer and the eloquent; rather the meaning is that, because of his greater eloquence, he expounds more clearly, answers doubts, and argues with the disbelievers. The majority read "ridan" with a hamza; Abu Ja'far, Nafi', and the two Madinans read it with the hamza omitted and its vowel transferred to the dal; the well-known reading of Abu Ja'far is with the transfer, and without hamza or tanwin, and its basis is that he treated the connected speech as pausal. 'Asim and Hamza read "yusaddiqani" with a damma on the qaf, so it may be a descriptive attribute of "ridan," and it may be a circumstantial clause or a resumed statement (isti'naf). The rest of the seven read it with a sukun. Ubayy and Zayd ibn 'Ali read "yusaddiquni," with the pronoun referring to Pharaoh and his people. Ibn Khalawayh said: this is evidence for one who reads with the jussive, because if it were in the nominative it would say "yusaddiqunani." End. The jussive is as a response to the imperative. The meaning of "yusaddiquni" is: I hope for their confirmation of me, so He answered his request and said: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother﴾. Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-Hasan read "'ududaka" with two dammas. From al-Hasan: with a damma on the ayn and sukun on the dad. From some of them: with a fatha on the ayn and a kasra on the dad; and with both fatha, which 'Isa read. It is also said "'add" with a fatha on the ayn and sukun on the dad, and I know of no one who read with it. The "'adud" is the well-known limb, and it is the support of the hand, and with its strength the hand becomes strong. The poet said:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not a hand except a hand which has no upper arm."

The meaning in it is: We will strengthen you through your brother. It is said in good: "shadda Allahu 'adudaka" (may Allah strengthen your arm), and in evil: "fatta Allahu fi 'adudika" (may Allah weaken you in your arm). And "al-sultan" is the proof, the dominance, and the empowerment.

﴿So they will not reach you﴾, that is, with harm, or to harming you both. "Bi-ayatina" may be connected to His saying "wa-naj'alu," or to "yasilun," or to "al-ghalibun," and if it is a relative clause according to the view of one who permits that the adverbial phrase and prepositional phrase precede the relative clause of "al," and if in his view it is a relative clause by way of expansion (ittisa'), or it is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "go with Our signs," just as "fi tis'i ayat" (among nine signs) is connected to "idhhab" (go); or by way of explanation (bayan), in which case the governing element is omitted. These are transmitted parsings. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may be an oath whose answer is "fa-la yasilun" (so they will not reach you), placed before it, or it is from the idle oath (laghw al-qasam). End. As for it being an oath whose answer is "fa-la yasilun," this does not hold according to the majority, because the answer of an oath is not entered by the fa'. As for his saying "or from the idle oath," it seems he means, and Allah knows best, that no answer is mentioned for it, but it is omitted because it is indicated, meaning: "by Our signs you will surely prevail." (p-119)

﴿So when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿And cast down your staff." But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in flight and did not return. "O Moses, come forward and do not fear; indeed you are among the secure.﴾ ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without harm. And draw your arm close to your side against fear. These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs; indeed they have been a defiantly disobedient people."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I killed a soul from among them, so I fear that they will kill me.﴾ ﴿And my brother Aaron, he is more eloquent in speech than I, so send him with me as a helper, to confirm me. Indeed I fear that they will deny me."﴾ ﴿He said, "We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will give you both authority, so they will not reach you. By Our signs, you and whoever follows you will be the victors."﴾.

The "min" in "min shati'" is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), and "min al-shajara" is likewise, since it is a substitute (badal) for the first, meaning "from the direction of the tree." All these opinions regarding "al-ayman" have been related. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli and Maslama read "fi al-buq'a" with a fatha on the ba'. Abu Zayd said: "I heard from the Arabs: 'hadhihi buq'a tayyiba' (this is a good spot), with a fatha on the ba'." The spot is described as blessed because of the signs of Allah and His lights that it was singled out with, and His speaking to Moses, peace be upon him, or because of the provisions and good fruits it contained. "Fi al-buq'a" is connected to "nuwdiya," or it may be in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "shati'." "Al-shajara" is a jujube tree (unnab), or a... (in the reports) a thorny bush ('ulayq), or an acacia (samura), or a thorny shrub ('awsaj), these being the opinions. It came in Ta-Ha: ﴿O Moses, I am your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 11], and in al-Naml: ﴿Called out: blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾ [al-Naml: 8], and here: ﴿was called from the shore﴾. Al-Hasan said: He called him with the call of revelation (wahy), not the call of speech. The discussion of the parallel of His saying ﴿and cast down your staff. But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in flight and did not return﴾ has already preceded. Then He commanded him, saying: ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket﴾, and the "jayb" is the opening of the robe from where the head comes out, and the sleeve of the robe was extremely tight. The discussion of ﴿it will come out white without harm﴾ has already preceded. "Al-janah" (wing) here has been interpreted as the hand, as the upper arm (adud), as the side (i'taf), and as what lies below the upper arm down to the wrist, and as the collar of his tunic. "Al-rahb" means fear, and the readings concerning it will come. It has been said that with a fatha on the ra' and ha', it means "the sleeve," in the dialect of Banu Hanifa and Himyar, and al-Asma'i heard a speaker say: "Give me what is in your rahb," meaning in your sleeve. The apparent meaning of ﴿draw your janah close to you from the rahb﴾ is to be taken literally.

Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: He commanded him to press his upper arm and forearm, which is the wing, to his side, so that his fright would be lightened by that. It is the nature of a person that when he does this at the time of his fright, his heart becomes strong. It has been said: When the staff turned into a snake, Moses was frightened and trembled, and he protected himself with his hand, as the one who fears something does; so it was said to him: "Put your hand under your upper arm in place of your protecting yourself with it," then he brought it out white so that another miracle would appear. This opinion was expounded by al-Zamakhshari, because it is like a repetition of His saying: ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket﴾. He himself said: "The janah here is the hand." He said: "Because the two hands of a person are like the two wings of a bird, and when he puts his right hand under his left upper arm, he has drawn his wing to himself." It has been said: The meaning is that when a matter terrifies you because of the glare of its light, draw it to yourself and you will be calm. A group said: It is a figurative usage (majaz); He commanded him to resolve upon what He commanded him, as the Arabs say: "shidda hayazimaka wa-rbut jash'aka" (gird your loins and steady your heart), meaning: "exert yourself in your affair and leave off fear." This is because his fear and fright had multiplied in more than one place. This was said by Abu 'Ali, and it is as if the fright made him fly, and the instrument of flying is the wing. So it was said to him: "Be still and do not fear, and fold the spread of your wing to yourself out of fear." Al-Zamakhshari also mentioned this opinion, and he said: "The second is that by drawing his wing to himself is meant his steadfastness, his self-restraint and his firmness at the transformation of the staff into a snake, so that he would not tremble or be afraid, as a metaphor (isti'ara) borrowed from the action of a bird, because when it fears it spreads its wings and lowers them; otherwise its wings are folded to it and tucked up." The meaning of ﴿from the rahb﴾ is "because of the rahb," that is: if fear afflicts you at the sight of the snake, then draw your wing to yourself. He made the fear that used to befall him the cause and reason for what he was commanded regarding folding his wing to himself. Then I wish I knew: how is its position in the verse, and how does the separation (fasl) give it, like the rest of the words of the revelation? "Over two swift [horses], in which they set out one evening."

﴿So when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿And cast down your staff." These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs; indeed they have been a defiantly disobedient people."﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I killed a soul from among them, so I fear that they will kill me.﴾ ﴿And my brother Aaron, he is more eloquent in speech than I, so send him with me as a helper, to confirm me. "Bi-ayatina" may be connected to His saying "wa-naj'alu," or to "yasilun," or to "al-ghalibun," and if it is a relative clause according to the view of one who permits that the adverbial phrase and prepositional phrase precede the relative clause of "al," and if in his view it is a relative clause by way of expansion (ittisa'), or it is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "go with Our signs," just as "fi tis'i ayat" (among nine signs) is connected to "idhhab" (go); or by way of explanation (bayan), in which case the governing element is omitted. These are transmitted parsings. Al-Zamakhshari said: It may be an oath whose answer is "fa-la yasilun" (so they will not reach you), placed before it, or it is from the idle oath (laghw al-qasam). End. As for it being an oath whose answer is "fa-la yasilun," this does not hold according to the majority, because the answer of an oath is not entered by the fa'. As for his saying "or from the idle oath," it seems he means, and Allah knows best, that no answer is mentioned for it, but it is omitted because it is indicated, meaning: "by Our signs you will surely prevail." (p-119)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verse 36–43:

﴿So when Musa came to them with Our signs, clear proofs, they said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we never heard of this among our forefathers, the earliest ones."﴾ ﴿Musa said, "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him, and who will have the good outcome of the abode. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾ ﴿Pharaoh said, "O chiefs, I know of no god for you other than myself. So kindle for me, O Haman, [a fire] upon the clay and make for me a tower that I may look upon the god of Musa, though I think him to be among the liars."﴾ ﴿And he and his soldiers became arrogant in the land without right, and they thought that they would not be returned to Us.﴾ ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea. So see how was the end of the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised.﴾ ﴿And We had certainly given Musa the Scripture after We had destroyed the former generations as a source of insight for the people, and guidance and mercy, that they might remember.﴾

﴿بِآياتِنا﴾ (with Our signs) are the staff and the hand.

﴿بَيِّناتٍ﴾ means clear in indicating his truthfulness, and that it is an extraordinary, miraculous matter. They ceased resisting and opposing him, so they reverted to slander and lying, and attributed it to being magic, because they see a thing in one state, then see it in another state, then it returns to the first state. So they claimed that it was magic that Musa fabricates and attributes falsely to God, and therefore it is not a miracle. Then, together with their claim that it is fabricated magic, and their lie in that, they went further in lying, saying that they had never heard of this among their fathers, meaning in the time of their fathers and their days. And "among our fathers" is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning "this," that is, something like this existing in the days of our fathers. When they denied hearing of the like of this in the earlier time, it became established that what Musa claimed is a novelty, to which nothing similar had preceded, and this indicates that it is fabricated against God. They were lying in that, and the means by which they heard reports of the earlier messengers, Musa being in their time. Do you not see the saying of a believer from the family of Pharaoh: ﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs﴾ [Ghafir: 34]?

When Musa saw what they countered him with, namely that what he brought was magic, and the absence of hearing of the like in the earlier time, ﴿Musa said, "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him"﴾, since He qualified him for prophethood, sent him with guidance, and promised him a good final outcome, and he means by this himself; and had he been as they claim, He would not have sent him. Then he drew attention to the cause that makes success impossible, which is wrongdoing (ẓulm), meaning placing a thing other than its place, since they were called to belief in God and brought miracles, yet they claimed divinity and attributed that miraculous matter to magic. The "outcome of the abode" (ʿāqibat al-dār), although it may apply to both the praiseworthy and the blameworthy, has been used most often for the praiseworthy, so if it is not restricted, it is understood in that sense. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Those will have the good outcome of the abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 22], ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence﴾ [al-Ra'd: 23]? And He said: ﴿And the disbelievers will know to whom belongs the good outcome of the abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 42]. Ibn Kathir recited "Qāla Mūsā" without a waw; the rest of the seven read it with the waw. The rationale for the majority reading is that when he brought them the clear proofs, they said "such and such," and Musa said "such and such," so the observer distinguishes the difference between the two statements and the corruption of one of them, since they stand opposed, and thus he knows with certainty that the statement of Musa is the truth and guidance. The rationale for Ibn Kathir's reading is that it is a place of recitation: when they said "such and such," Musa said "such and such."

Pharaoh denied to his chiefs that he knew of a god other than himself, intending by this the negation of its existence, meaning: you have no god other than me. It is also possible that a god for them was not known to him, but was only supposed, so the negation is on its apparent meaning. This is indicated by his saying: ﴿And I think him to be among the liars﴾, and he was lying in the negation of his knowledge of a god other than himself. Do you not see his saying at the time of his drowning: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾ [Yunus: 90]? Pharaoh continued in his deception, called his minister Haman, and ordered him to kindle fire upon the clay. It was said: he was the first to make baked brick, and he did not say "bake the brick," because Haman had no prior knowledge of that, so Pharaoh is the one who teaches him what to do.

﴿فاجْعَلْ لِي صَرْحًا﴾ means build for me, ﴿that I may look upon the god of Musa﴾. He gave his people the impression that the god of Musa can be reached and overcome, while he, knowing with certainty that this is impossible for him, yet because of his people's foolishness, ignorance, and extreme blindness, it was possible in their eyes; and the very region of Egypt requires of its people belief in impossibilities and susceptibility to illusions and imaginings. There is no doubt that among Pharaoh's people there were those who believed his claim to be false, but agreed with him out of fear of his power and aggression, just as we have seen it happen to many intelligent people when a chief in their presence narrates an impossible story, they agree with him about that story. The command to build the tower does not indicate that it was built, and this has been disputed: it was said, he built it, and one who described it mentioned things that God alone knows; and it was said, it was not built. "Iṭṭalaʿa" (to look upon) in the sense of "ṭalaʿa" (to ascend): one says "ṭalaʿa ilā al-jabal" and "iṭṭalaʿa" with one meaning, that is, he ascended, so the form iftaʿala is used with the sense of the bare verb.

﴿وبغير الحق﴾ (and without right), since they had no right to that, so they were falsifiers in their arrogance, in that he claimed divinity and they agreed with him in that; and greatness in reality belongs only to God. Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, and Nafi' read "lā yurjaʿūn" in the active voice; the majority read it in the passive voice. "Al-ard" here is the land of Egypt.

﴿فَنَبَذْناهم في اليَمِّ﴾ is a metaphor for causing them to enter the sea until they drowned; they were likened to pebbles thrown by the one who casts them from his hand. From it comes "nabdh al-nawāh" (throwing away the date-stone), and the saying of the poet:

I looked at its title and cast it aside, as you cast away a worn-out sandal from your sandals.

The people of Pharaoh and Pharaoh, although they went to the sea by their own choice in pursuit of the Children of Israel, what gathered them of the preordained decree and their drowning in the sea is God's casting them away. "Ja'ala" here means "ṣayyara" (to make), that is, We made them leaders, models for the disbelievers who follow them in their misguidance, just as there are leaders of good who are followed, and they became renowned for that, and their story remained. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And We made them" means "We called them," "leaders" means "callers to the Fire," and we said: they are leaders, callers to the Fire, and it is from your saying "ja'alahu bakhīlan wa fāsiqan" when you call him and say: he is stingy and wicked. The lexicographers explain his wickedness and stinginess as "ja'alahu bakhīlan wa fāsiqan," and from it is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. The meaning of calling them to the Fire is calling them to its causes, which is disbelief. End of quotation. He interpreted "ja'alnāhum" as "da'awnāhum" rather than "ṣayyarnāhum," following his Mu'tazilite school, because making them leaders would involve creating that state in them, and the Mu'tazilites permit this from God but do not attribute it to Him. He said: it is permissible that "khadhalnāhum" (We forsook them) until they became leaders of disbelief. The meaning of forsaking is withholding the favours, and one withholds them only from one who is known will not benefit from them, namely one who is set upon disbelief, whom signs and warnings do not avail. End of quotation, and this too follows the Mu'tazilite method.

﴿لَعْنَةً﴾ means expulsion and removal. "The Day of Resurrection" is joined to "in this world."

﴿مِنَ المَقْبُوحِينَ﴾ Abu 'Ubayda said: "among the destroyed." Ibn 'Abbas said: "among those disfigured in form, through blackness of faces and blueness of eyes." It was also said: "among the distanced."

When the Exalted mentioned what Pharaoh and his people came to, of God's wrath upon them and their drowning, He mentioned what He bestowed upon His messenger Musa, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Musa the Scripture﴾, which is the Torah, and it is the first book in which obligatory duties and rulings were revealed.

﴿مِن بَعْدِ ما أهْلَكْنا القُرُونَ الأُولى﴾ refers to the people of Nuh, Hud, Salih, and Lut. It is said: no town was destroyed after the revelation of the Torah except the town whose people were transformed into apes. "Baṣā'ir" is in the accusative as a circumstantial phrase, meaning ways of guidance by which one gains insight.

I looked at its title and cast it aside, as you cast away a worn-out sandal from your sandals.

"Ja'ala" here means "ṣayyara" (to make), that is, We made them leaders, models for the disbelievers who follow them in their misguidance, just as there are leaders of good who are followed, and they became renowned for that, and their story remained.
