(p-124) Al-Zamakhshari said: "Awa lam yakfuru" (Did they not disbelieve) means the fathers of their kind, and whoever holds their creed shares their creed, and their obstinacy is their obstinacy; they are the disbelievers of the time of Musa, "bima utiya Musa" (in what was given to Musa). And from al-Hasan: there was already a basis among the Arabs in the days of Musa, so its meaning according to this is: Did not their fathers disbelieve? They said of Musa and Harun: "Two sorceries that back each other up" (saahiran tazaharaa), that is, they cooperated. End of quotation. "Min qablu" (before): it may be connected to "yakfuru" and to "utiya."

The majority read: "saahiran" (two sorcerers). Mujahid said: Musa and Harun. Al-Hasan said: Musa and Isa. Ibn Abbas said: Musa and Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Hasan also said: Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud], Zayd ibn Ali, and the Kufans read: "sihraan" (two magics). Ibn Abbas said: the Torah and the Qur'an. It was also said: the Torah and the Injil, or Musa and Harun were called two magics as a form of emphasis.

"Tazaharaa" means they cooperated. The majority read "tazaharaa" as a past verb on the pattern of tafaa'ala. Talhah and al-A'mash read "izzaharaa" with a hamzat al-wasl and a shaddah on the zay, and likewise it is in the reading of Abdullah; its original form is "tazaharaa," and the ta' was assimilated into the za', so a hamzat al-wasl was brought in because of the sukun of the assimilated ta'. Mahbub from al-Hasan, Yahya ibn al-Harith al-Dhimari, Abu Haywa, and Abu Khallad from al-Yazidi read "tazzaharaa" with a ta' and a shaddah on the za'. Ibn Khalawayh said: its shaddah is a grammatical error, because it is a past verb, and the shaddah is only used in the present tense. Sahib al-Lawami said: I do not know its basis. Sahib al-Kamil fi al-Qira'at said: it has no meaning. End of quotation. However, it has an explanation in the language: it is a present tense verb from which the nun has been dropped, and the dropping of it has occurred in a few instances in speech and in poetry. "Saahiran" is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "antuma saahiraani tatazaharaani" (you two are two sorcerers who back each other up); then the ta' was assimilated into the za' and the nun was dropped, and the pronoun of address was observed. If it were read "yazzaharaa" with a ya', taking into account "saahiraan," it would have a basis, or by estimating "they two are sorcerers that back each other up."

"Wa qaluu inna bikullin kaafiruun" (And they said: Indeed we disbelieve in each of them), that is, in each of the two sorcerers or the two sorceries. Then Allah commanded him to proclaim this verse, which is His saying: "Qul fa'tuu" (Say: Then bring), that is, you, O deniers of these books, which contain the command to acts of worship and noble character, forbid disbelief and blameworthy traits, and for which Allah promised great reward. "If your denial is for some reason, then bring a Book from Allah which gives better guidance than these two, I will follow it with you." The pronoun in "minhaa" refers to what was revealed to Musa and to Muhammad (ﷺ) (may Allah bless them both and grant them peace). Making their bringing of such a book conditional on truthfulness is a matter that is certain and established: it will not happen, and their truthfulness is impossible, just as it is impossible that they bring a Book from Allah that is more guided than the two Books. It is also permissible that the condition is intended as mockery of them. Zayd ibn Ali read "atta'bi'uhu" with a raf' on the 'ayn as a new sentence, meaning: I follow it.

"Fa-in lam yastajiibuu laka" (And if they do not respond to you). Ibn Abbas said: it means if they do not believe in what you have brought of proofs, and they are not able to bring a Book that is better. Istijabah (responding) implies a call, and he (ﷺ) always calls to faith; that is, if they do not respond to you after the miracles contained in your Book that was revealed have become clear to them. Or the saying "fa'tuu bikitab" may itself be the call, since it is a request from them and a call upon them to bring it. It is known that they will not respond by bringing a Book from Allah. So know that they have nothing but the following of mere desire, not the following of evidence. "Istajaba" means "ajaba," and it is transitive to the one called with "li" and without it, as He said: "Fastajaba lahu rabbuhu" (Yusuf 34), "Fastajabnaa lahu wa wahabnaa lahu Yahyaa" (al-Anbiya 90), "Fa-in lam yastajiibuu lakum" (Hud 14). "Fa lam yastajibhu 'inda dhaalika mujiibu"
So he transitively used it without "li." As for the verse, its meaning is: "lam yastajib du'aa'," with the omission of the modifier. End of quotation.

"Bi-ghayri hudan" (without guidance) is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and this circumstance is a restriction on following desire, because a person may follow what he desires, and that which he desires may contain guidance from Allah, since all desires are divided into those that contain guidance (p-125) and those that do not contain guidance; therefore it is restricted by this circumstance. Al-Zamakhshari said: meaning forsaken, left to his own desire. End of quotation, and this is according to the path of the Mu'tazila.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verses 44–50 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Moses the command, nor were you among the witnesses.﴾ ﴿But We produced generations, and the lifetime grew long for them. And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan, reciting Our verses to them, but We were ever sending messengers.﴾ ﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount when We called out, but it was a mercy from your Lord, that you might warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that perhaps they might be mindful.﴾ ﴿And had it not been that a misfortune might befall them because of what their hands had sent forth, and they should say, "Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs and be among the believers?"﴾ ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?" Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before? They said, "Two sorceries backing each other," and they said, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in both."﴾ ﴿Say, "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guided than these two, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿But if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their own desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

When Allah (Exalted) had related the accounts of Moses and the remarkable events that befell him, namely his being conceived at the time when the sons were being slaughtered, his being cast into the sea in a chest, his being returned to his mother, Pharaoh's adoption of him, his being granted judgment and knowledge, his killing of the Copt, his leaving his homeland in flight, his marriage connection with Shu'ayb, his tending of Shu'ayb's sheep for many long years, his return to Egypt, his losing the way, Allah's conversing with him, the manifesting through his hands of those two great miracles, namely the staff and the hand, his being commanded to go to Pharaoh, his dialogue with him, Pharaoh's denial and his destruction along with his people, and the favour bestowed upon Moses in giving him the Torah, Allah (Exalted) revealed all of that to Muhammad, His Messenger (ﷺ). He reminded him of His bounty upon him in this regard, and of the unseen matters that He had specially granted him, which neither he nor his people had known. So He said: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Moses the command.﴾

As for "al-amr" (the command), it has been said: it is prophethood and the judgment that Allah gave Moses. It has also been said: the command is the command to Muhammad (peace be upon him) that he should be among his community, and this interpretation harmonises with what follows it, His saying: ﴿But We produced generations.﴾ It has also been said: the command is the destruction of Pharaoh by water, and "bi-janib al-gharbi" (on the western side) is to be understood as the sea (al-yamm).

He began first by negating a specific matter, which is that he was not present (p-122) at the time when Allah decreed the command to Moses. Then he repeated it by saying that he was not among the witnesses. The meaning, and Allah knows best, is: not among the witnesses to all that We informed you of. Thus it is a negation of his witnessing all that happened to Moses, so it was a generality after a specification.

As for "bi-janib al-gharbi": according to some, it is an idafa (construct) of the qualified noun to its qualifier; according to others, the noun has been omitted and the qualifier put in its place. On the first view the original is "bi-l-janib al-gharbi," and on the second the original is "bi-janib al-makan al-gharbi." The preference between the two views is mentioned in grammar (nahw).

As for "al-gharbi": Qatadah said it is the western side of the mountain. Al-Hasan said: Allah sent Moses to the west. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the place where the sun, the moon and the stars set. It has been said: here there is a western mountain. It has been said: al-gharbi is of the valley, and it has been said: of the sea.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning is: you, O Muhammad, were not present at these unseen matters about which you are informed, but they came to you by Our revelation. That is to say, it was incumbent that one should hasten to believe in you, but the matter stretched over the generations which We produced age after age, so their wisdom faded and their ignorance and error became firmly established.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-gharb is the place lying on the western side, which is the place where Moses' appointed time on the Mount occurred, and where Allah wrote for him on the tablets. The command decreed to Moses is the revelation that was revealed to him. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: you were not present at the place where We revealed to Moses, nor were you among the company of those who witnessed the revelation to him, or [witnessing] upon the revelation to him, namely his deputies whom he chose for the appointed time, so that you might learn from the body of the witnesses what happened to Moses at his appointed time, the writing of the Torah for him on the tablets, and other things.

(If you ask): how does His saying ﴿But We produced generations﴾ connect with this statement, and in what respect is it a corrective (istidrak) to it? (I answer): its connection to it and its being a corrective lies in the fact that its meaning is: But We produced, after the era of the revelation until your era, many generations, so the lifetime stretched over the last of them, and that is the generation in which you exist.

﴿The lifetime grew long﴾: that is, the period of the cessation of revelation, and the sciences were effaced, so it became necessary to send you to them. So We sent you and taught you knowledge of the stories of the prophets and the story of Moses. It is as if He said: you were not a witness to Moses and what happened to him, but We revealed it to you. Thus He mentioned the cause of the revelation, which is the lengthening of the interval, and indicated the effect through it, in accordance with Allah's custom of brevity. Therefore this istidrak (corrective statement) resembles the two istidraks after it.

﴿And you were not dwelling﴾: that is, residing among the people of Madyan, who were Shu'ayb and the believers.

﴿Reciting to them Our verses﴾: reading to them, learning from them, meaning the verses in which is the story of Shu'ayb and his people. But We sent you and informed you of them and taught them to you.

﴿When We called out﴾: he means the calling out to Moses on the night of the secret conversation and speaking with him. But We taught you. It has been said: ﴿So the lifetime grew long for them﴾ and prophethood became dormant, the laws were effaced, and much of them was distorted. The completion of the statement is implied, and its estimate is: We sent you renewing those reports, distinguishing the truth from what had been disputed among them, as a mercy from Us. It has been said: it is possible that the meaning is: you were not among the witnesses at that time, and between you and Moses there were generations whose lifetimes stretched long, and you now relate those circumstances by way of direct witnessing and vision, through Our inspiration to you as a miracle for you. It has been said: "tatlu" (reciting) is a circumstantial clause (hal), and it has been said: it is a new independent statement, meaning: you now recite the story of Shu'ayb, but We sent you as a messenger, and We sent down to you a Book in which these forgotten reports are contained, which you recite to them, and had it not been for you, I would not have informed them of what they did not witness.

Al-Farra' said: ﴿And you were not dwelling﴾ among the people of Madyan with Moses, so that you would see him and hear his speech, and now you are ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾, that is, to your community, so it is disconnected [from what precedes]. End of quotation. It has been said: if he was not present at that place, then what is the meaning of ﴿nor were you among the witnesses﴾? Ibn 'Abbas said: the estimate is: you did not attend that place, and even had you attended, you would not have witnessed those events, for it is possible that there was [someone] there who would neither witness nor see. Muqatil said: he did not witness the people of Madyan so as to read their report to the people of Makkah, but We sent you to the people of Makkah, and sent down to you these reports, and had it not been for that, you would not have known. Al-Dahhak said: he says: you, O Muhammad, were not the messenger to the people of Madyan, reciting to them the verses of the Book, but rather it was another, (p-123) but We were ever sending a messenger in every age: We sent Shu'ayb to Madyan, and We sent you to the Arabs so that you would be the seal of the prophets. End of quotation.

Al-Tabari said: ﴿When We called out﴾ with [the words]: "I will write it for those who fear [Me]." And from Abu Hurayrah: that at that time a voice was called out from heaven: "O community of Muhammad, I have answered you before you called upon Me, and I have forgiven you before you asked Me." Then Moses (peace be upon him) said: "O Allah, make me of the community of Muhammad." So the meaning is: when We called out by Your command, and We informed you of your prophethood.

The majority read ﴿mercy﴾ in the accusative (raḥmatan), so it is estimated: "but We made you a mercy," and it is estimated: We informed you and made you aware as a mercy. 'Isa and Abu Haywah read it in the nominative (raḥmatun), and they estimated: "but he is a mercy," or "he is a mercy," or "you are a mercy."

﴿That you might warn a people to whom no warner had come﴾: that is, in the period of the interval between you and 'Isa, which is about five hundred and fifty years or so. The answer to (lawla) is omitted. The meaning is: had it not been that they would say, when they are punished for what they had sent forth of polytheism and sins, "Why did You not send to us a messenger?", arguing with that against us, [We sent messengers]. That is: We only sent the messengers to remove this excuse, as He said: ﴿So that there would not be for people any argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa': 165], and [so that] you would not say: ﴿There came to us no bringer of good tidings nor warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19]. The estimate of the answer is: We did not send messengers to them, this is the statement of al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its estimate is: We would have hastened to punish them with what they deserve.

The misfortune (muṣība) is the punishment. Since most actions are performed by the hands, every deed was expressed by the earning of the hands, even deeds of the hearts, as an extension of speech, and making the minority follow the majority, and giving the majority precedence over the minority.

The fa' in ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ is for conjunction with "tuṣība" [it might befall them]; the second lawla is for urging (taḥḍīḍ). And in "fa-nattabi'a" the fa' is the answer to the urging.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): how is this meaning valid, when the punishment has been made the cause of the sending, not the saying, since the particle of prevention (ḥarf al-imtina') enters upon it and not upon the saying? (I answer): the saying is what is intended, so that it would be the cause of the sending of the messengers, but since the punishment was the cause of the saying, its existence was dependent upon its existence. The punishment was made as if it were the cause of the sending through the medium of the saying. Thus lawla was placed before it, and the saying was brought joined to it by the fa' which gives the meaning of causation. Its meaning reduces to your saying: "And had it not been for their saying this, ﴿when a misfortune befalls them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 156], We would not have sent [messengers]." But this method was chosen for a subtle reason, which is that they were not punished, for example, for their disbelief, while they had seen what they were compelled by to the certain knowledge. They did not say: "Why did You not send to us a messenger?", and the cause of this saying of theirs is only the punishment and nothing else, not regret over what they missed of faith in their Creator. In this there is, of the strong testimony to the firmness and deep-rootedness of their disbelief, what is not hidden, like their saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would go back to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28]. End of quotation.

As for "al-Haqq" (the Truth): it is the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), who came with the inimitable Book which cut off their excuses. It has been said: it is the Qur'an.

﴿Like what was given to Moses﴾. ﴿Before﴾: that is, before the Book that was sent down all at once, and the turning of the staff into a serpent, the splitting of the sea, and other signs. They proposed that out of obstinacy and stubbornness, just as they said: "Why was not a treasure sent down upon him?" and other such proposals they made. This statement that they uttered is from the teaching of the Jews to the Quraysh; they said to them: "Will he not bring a manifest sign like the signs of Moses?" So Allah answered them that they disbelieved in the signs of Moses, and what occurred from them concerning the signs of Moses is what occurred from these [people] concerning the signs of the Messenger.

The pronoun in ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ refers to the Jews, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. It has been said: the speaker of that is the Arabs, by instruction, as we have said. It has been said: the speaker of that is the Jews. It appears to me that it refers to the Quraysh, who said: "Why was he not given (*lawla ūtiya*)," meaning Muhammad, "the like of what was given to Moses?" That is because their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a denial of Moses (peace be upon him), and their attribution of sorcery to the Messenger is like their attribution of sorcery to Moses, since the prophets are of one valley. Whoever attributes to one of the prophets what is not fitting has attributed it to all the prophets. All the pronouns harmonise in this, in His saying: ﴿Say, "Then bring a Book from Allah"﴾. Although the apparent meaning of "qala" (saying) is verbal utterance, it may also apply to belief, and they, in terms of denying prophethoods, believed that what appeared at the hands of the prophets of signs was only a kind of sorcery.

Then he repeated it by saying that he was not among the witnesses. The meaning, and Allah knows best, is: not among the witnesses to all that We informed you of. Thus it is a negation of his witnessing all that happened to Moses, so it was a generality after a specification.

As for "bi-janib al-gharbi": according to some, it is an idafa (construct) of the qualified noun to its qualifier; according to others, the noun has been omitted and the qualifier put in its place. On the first view the original is "bi-l-janib al-gharbi," and on the second the original is "bi-janib al-makan al-gharbi." The preference between the two views is mentioned in grammar (nahw).

As for "al-gharbi": Qatadah said it is the western side of the mountain. Al-Hasan said: Allah sent Moses to the west. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the place where the sun, the moon and the stars set. It has been said: here there is a western mountain. It has been said: al-gharbi is of the valley, and it has been said: of the sea.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning is: you, O Muhammad, were not present at these unseen matters about which you are informed, but they came to you by Our revelation. That is to say, it was incumbent that one should hasten to believe in you, but the matter stretched over the generations which We produced age after age, so their wisdom faded and their ignorance and error became firmly established.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-gharb is the place lying on the western side, which is the place where Moses' appointed time on the Mount occurred, and where Allah wrote for him on the tablets. The command decreed to Moses is the revelation that was revealed to him. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: you were not present at the place where We revealed to Moses, nor were you among the company of those who witnessed the revelation to him, or [witnessing] upon the revelation to him, namely his deputies whom he chose for the appointed time, so that you might learn from the body of the witnesses what happened to Moses at his appointed time, the writing of the Torah for him on the tablets, and other things.

(If you ask): how does His saying ﴿But We produced generations﴾ connect with this statement, and in what respect is it a corrective (istidrak) to it? (I answer): its connection to it and its being a corrective lies in the fact that its meaning is: But We produced, after the era of the revelation until your era, many generations, so the lifetime stretched over the last of them, and that is the generation in which you exist.

﴿The lifetime grew long﴾: that is, the period of the cessation of revelation, and the sciences were effaced, so it became necessary to send you to them. So We sent you and taught you knowledge of the stories of the prophets and the story of Moses. It is as if He said: you were not a witness to Moses and what happened to him, but We revealed it to you. Thus He mentioned the cause of the revelation, which is the lengthening of the interval, and indicated the effect through it, in accordance with Allah's custom of brevity. Therefore this istidrak (corrective statement) resembles the two istidraks after it.

﴿And you were not dwelling﴾: that is, residing among the people of Madyan, who were Shu'ayb and the believers.

﴿Reciting to them Our verses﴾: reading to them, learning from them, meaning the verses in which is the story of Shu'ayb and his people. But We sent you and informed you of them and taught them to you.

﴿When We called out﴾: he means the calling out to Moses on the night of the secret conversation and speaking with him. But We taught you. It has been said: ﴿So the lifetime grew long for them﴾ and prophethood became dormant, the laws were effaced, and much of them was distorted. The completion of the statement is implied, and its estimate is: We sent you renewing those reports, distinguishing the truth from what had been disputed among them, as a mercy from Us. It has been said: it is possible that the meaning is: you were not among the witnesses at that time, and between you and Moses there were generations whose lifetimes stretched long, and you now relate those circumstances by way of direct witnessing and vision, through Our inspiration to you as a miracle for you. It has been said: "tatlu" (reciting) is a circumstantial clause (hal), and it has been said: it is a new independent statement, meaning: you now recite the story of Shu'ayb, but We sent you as a messenger, and We sent down to you a Book in which these forgotten reports are contained, which you recite to them, and had it not been for you, I would not have informed them of what they did not witness.

Al-Farra' said: ﴿And you were not dwelling﴾ among the people of Madyan with Moses, so that you would see him and hear his speech, and now you are ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾, that is, to your community, so it is disconnected [from what precedes]. End of quotation. It has been said: if he was not present at that place, then what is the meaning of ﴿nor were you among the witnesses﴾? Ibn 'Abbas said: the estimate is: you did not attend that place, and even had you attended, you would not have witnessed those events, for it is possible that there was [someone] there who would neither witness nor see. Muqatil said: he did not witness the people of Madyan so as to read their report to the people of Makkah, but We sent you to the people of Makkah, and sent down to you these reports, and had it not been for that, you would not have known. Al-Dahhak said: he says: you, O Muhammad, were not the messenger to the people of Madyan, reciting to them the verses of the Book, but rather it was another, (p-123) but We were ever sending a messenger in every age: We sent Shu'ayb to Madyan, and We sent you to the Arabs so that you would be the seal of the prophets. End of quotation.

Al-Tabari said: ﴿When We called out﴾ with [the words]: "I will write it for those who fear [Me]." And from Abu Hurayrah: that at that time a voice was called out from heaven: "O community of Muhammad, I have answered you before you called upon Me, and I have forgiven you before you asked Me." Then Moses (peace be upon him) said: "O Allah, make me of the community of Muhammad." So the meaning is: when We called out by Your command, and We informed you of your prophethood.

The majority read ﴿mercy﴾ in the accusative (raḥmatan), so it is estimated: "but We made you a mercy," and it is estimated: We informed you and made you aware as a mercy. 'Isa and Abu Haywah read it in the nominative (raḥmatun), and they estimated: "but he is a mercy," or "he is a mercy," or "you are a mercy."

﴿That you might warn a people to whom no warner had come﴾: that is, in the period of the interval between you and 'Isa, which is about five hundred and fifty years or so. The answer to (lawla) is omitted. The meaning is: had it not been that they would say, when they are punished for what they had sent forth of polytheism and sins, "Why did You not send to us a messenger?", arguing with that against us, [We sent messengers]. That is: We only sent the messengers to remove this excuse, as He said: ﴿So that there would not be for people any argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa': 165], and [so that] you would not say: ﴿There came to us no bringer of good tidings nor warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19]. The estimate of the answer is: We did not send messengers to them, this is the statement of al-Zajjaj. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its estimate is: We would have hastened to punish them with what they deserve.

The misfortune (muṣība) is the punishment. Since most actions are performed by the hands, every deed was expressed by the earning of the hands, even deeds of the hearts, as an extension of speech, and making the minority follow the majority, and giving the majority precedence over the minority.

The fa' in ﴿fa-yaqulu﴾ is for conjunction with "tuṣība" [it might befall them]; the second lawla is for urging (taḥḍīḍ). And in "fa-nattabi'a" the fa' is the answer to the urging.

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): how is this meaning valid, when the punishment has been made the cause of the sending, not the saying, since the particle of prevention (ḥarf al-imtina') enters upon it and not upon the saying? (I answer): the saying is what is intended, so that it would be the cause of the sending of the messengers, but since the punishment was the cause of the saying, its existence was dependent upon its existence. The punishment was made as if it were the cause of the sending through the medium of the saying. Thus lawla was placed before it, and the saying was brought joined to it by the fa' which gives the meaning of causation. Its meaning reduces to your saying: "And had it not been for their saying this, ﴿when a misfortune befalls them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 156], We would not have sent [messengers]." But this method was chosen for a subtle reason, which is that they were not punished, for example, for their disbelief, while they had seen what they were compelled by to the certain knowledge. They did not say: "Why did You not send to us a messenger?", and the cause of this saying of theirs is only the punishment and nothing else, not regret over what they missed of faith in their Creator. In this there is, of the strong testimony to the firmness and deep-rootedness of their disbelief, what is not hidden, like their saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would go back to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28]. End of quotation.

As for "al-Haqq" (the Truth): it is the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), who came with the inimitable Book which cut off their excuses. It has been said: it is the Qur'an.

﴿Like what was given to Moses﴾. ﴿Before﴾: that is, before the Book that was sent down all at once, and the turning of the staff into a serpent, the splitting of the sea, and other signs. They proposed that out of obstinacy and stubbornness, just as they said: "Why was not a treasure sent down upon him?" and other such proposals they made. This statement that they uttered is from the teaching of the Jews to the Quraysh; they said to them: "Will he not bring a manifest sign like the signs of Moses?" So Allah answered them that they disbelieved in the signs of Moses, and what occurred from them concerning the signs of Moses is what occurred from these [people] concerning the signs of the Messenger.

The pronoun in ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ refers to the Jews, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. It has been said: the speaker of that is the Arabs, by instruction, as we have said. It has been said: the speaker of that is the Jews. It appears to me that it refers to the Quraysh, who said: "Why was he not given (*lawla ūtiya*)," meaning Muhammad, "the like of what was given to Moses?" That is because their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) is a denial of Moses (peace be upon him), and their attribution of sorcery to the Messenger is like their attribution of sorcery to Moses, since the prophets are of one valley. Whoever attributes to one of the prophets what is not fitting has attributed it to all the prophets. All the pronouns harmonise in this, in His saying: ﴿Say, "Then bring a Book from Allah"﴾. Although the apparent meaning of "qala" (saying) is verbal utterance, it may also apply to belief, and they, in terms of denying prophethoods, believed that what appeared at the hands of the prophets of signs was only a kind of sorcery.

(p-124) Al-Zamakhshari said: "Awa lam yakfuru" (Did they not disbelieve) means the fathers of their kind, and whoever holds their creed shares their creed, and their obstinacy is their obstinacy; they are the disbelievers of the time of Musa, "bima utiya Musa" (in what was given to Musa). And from al-Hasan: there was already a basis among the Arabs in the days of Musa, so its meaning according to this is: Did not their fathers disbelieve? They said of Musa and Harun: "Two sorceries that back each other up" (saahiran tazaharaa), that is, they cooperated. End of quotation. "Min qablu" (before): it may be connected to "yakfuru" and to "utiya."

The majority read: "saahiran" (two sorcerers). Mujahid said: Musa and Harun. Al-Hasan said: Musa and Isa. Ibn Abbas said: Musa and Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Hasan also said: Isa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both. Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud], Zayd ibn Ali, and the Kufans read: "sihraan" (two magics). Ibn Abbas said: the Torah and the Qur'an. It was also said: the Torah and the Injil, or Musa and Harun were called two magics as a form of emphasis.

"Tazaharaa" means they cooperated. The majority read "tazaharaa" as a past verb on the pattern of tafaa'ala. Talhah and al-A'mash read "izzaharaa" with a hamzat al-wasl and a shaddah on the zay, and likewise it is in the reading of Abdullah; its original form is "tazaharaa," and the ta' was assimilated into the za', so a hamzat al-wasl was brought in because of the sukun of the assimilated ta'. Mahbub from al-Hasan, Yahya ibn al-Harith al-Dhimari, Abu Haywa, and Abu Khallad from al-Yazidi read "tazzaharaa" with a ta' and a shaddah on the za'. Ibn Khalawayh said: its shaddah is a grammatical error, because it is a past verb, and the shaddah is only used in the present tense. Sahib al-Lawami said: I do not know its basis. Sahib al-Kamil fi al-Qira'at said: it has no meaning. End of quotation. However, it has an explanation in the language: it is a present tense verb from which the nun has been dropped, and the dropping of it has occurred in a few instances in speech and in poetry. "Saahiran" is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "antuma saahiraani tatazaharaani" (you two are two sorcerers who back each other up); then the ta' was assimilated into the za' and the nun was dropped, and the pronoun of address was observed. If it were read "yazzaharaa" with a ya', taking into account "saahiraan," it would have a basis, or by estimating "they two are sorcerers that back each other up."

"Wa qaluu inna bikullin kaafiruun" (And they said: Indeed we disbelieve in each of them), that is, in each of the two sorcerers or the two sorceries. Then Allah commanded him to proclaim this verse, which is His saying: "Qul fa'tuu" (Say: Then bring), that is, you, O deniers of these books, which contain the command to acts of worship and noble character, forbid disbelief and blameworthy traits, and for which Allah promised great reward. "If your denial is for some reason, then bring a Book from Allah which gives better guidance than these two, I will follow it with you." The pronoun in "minhaa" refers to what was revealed to Musa and to Muhammad (ﷺ) (may Allah bless them both and grant them peace). Making their bringing of such a book conditional on truthfulness is a matter that is certain and established: it will not happen, and their truthfulness is impossible, just as it is impossible that they bring a Book from Allah that is more guided than the two Books. It is also permissible that the condition is intended as mockery of them. Zayd ibn Ali read "atta'bi'uhu" with a raf' on the 'ayn as a new sentence, meaning: I follow it.

"Fa-in lam yastajiibuu laka" (And if they do not respond to you). Ibn Abbas said: it means if they do not believe in what you have brought of proofs, and they are not able to bring a Book that is better. Istijabah (responding) implies a call, and he (ﷺ) always calls to faith; that is, if they do not respond to you after the miracles contained in your Book that was revealed have become clear to them. Or the saying "fa'tuu bikitab" may itself be the call, since it is a request from them and a call upon them to bring it. It is known that they will not respond by bringing a Book from Allah. So know that they have nothing but the following of mere desire, not the following of evidence. "Istajaba" means "ajaba," and it is transitive to the one called with "li" and without it, as He said: "Fastajaba lahu rabbuhu" (Yusuf 34), "Fastajabnaa lahu wa wahabnaa lahu Yahyaa" (al-Anbiya 90), "Fa-in lam yastajiibuu lakum" (Hud 14). The poet said:

"Fa lam yastajibhu 'inda dhaalika mujiibu"
So he transitively used it without "li." Al-Zamakhshari said: this verb is transitive to the call and to the one called with "li," and the call is usually omitted when it is transitive to the one called, so one says: "Istajaba Allahu du'aahu" and "istajaba lahu," but one hardly says "istajaba lahu du'aahu." As for the verse, its meaning is: "lam yastajib du'aa'," with the omission of the modifier. End of quotation.

"Wa man adallu" (And who is more astray), that is, no one is more astray. "Bi-ghayri hudan" (without guidance) is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and this circumstance is a restriction on following desire, because a person may follow what he desires, and that which he desires may contain guidance from Allah, since all desires are divided into those that contain guidance (p-125) and those that do not contain guidance; therefore it is restricted by this circumstance. Al-Zamakhshari said: meaning forsaken, left to his own desire. End of quotation, and this is according to the path of the Mu'tazila.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verses 51–57:

﴿We have caused the Word to reach them, so that they may be mindful.﴾ ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it.﴾ ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say, "We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims before it."﴾ ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they endured patiently, and they repel evil with good, and they spend from what We have provided them.﴾ ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek out the ignorant."﴾ ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills, and He knows best those who are guided.﴾ ﴿And they say, "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land." Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary, to which the fruits of everything are brought, as a provision from Us? But most of them do not know.﴾

The reciters agreed on ﴿وصّلنا﴾ (waṣṣalnā) with the ṣād shaddah (doubled). Al-Hasan read it with the ṣād unshaddah. The pronoun in ﴿لهم﴾ (lahum) refers to the Quraysh. Rifa'ah al-Qurazi said: it was revealed concerning ten Jews, and I was one of them.

The majority said: ﴿وصّلنا﴾ means: We followed the Qur'an, with its parts joined to one another, in admonitions, warnings, and the call to Islam. Al-Hasan said: it includes the mention of the nations that were destroyed. Mujahid said: We made it into connected pieces, since it is of various kinds of speech with different meanings. Ibn Zayd said: We joined for them the report of the Hereafter to the report of this world, until it was as if they were witnessing the Hereafter. Al-Akhfash said: We completed the joining of one thing to another, and the original meaning of tawassul (connecting) is in a rope, which is joined part to part. The poet said:

*Say to the sons of Marwan: "What has happened to my covenant,*
*that it is bound with a weak rope which is always being joined?"*

These sayings all mean: the conveying of meanings in it to them. Another group said: the joining refers to the words, meaning: We made for them a speech that is inimitable and that indicates your prophethood.

The "People of the Book" here are a group of Jews who had embraced Islam, and the disbelievers used to harm them. Or they are Bahira the monk, or the Negus, or Salman the Persian. Or Ibn Salam, Abu Rifa'ah, and his son, among ten Jews who embraced Islam. Or forty people of the Gospel who had believed in the Messenger before his mission; thirty-two from Abyssinia who came with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib; and eight who came from Syria: Bahira, Abraha, Ashraf, Arbad, Tammam, Idris, Nafi', and Radd, or Ibn Salam, and Tamim al-Dari, and al-Jarud al-Abdi, and Salman, seven sayings, the last of which is that of Qatadah. The apparent meaning is that these are examples of those among them who believed. The pronoun in ﴿به﴾ (bihi) refers to the Word, which is the Qur'an. Al-Farra' said: it refers to the Messenger. He also said: if it refers to the Qur'an, that is correct, because they have said, "Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord." End of quotation.

﴿إنه الحق من ربنا﴾ (Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord) is a reason given for believing in it, because its being a truth from God makes it fitting that we believe in it.

﴿إنا كنا من قبله مسلمين﴾ (Indeed, we were Muslims before it) is an explanation of their saying ﴿آمنا به﴾ (We believe in it), meaning: our belief in it is ancient, since the earlier forefathers of our fathers read what is in the first Book and informed their sons of it. So we were Muslims before its revelation and its recitation to us. Islam is the attribute of every monotheist who affirms the revelation. The giving of the reward twice is because he believed in his own Book and in the Qur'an. This was explained by their patience, that is, in bearing the obligations of the earlier Law which they had, and this Law, and what they suffered of harm. In a hadith: "Three people will be given their reward twice by God: a man from the People of the Book who believed in his prophet and believed in me..." and the hadith continues.

﴿ويدرؤون﴾ (and they repel) means they push away ﴿بالحسنة﴾ (with the good deed), which is obedience, ﴿السيئة﴾ (the evil deed), which is the disobedience that came before, or with forbearance the harm; and that is among the noble characteristics. Ibn Mas'ud said: they repel shirk by the testimony that there is no god but God. Ibn Jubayr said: they repel the wrong with the right. Ibn Zayd said: they repel evil with good. Ibn Salam said: they repel ignorance with knowledge, and anger by restraining it. In the instruction of the Messenger ﷺ to Mu'adh: "Follow the evil deed with a good deed, and it will erase it, and treat people with good character." And ﴿اللغو﴾ (al-laghw, idle talk) is worthless speech. Mujahid said: it is harm and insult. al-Dahhak said: it is shirk. Ibn Zayd said: it is what the Jews changed of the description of the Messenger; a group of them heard it, disliked it, and turned away.

﴿ولكم أعمالكم﴾ (and for you are your deeds) is addressed to the speaker of the idle talk, which is understood from His saying ﴿وإذا سمعوا اللغو أعرضوا عنه﴾ (And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it).

﴿سلام عليكم﴾ (Peace be upon you): al-Zajjaj said: it is a peace of parting, not a greeting of salutation.

﴿لا نبتغي الجاهلين﴾ (We do not seek out the ignorant) means: we do not seek their company.

﴿إنك لا تهدي من أحببت﴾ (Indeed, you do not guide whom you love) means: you are not able to create guidance in him. There is no contradiction between this and His saying ﴿وإنك لتهدي إلى صراط مستقيم﴾ (And indeed, you guide to a straight path) [al-Shura: 52], because the meaning of that is: you guide, i.e., you show the way. The Muslims have agreed that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Talib, and his conversation with the Messenger of God ﷺ at the time of his death is well known. Al-Zamakhshari said: you cannot cause everyone you love to enter Islam, because you do not know who is sealed upon his heart apart from others; but God causes to enter Islam whom He wills, and He is the one who knows that he is not sealed upon his heart, and that the divine favors (lutf) benefit him, so His favors draw him near until they call him to acceptance. End of quotation.

﴿وهو أعلم بالمهتدين﴾ (and He knows best those who are guided) means: those who accept among those who do not accept. End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilites (ilitizal, the Mu'tazilite school) regarding the matter of the divine favors.

They said: the pronoun in ﴿وقالوا﴾ (and they said) refers to the Quraysh. It was said that the speaker was al-Harith ibn Uthman ibn Nawfal ibn Abd Manaf: "You are upon the truth, but we fear that if we follow you and oppose the Arabs, we will be snatched away." So this is what is meant, and we are only a few people, a small number, likely to be snatched away from our land.

Their saying ﴿الهدى معك﴾ (the guidance is with you) means: according to your claim. So God cut off their argument, since they were disbelievers in God, worshippers of idols, who had been made secure in their sanctuary while people outside it were fighting one another; they dwelt in a land without crops, to which the food they needed was brought. So how much more so once they believed and were guided? He, exalted is He, prepares the land for them and gives them dominion over the land, as He promised them, and what He promised came to pass. The description of the sanctuary as secure is metaphorical, since those who are secure in it are its inhabitants. ﴿ثمرات كل شيء﴾ (the fruits of everything) is a general term with a specific sense, meant to indicate abundance. Al-Minqari read ﴿يُتخطَّف﴾ (yutakhattaf) with a raised fa' (damma), like His saying ﴿أينما تكونوا يدرككم﴾ (Wherever you are, death will overtake you) [al-Nisa: 78], with the raised kaf (damma), meaning: then it overtakes you, i.e., then He overtakes you. And His saying ﴿من يفعل الحسنات الله يشكرها﴾ (Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them): meaning "then it is snatched," and "then God rewards them." This is an anomalous reading. Nafi' and a group from Ya'qub, and Abu Hatim from Asim, read ﴿تُجبى﴾ (tujba) with the feminine ta'; the rest read it with the ya'. The majority read ﴿ثمرات﴾ (thamarat) with two fatahs; Aban ibn Taghlib read it with two dammas; and some read it with a fatha on the tha' and sukun on the mim.

﴿رزقًا﴾ (rizqan, as provision) is in the accusative as a verbal noun from the meaning: because His saying ﴿يُجبى إليه ثمرات﴾ (to which the fruits are brought) means "with the provision of fruits." Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the subject of the causal verb is omitted, meaning: We drive to it the fruits of everything. And even if rizq is not a verbal noun but means "the thing provided," it can be accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from thamarat, and the specification is made acceptable by the annexation.

﴿أكثرهم لا يعلمون﴾ (But most of them do not know) means: they are ignorant that this provision is from Us.

The majority read ﴿ثمرات﴾ (thamarat) with two fatahs; Aban ibn Taghlib read it with two dammas; and some read it with a fatha on the tha' and sukun on the mim.

﴿رزقًا﴾ (rizqan, as provision) is in the accusative as a verbal noun from the meaning: because His saying ﴿يُجبى إليه ثمرات﴾ (to which the fruits are brought) means "with the provision of fruits." Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the subject of the causal verb is omitted, meaning: We drive to it the fruits of everything. And even if rizq is not a verbal noun but means "the thing provided," it can be accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from thamarat, and the specification is made acceptable by the annexation.

﴿أكثرهم لا يعلمون﴾ (But most of them do not know) means: they are ignorant that this provision is from Us.

This is a warning to the people of Makkah about the evil end of a people who were in a similar condition, enjoying God's favour through resting in the shade of security and ease of life. They were ungrateful for the blessing and met it with insolence and exultation, so God destroyed them and ruined their dwellings. ﴿Ma'ishatahā﴾ (its livelihood) is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification) according to the school of the Kufans, or is like the object (*mushabbah bil-maf'ul*) according to some of them. Or it may be an adverbial accusative of time (*zarf*), with the sense of "the days of its livelihood," as in your saying, "I came at the time of the setting of the star," according to al-Zajjaj.

﴿Fa-tilka masākinuhum﴾ (So those are their dwellings): he points to them, meaning you see them as ruins, passing by them as one passes the rock-dwellings of Thamud. They perished and were annihilated, and the dwellings have already been mentioned. As for ﴿tuskan﴾ (inhabited), it is possible that the exception in His words ﴿illā qalīlan﴾ (except a little) refers to the dwellings, meaning: except for a little of them that were inhabited. It is also possible that it refers to the verbal noun implied by "lam tuskan" (was not inhabited), meaning: except for a little habitation, that is, none dwelt in them except the traveller and the passer-by on the road.

﴿Wa-kunnā naḥnu al-wārithīn﴾ (And We were the inheritors): that is, of those dwellings and others, as in His words, ﴿Indā naḥnu narithu al-arḍ﴾ (Indeed We are the inheritors of the earth) [Maryam: 40]. They were emptied of their inhabitants and so fell into ruin.

A poet said:
*The traces are left behind by their owners for a time, and then annihilation overtakes them and they follow after.*

The apparent meaning is that ﴿al-qurā﴾ (the towns) is general, referring to the towns that were destroyed. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, does not destroy them at every time. ﴿Ḥattā yabʿatha fī ummi-hā﴾ (until He sends into their mother): that is, the chief of them, to which those towns return and from which they obtain provisions, and in which is their great one who rules over those towns.

﴿Ḥattā yabʿatha fī ummi-hā rasūlan﴾ (until He sends in its mother a messenger) is for establishing the proof and cutting off excuses. It is possible that by the towns is meant the towns of the Messenger's age, so that the mother of the towns is Makkah, the Messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), the seal of the prophets, and the wrongdoing of its people is disbelief and sins.

﴿Wa-mā ūtītum min shay'in﴾ (And whatever you have been given of a thing): that is, of goodness that pleases you and in which you take pride. ﴿Fa-matā'u al-ḥayāt al-dunyā wa-zīnatuhā﴾ (is the enjoyment of the life of this world and its adornment): you enjoy it for a few days. ﴿Wa-mā ʿinda Allāh﴾ (and what is with God) of lasting, everlasting bliss prepared for the believers ﴿khayrun﴾ (is better) than your enjoyment. ﴿Afalā ta'qilūn﴾ (Will you not then reason?) is a rebuke to them. Abu ʿAmr read *ya'qilūn* (with the letter ya), turning away from addressing them and addressing others, as if he said: look at these people and the feebleness of their minds. The majority read it with *ta'* from above, addressing them and rebuking them for having neglected reason regarding the outcome. Abu ʿAli in *al-Ḥujja* attributed this reading to Abu ʿAmr alone, while in *al-Taḥrīr wa-al-Taḥbīr* it is reported from Abu ʿAmr as between *ya'* and *ta'*. ﴿Afa-man wa'adnāhu﴾ (Is then one whom We have promised) describes the difference between the two men: one who was promised ﴿wa'dan ḥasanan﴾ (a good promise), which is the reward, and so he meets it, and one who was given enjoyment in the life of this world, and then was brought to the Fire. The apparent meaning of the verse is general, covering both the believer and the disbeliever. It has been said that it was revealed about the Messenger (ﷺ) and Abu Jahl. It has been said: about Hamzah and Abu Jahl. It has been said: about ʿAli and Abu Jahl. It has been said: about ʿAmmar and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It has also been said that it was revealed about the believer and the disbeliever in general, and the word *al-muḥḍarīn* (those brought forward) became dominant for those brought to the Fire, as in His words, ﴿La-kunta min al-muḥḍarīn﴾ (you would have been among those brought forward) [al-Saffat: 57], and ﴿Fa-kadhdhabūhu fa-innahum la-muḥḍarūn﴾ (but they denied him, so they will surely be brought forward) [al-Saffat: 127].

The *thumma* (then) in ﴿thumma huwa yawma al-qiyāmati mina al-muḥḍarīn﴾ indicates a delay in the state of being brought forward from the state of enjoyment, due to the delay of its time from that time. Ṭalḥah read *a-man wa'adnāhu* without the *fa'*.

(p-128) When he mentioned that those who enjoyed worldly pleasures would be brought to the Fire, he went on to mention some of the conditions of the Day of Resurrection, meaning: remember their condition on the day when God calls out to them. His calling to them may be through an intermediary or without one. ﴿Then He will say: "Where are My partners?"﴾ That is, according to your claim. This question is asked in a tone of reproach and rebuke. The "partners" are those they worshipped besides God, whether an angel, a jinn, a human, a star, an idol, or other things. The two objects of ﴿you claimed﴾ are omitted, the first of which is the pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun, and the sense is: "you claimed them to be partners." Since this question left them speechless, because those partners they had worshipped were absent, though they themselves had been brought into existence in the Hereafter, they swerved from giving an answer and turned to speech that was of no use.

﴿Those against whom the Word has been justified will say﴾ That is, the devils and the leaders and heads of disbelief. "Haqqa" means the Word was obligated against them, that is, its requirement, which is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together﴾ (Hud 11:119). "Hā'ulā'" is the subject (mubtada'), "alladhīna aghwaynā" is the attribute (sifah) of it, and "aghwaynāhum kamā ghawaynā" is the predicate (khabar). "Kamā ghawaynā" is an attribute of the verb that corresponds to "aghwaynāhum," meaning: "so they went astray just as we went astray," that is, we were the cause of their going astray, and they accepted it from us. This parsing was stated by al-Zamakhshari. Abu 'Ali said: this way is not permissible, because the predicate contains no addition beyond what is in the attribute of the subject. He said: "If you say: it has been connected with His saying 'kamā ghawaynā,' and there is an addition in it," it is answered that an adverbial complement (ẓarf) added does not make it a fundamental part of the sentence, because adverbial complements are relative clauses. The clauses that follow this have already been discussed. Praise in the Hereafter is their saying: ﴿Praise be to God, who has removed from us all grief﴾ (Fatir 35:34), ﴿Praise be to God, who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾ (al-Zumar 39:74), ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ (al-Zumar 39:75). Praising God there is for pleasure, not for obligation. A ḥadīth says: "They will be inspired to glorify and sanctify (God)." Ibn Muhaysin read "mā tukinnu," with a fatha on the tā' and a ḍamma on the kāf.

﴿And to Him belongs the judgment﴾ That is, the judgment among His servants and the decisive decision. "Ara'aytum" means "tell me," and it may be made to govern the night, "ara'aytum" and "ja'ala" both demanding it, so the second is made to operate. The second "ara'aytum" clause is the interrogative clause, and the pronoun referring back to the night is omitted; its estimate: "who is a god other than God who brings you light after it?" In the chapter of disputing governing verbs (tanāzuʿ), it is not required that the two competing verbs be equal in their mode of transitivity in every respect; rather the demand may differ, so this one demands it as subject, that one as object, another as object, and another as adverbial complement. Likewise, "ara'aytum" has as its second object an interrogative clause, usually, and the second object of "ja'ala" if it means "made" (ṣayyara) cannot be an interrogative; if it means "created" or "brought into existence," and what follows its object is in the accusative, then that accusative is a circumstantial (ḥāl). ﴿Sarmadan﴾ is said to derive from "sarmad," so its mīm is extra, and its pattern is "fa'lal." The extra letter is not added in the middle or at the end by analogy; these are words preserved as they are mentioned in the science of morphology. He used ﴿light﴾, which is the sunlight, and did not use the phrase with "daytime" in which they engage in activities, as He used ﴿at night in which you rest﴾, because the benefits of light are abundant and not limited to livelihood alone, whereas darkness is not in that rank; for this reason it was paired with light.

﴿Will you not hear?﴾ Because hearing perceives what sight perceives, through mention of its benefits and description of its advantages, and it was paired with the night.

﴿Will you not see?﴾ Because someone other than you sees, from the benefit of the darkness, what you see from the stillness and the like, said al-Zamakhshari. And "from His mercy" (min rahmatihi) here indicates cause, meaning: and because of His mercy toward you, ﴿He made for you the night and the day﴾. Then he gave the reason for the making of each of them. He began with the reason for the first, which is the night, and it is: ﴿that you may rest therein﴾. Then (he gave) the reason for the second, which is: "and that you may seek of His bounty." Then (he gave) what resembles a reason for the making of these two things, which is: ﴿and that you may seek of His bounty﴾. Then (he gave) what resembles a reason for the making of these two things, which is: "so that you may give thanks" (la'allakum tashkurun), meaning, for this mercy and blessing.

This type of the science of rhetorical embellishment (ʿilm al-badīʿ) is called al-tafsir (a device in which one mentions several things and then explains each of them with what suits it). From it is the saying of Ibn Juyush:

*A man in a muqarṭaq (robe) delights the boon companion with his face,*
*instead of his full cup and his ewer.*

*The effect of the wine, its color and its taste,*
*are in his two eyes, his two cheeks and his saliva.*

The pronoun in "fihi" (in it) refers to the night. As for "fadlihi" (His bounty), it may refer to Allah, and the implied meaning is: "from His bounty," i.e., from the bounty of Allah in it, i.e., in the day. It was omitted because the meaning indicates it, and because of the earlier word "fihi" (in it). It is also possible that it refers to the day, meaning: from the bounty of the day. He attributed it to the pronoun of the day in a metaphorical sense, since the bounty is present in it, so it was attributed to it, as in His saying: ﴿Rather, it is the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba: 33].

(p-131) **[Verse 74]** ﴿On the Day He calls to them, He will say, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿And We will draw forth from every nation a witness, and We will say, "Bring your proof." Then they will know that the truth belongs to God, and what they used to fabricate will vanish from them.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa, but he oppressed them. We had given him treasures whose keys would weigh heavily upon a band of strong men, when his people said to him, "Do not exult. Indeed, God does not love the exultant."﴾ ﴿But seek, through what God has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world. Do good as God has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the land. Indeed, God does not love the corrupters."﴾ ﴿He said, "I was given it only on account of knowledge I possess." Did he not know that God had destroyed before him generations that were greater than him in strength and more abundant in wealth? The guilty will not be asked about their sins.﴾ ﴿So he went out before his people in his adornment. Those who desired the life of this world said, "Would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given. Indeed, he is possessed of great fortune."﴾ ﴿But those who had been given knowledge said, "Woe to you! The reward of God is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds, and it is granted only to the steadfast."﴾ ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. He had no group to help him against God, nor was he one of those who could defend himself.﴾ ﴿And by the morning, those who had coveted his position said, "Woe! It seems that God widens provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts it. Had God not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. Woe! It seems the disbelievers will not prosper."﴾.

The discussion of His saying: (Wa-yawma yunadihim) has already been addressed, and it is repeated here for emphasis and reinforcement. (Wa-naza'na) means: We separated and brought forth swiftly from every nation of the nations. (Shahidan), meaning the prophet of that nation, because he is the witness over it, as He said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness over these people?﴾ [An-Nisa': 41]. It is also said: (shahidan) means just and choice persons. According to this view, (al-shahid) is a generic noun (ism al-jins), and the witness testifies against that nation regarding what proceeded from it and how it responded when it was called to monotheism, and that its prophet had conveyed to them the message of their Lord. (Fa-qulna), meaning to the assembly: ﴿Bring your proof﴾, meaning your argument concerning what you were upon in the world of disbelief and opposition to this witness. ﴿Then they will know that the truth belongs to God﴾, not to their idols, nor to what they worshipped besides God. (Wa-dalla 'anhum), meaning: it vanished from them with the absence of a lost thing. ﴿What they used to fabricate﴾ of falsehood and vanity.

Qarun is non-Arabic (a'jami): it is not declined because of foreignness and being a proper name. It is also said that the meaning of "was of his people" is: he was among those who believed in him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He was an Israelite by consensus." End of quote. There has been disagreement about his kinship to Musa, peace be upon him, a disagreement that is confused and contradictory. The most plausible view is what Ibn 'Abbas said: that he was the son of Musa's paternal uncle, namely Qarun ibn Yashhur ibn Qahith, the grandfather of Musa, because genealogists recorded his lineage thus. He was called "al-Munawwar" because of the beauty of his appearance, and he was the most learned of the Children of Israel in the Torah and the best at reciting it. Then he became a hypocrite, just as the Samiri did.

﴿So he oppressed them﴾: they mentioned among the forms of his oppression: disbelief, arrogance, his envy of Musa regarding prophethood, and of Harun regarding the sacrificial offering and the sacrifice, his oppression of the Children of Israel when Pharaoh made him their ruler, and his scheming to bring a prostitute who would falsely accuse Musa of approaching her, thereby exposing him before an assembly of the Children of Israel. And among his arrogance was that he lengthened his garments by a span.

﴿We had given him treasures﴾: it is said that God caused him to find a treasure from the treasures of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It is also said that his wealth was called treasures because he withheld the payment of zakat, and because of this he became hostile to Musa, peace be upon him, at the very beginning of his enmity. The word (ma) is a relative pronoun whose relative clause is "inna" and its operands. Al-Nahhas said: "I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman, meaning al-Akhfash al-Saghir, say: 'How ugly is what the Kufans say about relative clauses, that the relative clause of (alladhi) cannot be "inna" and what it governs (p-132) within it, and in the Qur'an there is: ﴿what indeed its keys﴾.'" End of quote. The discussion of (mafatih) has already been addressed in Surat al-An'am. Here they said: it means the keys (maqalid) of his treasuries. Al-Suddi said: it means the treasuries themselves. Al-Dahhak said: its containers and receptacles. Al-A'mash read (mafatihahu) with a yāʾ, plural of (miftah), key. They also mentioned, concerning the great number of his keys, things that are false or close to falsehood, so I have not written them down. Abu Zayd said: "Nu'tu bil-'amal" means when you rise up with the work. The poet said:

*When we find a successor, a wretched successor, a servant who, when burdened with the load, gives way.*

He says: (na'a yanu'u) means he rose up under a weight. The poet said:

*Its hindquarters strain, so its standing is slow, and it walks at ease, yet soon it is breathless.*

Abu 'Ubayda said: it is inverted (maqlub), and its original form is: (la-tanu'u biha al-'usbatu), meaning, it rises up with it, the band. Inversion (al-qalb), according to our companions, belongs mainly to poetry. The correct view is that the (ba') is for transitivity (al-ta'diya), meaning: it makes the band give way, just as you say "dhahabtu bihi" and "adhhabtuhu," and "ji'tu bihi" and "aja'tuhu." This is reported from al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and al-Farra', and al-Nahhas chose it. Its meaning is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih, and al-Suddi. The Arabs say: "na'a al-himlu bil-ba'ir" when it made the camel heavy. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible to attribute (tanu'u) to the keys, because they rise with difficulty when the one who lifts them strains, and this is common in "na'a al-himlu bil-ba'ir" and similar expressions, so consider it. Budayl ibn Maysara read (la-yanu'u) with a yāʾ and masculine form, taking into account the omitted noun in the construction: the estimated meaning is: "Indeed, the weight of its keys," or "its amount," or something like that. Al-Zamakhshari said: its explanation is that (mafatih) is interpreted as treasuries, and it is given the ruling of what it is annexed to, through association and connection, like his saying: "dhahabat ahl al-Yamama" (the people of Yamama went). End of quote. He means that the keys acquired masculine gender from the pronoun referring to Qarun, just as the word (ahl) acquired feminine gender from its annexation to Yamama, so it was said: "dhahabat." Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that Budayl ibn Maysara read: "ma inna miftahahu" in the singular, so his reading (la-yanu'u) with a yāʾ does not require interpretation. The explanation of (al-'usbah) has already been given in Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him. And before the explanation of (al-mafatih) it was mentioned whether they are the keys, or the treasuries themselves, or the containers and receptacles. And from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan: the keys are wealth.

Ibn 'Abbas said: his treasuries were carried by forty strong men, and they were four hundred thousand, each man carrying ten thousand. Abu Muslim said: what is meant by the keys is knowledge and comprehension, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿With Him are the keys of the Unseen﴾ [Al-An'am: 59]. The meaning is: We gave him treasures whose preservation and knowledge of them would indeed burden a band, meaning these treasures, because of their abundance and the variety of their kinds, would exhaust those who are in charge of guarding them.

﴿When his people said to him, "Do not exult"﴾: they forbade him from the arrogant exultation, which is absorption, dissolution of the soul, insolence, and self-admiration. Only one who is at peace with the world and heedless of the matter of the Hereafter rejoices in the world's turning toward him, whereas one who considers himself about to part soon from the blossom of this world does not rejoice in it. Abu al-Tayyib said:

*The greatest grief to me, in joy, is one whose possessor is sure of departing from it.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: the position of (idh) is in the accusative, governed by (tanu'u). End of quote. This is very weak, because the weighing down of the band by the keys is not restricted to the time of his people's saying to him, "Do not exult." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is related to His saying: ﴿so he oppressed them﴾, and this is also weak, because his oppression of them was not restricted to that time. Al-Hawfi said: its governing verb is omitted, its estimate being: "Remember." Abu al-Baqa' said: "(idh qala lahu)" is an adverbial complement for "atayna-hu," and this is also weak, because the giving did not occur at the time of that saying. He also said: it is permissible that it be an adverbial complement for an omitted verb indicated by the context, meaning: he oppressed them ﴿when his people said to him﴾. End of quote. It seems that the estimate should be: he then displayed boasting and exultation over what he had been given of treasures ﴿when his people said to him, "Do not exult."﴾ And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not exult in what He has given you﴾ [Al-Hadid: 23], and the Arabs praise the abandonment of exultation when good comes. The poet said:

*I am not one who exults when fortune delights me, nor one who frets over its changing turns.*

Another said:

*If we meet a man who is generous, let us not be counted among those who rejoice in good, nor stumble from harm.*

It was also read: (al-farihin), with the active participle, reported by 'Isa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi. And (la yuhibbu) is a description of action, not a description of essence, meaning in the sense of will, because exultation is a matter that has already occurred. So the meaning is: He does not show His blessing upon them, nor does His mercy encompass them. And when they forbade him from insolent exultation, they commanded him to seek, in what God had given him of treasures and abundance of provision, the reward of the Hereafter, by doing acts of righteousness and making it provision for you toward the Hereafter.

﴿And do not forget your share of this world.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: its meaning is: do not waste your life by not doing righteous deeds in your world, since the Hereafter is only worked for in this world, so a person's share is his life and his righteous deeds in it. This interpretation contains admonition. Al-Hasan and Qatada said its meaning is: do not waste your portion of this world by enjoying the lawful and seeking it, meaning, by looking to the consequences of your worldly life. In this interpretation there is some gentleness. Al-Hasan also said: its meaning is: advance the surplus and hold back what you need to sustain you. Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. It was also said: they meant by his share the shroud, and this is a connected admonition, as if they said: you will leave all your wealth, and your share of it will be nothing but a shroud, as the poet said:

*Your share of all that you gather throughout the ages is two garments in which you will be lodged, and spices for embalming.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: that you take from it what suffices you and sets you right. This is close to the saying of al-Hasan. ﴿And do good﴾ to the servants of God, or through your thankfulness and obedience to God.

﴿As God has done good to you﴾ with those blessings with which He has entrusted you. The particle (ka) is for comparison, and it may apply to some attributes, because the resemblance of a servant's goodness to God's goodness in all attributes is impossible. So the comparison falls upon the absolute notion of goodness. Or (ka) may be for causation, meaning: do good for the sake of God's goodness to you.

﴿And do not seek corruption﴾, meaning: what you are upon of insolence and wrongdoing. (ʿalā ʿilm), where (ʿilm) is a verbal noun, may be read as annexed to what follows and as annexed to God. The majority said: he claimed that he possessed a knowledge that entitled him to be the owner of those treasures. It was said: the knowledge of the Torah and its memorization, and he was one of the seventy whom Musa chose for the appointed time, and this was a deception. Abu Sulayman al-Dani said: that is the knowledge of trade and the ways of gain, meaning: I was given it through my own understanding and effort. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the knowledge of alchemy (al-kimiya'), and Ibn al-Musayyab said: Musa, peace be upon him, knew alchemy, which is the transformation of lead and copper into gold. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "upon knowledge of making gold," but this is probably not authentically reported from him or from Ibn al-Musayyab. Al-Zajjaj denied the knowledge of alchemy and said: it is false and has no reality. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verse 74–82 (part 2 of 2):

The people of Egypt have often been fond of seeking things that are impossible and superstitious. Among these: drawing water underground (taghwir al-ma'), serving images depicted as lines on walls, and their claim that those lines move when they are served with various kinds of services for them and with alchemy (al-kimya'). Even their shaykhs of knowledge, who among them hold the appearance of sainthood (al-wilaya), demand this from the most ignorant of the newcomers from the Maghrib. Ibn Zayd and others said: he meant "I have been given it on knowledge" (﴿أوتيته على علم﴾) from God and a special grant from Him intended for me, that is, nothing of what you say binds me in it. Then he made his saying "with me" (ʿindi) like one who says: "in my belief and in what I see." Mujahid said: "on knowledge" means "on a good that God knew to be with me." The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Did he not know﴾ is an affirmation of his knowledge of that and a warning of his error in his self-deception, that is: he knew that God had destroyed before him generations who were stronger than him and richer, because he had read it in the Torah, and Moses informed him of it, and he heard it in the histories. As if it were said: did he not know, among what he has of knowledge? This is so that he not be deceived by the abundance of his wealth and his strength. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it be a description of his knowledge of that, because when he said ﴿I have been given it on knowledge with me﴾ he became puffed up with knowledge and magnified himself by it, it was said: does he have with him the like of that knowledge which he claims? He saw himself as deserving of every blessing, and he did not know this beneficial knowledge so as to protect himself from the fate of the ruined. End.

﴿And more abundant in number﴾ either refers to wealth, or to a group who surround and serve him. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: ﴿Did he not know﴾ with the preponderance that (p-134) Qarun had become intoxicated with knowledge of himself according to his own claim.

The majority read (wa-la yus'alu) in the passive voice, with al-mujrimun (the criminals) as its subject, and it is connected to what precedes it, as Muhammad ibn Ka'b said. The pronoun in (dhunubihim) refers to those of the generations who were destroyed, that is: those other than them of the guilty are not questioned, nor are those who did not commit crime questioned about those whom God destroyed; rather ﴿every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38]. It was also said: those of the generations whom He destroyed, He knew their sins, so He had no need to question them about them. It was also said: it is a new statement about the situation on the Day of Resurrection. Qatada said: they are not asked about their sins because they are manifest and numerous, for they enter the Fire without reckoning. Qatada and Mujahid also said: the angels do not ask them about their sins, because they recognize them by their marks of blackness and disfigurement, as in His saying: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. It was also said: they are not asked with a question of rebuke and reproach. Abu Ja'far, in one transmission, read: "wa-la tas'al" with the ta' and jazm, and "al-mujrimin" in the accusative. Ibn Sirin and Abu al-ʿAliya read likewise "wa-la tas'al" as a prohibition addressed to the one addressed, and Ibn Abi Ishaq did not permit this unless "al-mujrimin" with the ya' is in the accusative position, the verb falling upon it. The author of al-Lawami' said: the apparent is what he said, and I have not received anything about the accusative of al-mujrimin. If they left it in its nominative, it has two aspects: the first: that the ha' and mim in ﴿ʿan dhunubihim﴾ refer to what preceded of the generations, and the nominative of "al-mujrimin" is by an implied subject, its estimate being: "they are the criminals," or "those are the criminals," and similar to it ﴿the repenting, the worshipping﴾ [al-Tawba: 112] in al-Tawba. The second: that it be a substitute for the original ha' and mim in (dhunubihim), for they, though in the genitive position by the annexation to them, their origin is the nominative, because the annexation to them is in the position of the annexation of the verbal noun to the active participle; so on that basis "al-mujrimun" is carried to the original, as we have previously mentioned that some of them read: ﴿that He should strike an example, a gnat﴾ [al-Baqara: 26] in the genitive, on the basis that it is a substitute for the original of "example," and "ma" is superfluous in it, its estimate being: "he is not ashamed to strike an example of a gnat," that is: to strike a gnat. Regarding this, it was explained that with the separation by the verbal noun, the governor reaches the object, then the gnat was substituted from it without my knowing any trace of a state in it. As for his saying "dhunub," it is a plural; if it is the plural of a verbal noun, there is a disagreement about its governing. As for his saying "as we have previously mentioned that some of them read," he mentioned in al-Baqara that he heard that, and we do not know any trace in it, so he should not make it a recitation.

When He mentioned Qarun, his description, what He gave him of treasures, and his exultation in that, the exultation of the exultant, and his claim that what he was given of that he was given on knowledge, He mentioned what arises from arrogance and joy in what he was given, and so He said: ﴿So he went out to his people in his adornment﴾, and it was a Saturday; that is: he displayed the most that he was able to of clothing, mounts, and the adornment of the world. Jabir and Mujahid said: in red garments. Ibn Zayd said: he and his retinue were in saffron-dyed garments. It was said: in garments of purple. It was said: on a white mule over which was purple, and over it a saddle of gold, and with him four thousand on his style. It was said: upon them and upon their horses was red brocade, and on his right were three hundred boys, and on his left three hundred white maidens upon whom were jewelry and brocade. It was said: in ninety thousand, upon them the saffron garments, and it was the first day in which saffron was seen. Other modes were said.

﴿Those who desired the life of this world said﴾: it was said: they were believers. Qatada said: they wished for it in order to draw near to God by it. It was said: out of desire for ease and wealth. It was said: they were disbelievers, and they wished ﴿the like of what Qarun was given﴾ and did not mention the end of his blessing, and this is from envy (al-ghibta).

﴿Indeed he is of great fortune﴾, that is: a great rank, said by al-Dahhak. It was said: a great portion of the world. The ḥaẓẓ (fortune) is luck and good fortune; it is said: "So-and-so is of fortune, lucky, and fortunate."

﴿And those who were given knowledge said﴾ among them: Yusha ʿ. Knowledge: the knowing of reward and punishment, or trust in God, or reporting, are sayings. (Woe to you) is a supplication with evil.

﴿The reward of God﴾, which is what He has prepared in the Hereafter for the believer, is ﴿better﴾ than what Qarun was given.

﴿And none receives it﴾, that is: this wisdom, which is the knowing of God's reward. It was said: Paradise and its bliss. It was said: this statement, which is their saying: ﴿The reward of God is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds﴾, with which He rebuked them.

﴿Except the patient﴾ in obedience and in restraining their souls from desires.

A portion of the account of Qarun and his envy of Moses has preceded (p-135). Among his envy was that he set a reward for a prostitute, on condition that she accuse Moses of seeking her and of fornication, and that she repented to God and confessed that Qarun was the one who had set for her a reward to accuse Moses of that. So God commanded the earth to obey him, and He said: "O earth, seize him and his followers," and they were swallowed up, in a long narrative of which God knows best.
