When Qarun and those with him were swallowed up, the Children of Israel said: Moses only prayed against Qarun so that he might seize his house and treasures, so he called upon God until He swallowed up his house and his wealth. And ﴿min﴾ is superfluous, that is: from a group which conveys the comprehensiveness of the categories. And when the sentence is negated and he was not able to help him, the negation of the one from his support is more emphatic.

﴿And he was not of those who were given victory﴾, that is: he was not, in himself, of those who could defend against the punishment of God.

﴿And those who had wished for his place yesterday morning﴾ is a substitute; and "asbaḥa" (became), if it is taken in its apparent sense, means that the swallowing up of him and his house was at night, and that is the most frightful of punishments, since night is the place of rest and tranquility. And "al-ams" (yesterday) may be intended as past time, and it may be intended as what was before the day of the swallowing, which is the day of wishing, and this is indicated by the conjunction with "fa" which implies sequence in His saying: ﴿So We caused to sink﴾; so the punishment followed his going out in his adornment, and in that is the hastening of punishment. "Makanahu" means his rank in the world, in wealth, retinue, and followers. "Wayka" according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh is a verb-name like "ṣah" and "mah," and its meaning is: "I am amazed." Al-Khalil said: that is because the people regretted and said, regretting what had passed from them: "wayka," and everyone who regrets and shows his regret says "wayka." "Ka'anna" is the particle of comparison entering upon "anna," and it was written joined to the comparison particle because of frequent use. Sibawayh recited:

"Wayka, as if he who has wealth is one who is given, and he who is poor lives the life of hardship."

The verse belongs to Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl. Al-Farra' related that a woman said to her husband: "Where is your son?" He said: "Wayka'annahu behind the house," and according to this view, the pause is on "wayka." Al-Akhfash said: it is "waykaʾ," and the kaf should be a particle of address, without any place in the grammar, and its pause is "wayk," and from it is the saying of ʿAntara:

"And indeed he has healed my soul and cured its sickness: the cry of the horsemen, 'Waykа, ʿAntar, advance!'"

Al-Akhfash said: "anna" after it is open by the estimate of knowledge, that is: "I know that God..." And the poet said:

"Alas, waykа, the harm does not last, and bliss does not leave misery."

Al-Kisa'i, Yunus, Abu Hatim and others held that its origin is "waylaka," so the lam and the kaf were deleted in a place of genitive by annexation. So according to the first view, it was said the kaf is free of the meaning of comparison, as it was said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. According to the second view, the meaning is: "I am amazed, because God..." And according to the third view, "waylaka" is an expression of grief, and the meaning likewise: "because God..." Abu Zayd and a group with him said: "wayka'anna" is one particle in its entirety, and it means: "Have you not seen?" Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Kisa'i and Abu ʿUbayd said with the meaning: "Have you not seen?" al-Farra' said: "wayka" in the speech of the Arabs is like the saying of a man: "Do you not see the handiwork of God?" Ibn Qutayba related from some scholars that he said: the meaning of "wayka" is: "mercy upon you," in the dialect of Himyar.

When there issued from them the wish for Qarun's condition, and they witnessed the swallowing up, that was a restraint for them from love of the world, and a summons to contentment with God's decree, so they awakened to their error and said: "Wayka," then they said: ﴿Indeed God extends provision to whom He wills of His servants﴾ according to His will and wisdom, not because of honor with Him, and He restricts it for whom He wills, not because of contempt, but for His wisdom and decree as a trial. Al-A'mash read: "lawla man Allahu" with the omission of "an," and it is superfluous. It is related from him: "manna Allahi" with the nun raised and the annexation. The majority read: "la-khusifa" in the passive voice. Hafs, ʿIsma, Aban from ʿAsim, and Ibn Abi Hammad from Abu Bakr: in the active voice. Ibn Mas'ud, Talha, and al-A'mash: "la-nkhasafa bina," as in your saying "inqata'a bina," as if it were a reflexive verb, and the position of the doer is held by "bina." It is permissible that it be the verbal noun, that is: "the sinking sank," and the reflexive of "fa'ala" is not transitive to a direct object, so for that reason it was built (p-136) either for the building or for the verbal noun. And also from Ibn Mas'ud: "latukhussifa," with a ta' and a doubled sin, in the passive voice.

(p-131) **[Verse 74]** ﴿On the Day He calls to them, He will say, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿And We will draw forth from every nation a witness, and We will say, "Bring your proof." Then they will know that the truth belongs to God, and what they used to fabricate will vanish from them.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa, but he oppressed them. We had given him treasures whose keys would weigh heavily upon a band of strong men, when his people said to him, "Do not exult. Indeed, God does not love the exultant."﴾ ﴿But seek, through what God has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world. Do good as God has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the land. Indeed, God does not love the corrupters."﴾ ﴿He said, "I was given it only on account of knowledge I possess." Did he not know that God had destroyed before him generations that were greater than him in strength and more abundant in wealth? The guilty will not be asked about their sins.﴾ ﴿So he went out before his people in his adornment. Those who desired the life of this world said, "Would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given. Indeed, he is possessed of great fortune."﴾ ﴿But those who had been given knowledge said, "Woe to you! The reward of God is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds, and it is granted only to the steadfast."﴾ ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. He had no group to help him against God, nor was he one of those who could defend himself.﴾ ﴿And by the morning, those who had coveted his position said, "Woe! It seems that God widens provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts it. Had God not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. Woe! It seems the disbelievers will not prosper."﴾.

The discussion of His saying: (Wa-yawma yunadihim) has already been addressed, and it is repeated here for emphasis and reinforcement. (Wa-naza'na) means: We separated and brought forth swiftly from every nation of the nations. (Shahidan), meaning the prophet of that nation, because he is the witness over it, as He said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness over these people?﴾ [An-Nisa': 41]. It is also said: (shahidan) means just and choice persons. According to this view, (al-shahid) is a generic noun (ism al-jins), and the witness testifies against that nation regarding what proceeded from it and how it responded when it was called to monotheism, and that its prophet had conveyed to them the message of their Lord. (Fa-qulna), meaning to the assembly: ﴿Bring your proof﴾, meaning your argument concerning what you were upon in the world of disbelief and opposition to this witness. ﴿Then they will know that the truth belongs to God﴾, not to their idols, nor to what they worshipped besides God. (Wa-dalla 'anhum), meaning: it vanished from them with the absence of a lost thing. ﴿What they used to fabricate﴾ of falsehood and vanity.

Qarun is non-Arabic (a'jami): it is not declined because of foreignness and being a proper name. It is also said that the meaning of "was of his people" is: he was among those who believed in him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He was an Israelite by consensus." End of quote. There has been disagreement about his kinship to Musa, peace be upon him, a disagreement that is confused and contradictory. The most plausible view is what Ibn 'Abbas said: that he was the son of Musa's paternal uncle, namely Qarun ibn Yashhur ibn Qahith, the grandfather of Musa, because genealogists recorded his lineage thus. He was called "al-Munawwar" because of the beauty of his appearance, and he was the most learned of the Children of Israel in the Torah and the best at reciting it. Then he became a hypocrite, just as the Samiri did.

﴿So he oppressed them﴾: they mentioned among the forms of his oppression: disbelief, arrogance, his envy of Musa regarding prophethood, and of Harun regarding the sacrificial offering and the sacrifice, his oppression of the Children of Israel when Pharaoh made him their ruler, and his scheming to bring a prostitute who would falsely accuse Musa of approaching her, thereby exposing him before an assembly of the Children of Israel. And among his arrogance was that he lengthened his garments by a span.

﴿We had given him treasures﴾: it is said that God caused him to find a treasure from the treasures of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It is also said that his wealth was called treasures because he withheld the payment of zakat, and because of this he became hostile to Musa, peace be upon him, at the very beginning of his enmity. The word (ma) is a relative pronoun whose relative clause is "inna" and its operands. Al-Nahhas said: "I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman, meaning al-Akhfash al-Saghir, say: 'How ugly is what the Kufans say about relative clauses, that the relative clause of (alladhi) cannot be "inna" and what it governs (p-132) within it, and in the Qur'an there is: ﴿what indeed its keys﴾.'" End of quote. The discussion of (mafatih) has already been addressed in Surat al-An'am. Here they said: it means the keys (maqalid) of his treasuries. Al-Suddi said: it means the treasuries themselves. Al-Dahhak said: its containers and receptacles. Al-A'mash read (mafatihahu) with a yāʾ, plural of (miftah), key. They also mentioned, concerning the great number of his keys, things that are false or close to falsehood, so I have not written them down. Abu Zayd said: "Nu'tu bil-'amal" means when you rise up with the work. The poet said:

*When we find a successor, a wretched successor, a servant who, when burdened with the load, gives way.*

He says: (na'a yanu'u) means he rose up under a weight. The poet said:

*Its hindquarters strain, so its standing is slow, and it walks at ease, yet soon it is breathless.*

Abu 'Ubayda said: it is inverted (maqlub), and its original form is: (la-tanu'u biha al-'usbatu), meaning, it rises up with it, the band. Inversion (al-qalb), according to our companions, belongs mainly to poetry. The correct view is that the (ba') is for transitivity (al-ta'diya), meaning: it makes the band give way, just as you say "dhahabtu bihi" and "adhhabtuhu," and "ji'tu bihi" and "aja'tuhu." This is reported from al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and al-Farra', and al-Nahhas chose it. Its meaning is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih, and al-Suddi. The Arabs say: "na'a al-himlu bil-ba'ir" when it made the camel heavy. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible to attribute (tanu'u) to the keys, because they rise with difficulty when the one who lifts them strains, and this is common in "na'a al-himlu bil-ba'ir" and similar expressions, so consider it. Budayl ibn Maysara read (la-yanu'u) with a yāʾ and masculine form, taking into account the omitted noun in the construction: the estimated meaning is: "Indeed, the weight of its keys," or "its amount," or something like that. Al-Zamakhshari said: its explanation is that (mafatih) is interpreted as treasuries, and it is given the ruling of what it is annexed to, through association and connection, like his saying: "dhahabat ahl al-Yamama" (the people of Yamama went). End of quote. He means that the keys acquired masculine gender from the pronoun referring to Qarun, just as the word (ahl) acquired feminine gender from its annexation to Yamama, so it was said: "dhahabat." Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that Budayl ibn Maysara read: "ma inna miftahahu" in the singular, so his reading (la-yanu'u) with a yāʾ does not require interpretation. The explanation of (al-'usbah) has already been given in Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him. And before the explanation of (al-mafatih) it was mentioned whether they are the keys, or the treasuries themselves, or the containers and receptacles. And from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan: the keys are wealth.

Ibn 'Abbas said: his treasuries were carried by forty strong men, and they were four hundred thousand, each man carrying ten thousand. Abu Muslim said: what is meant by the keys is knowledge and comprehension, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿With Him are the keys of the Unseen﴾ [Al-An'am: 59]. The meaning is: We gave him treasures whose preservation and knowledge of them would indeed burden a band, meaning these treasures, because of their abundance and the variety of their kinds, would exhaust those who are in charge of guarding them.

﴿When his people said to him, "Do not exult"﴾: they forbade him from the arrogant exultation, which is absorption, dissolution of the soul, insolence, and self-admiration. Only one who is at peace with the world and heedless of the matter of the Hereafter rejoices in the world's turning toward him, whereas one who considers himself about to part soon from the blossom of this world does not rejoice in it. Abu al-Tayyib said:

*The greatest grief to me, in joy, is one whose possessor is sure of departing from it.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: the position of (idh) is in the accusative, governed by (tanu'u). End of quote. This is very weak, because the weighing down of the band by the keys is not restricted to the time of his people's saying to him, "Do not exult." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is related to His saying: ﴿so he oppressed them﴾, and this is also weak, because his oppression of them was not restricted to that time. Al-Hawfi said: its governing verb is omitted, its estimate being: "Remember." Abu al-Baqa' said: "(idh qala lahu)" is an adverbial complement for "atayna-hu," and this is also weak, because the giving did not occur at the time of that saying. He also said: it is permissible that it be an adverbial complement for an omitted verb indicated by the context, meaning: he oppressed them ﴿when his people said to him﴾. End of quote. It seems that the estimate should be: he then displayed boasting and exultation over what he had been given of treasures ﴿when his people said to him, "Do not exult."﴾ And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not exult in what He has given you﴾ [Al-Hadid: 23], and the Arabs praise the abandonment of exultation when good comes. The poet said:

*I am not one who exults when fortune delights me, nor one who frets over its changing turns.*

Another said:

*If we meet a man who is generous, let us not be counted among those who rejoice in good, nor stumble from harm.*

It was also read: (al-farihin), with the active participle, reported by 'Isa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi. And (la yuhibbu) is a description of action, not a description of essence, meaning in the sense of will, because exultation is a matter that has already occurred. So the meaning is: He does not show His blessing upon them, nor does His mercy encompass them. And when they forbade him from insolent exultation, they commanded him to seek, in what God had given him of treasures and abundance of provision, the reward of the Hereafter, by doing acts of righteousness and making it provision for you toward the Hereafter.

﴿And do not forget your share of this world.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: its meaning is: do not waste your life by not doing righteous deeds in your world, since the Hereafter is only worked for in this world, so a person's share is his life and his righteous deeds in it. This interpretation contains admonition. Al-Hasan and Qatada said its meaning is: do not waste your portion of this world by enjoying the lawful and seeking it, meaning, by looking to the consequences of your worldly life. In this interpretation there is some gentleness. Al-Hasan also said: its meaning is: advance the surplus and hold back what you need to sustain you. Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. It was also said: they meant by his share the shroud, and this is a connected admonition, as if they said: you will leave all your wealth, and your share of it will be nothing but a shroud, as the poet said:

*Your share of all that you gather throughout the ages is two garments in which you will be lodged, and spices for embalming.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: that you take from it what suffices you and sets you right. This is close to the saying of al-Hasan. ﴿And do good﴾ to the servants of God, or through your thankfulness and obedience to God.

﴿As God has done good to you﴾ with those blessings with which He has entrusted you. The particle (ka) is for comparison, and it may apply to some attributes, because the resemblance of a servant's goodness to God's goodness in all attributes is impossible. So the comparison falls upon the absolute notion of goodness. Or (ka) may be for causation, meaning: do good for the sake of God's goodness to you.

﴿And do not seek corruption﴾, meaning: what you are upon of insolence and wrongdoing. (ʿalā ʿilm), where (ʿilm) is a verbal noun, may be read as annexed to what follows and as annexed to God. The majority said: he claimed that he possessed a knowledge that entitled him to be the owner of those treasures. It was said: the knowledge of the Torah and its memorization, and he was one of the seventy whom Musa chose for the appointed time, and this was a deception. Abu Sulayman al-Dani said: that is the knowledge of trade and the ways of gain, meaning: I was given it through my own understanding and effort. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the knowledge of alchemy (al-kimiya'), and Ibn al-Musayyab said: Musa, peace be upon him, knew alchemy, which is the transformation of lead and copper into gold. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "upon knowledge of making gold," but this is probably not authentically reported from him or from Ibn al-Musayyab. Al-Zajjaj denied the knowledge of alchemy and said: it is false and has no reality. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verse 74–82 (part 2 of 2):

The people of Egypt have often been fond of seeking things that are impossible and superstitious. Among these: drawing water underground (taghwir al-ma'), serving images depicted as lines on walls, and their claim that those lines move when they are served with various kinds of services for them and with alchemy (al-kimya'). Even their shaykhs of knowledge, who among them hold the appearance of sainthood (al-wilaya), demand this from the most ignorant of the newcomers from the Maghrib. Ibn Zayd and others said: he meant "I have been given it on knowledge" (﴿أوتيته على علم﴾) from God and a special grant from Him intended for me, that is, nothing of what you say binds me in it. Then he made his saying "with me" (ʿindi) like one who says: "in my belief and in what I see." Mujahid said: "on knowledge" means "on a good that God knew to be with me." The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Did he not know﴾ is an affirmation of his knowledge of that and a warning of his error in his self-deception, that is: he knew that God had destroyed before him generations who were stronger than him and richer, because he had read it in the Torah, and Moses informed him of it, and he heard it in the histories. As if it were said: did he not know, among what he has of knowledge? This is so that he not be deceived by the abundance of his wealth and his strength. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it be a description of his knowledge of that, because when he said ﴿I have been given it on knowledge with me﴾ he became puffed up with knowledge and magnified himself by it, it was said: does he have with him the like of that knowledge which he claims? He saw himself as deserving of every blessing, and he did not know this beneficial knowledge so as to protect himself from the fate of the ruined. End.

﴿And more abundant in number﴾ either refers to wealth, or to a group who surround and serve him. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: ﴿Did he not know﴾ with the preponderance that (p-134) Qarun had become intoxicated with knowledge of himself according to his own claim.

The majority read (wa-la yus'alu) in the passive voice, with al-mujrimun (the criminals) as its subject, and it is connected to what precedes it, as Muhammad ibn Ka'b said. The pronoun in (dhunubihim) refers to those of the generations who were destroyed, that is: those other than them of the guilty are not questioned, nor are those who did not commit crime questioned about those whom God destroyed; rather ﴿every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38]. It was also said: those of the generations whom He destroyed, He knew their sins, so He had no need to question them about them. It was also said: it is a new statement about the situation on the Day of Resurrection. Qatada said: they are not asked about their sins because they are manifest and numerous, for they enter the Fire without reckoning. Qatada and Mujahid also said: the angels do not ask them about their sins, because they recognize them by their marks of blackness and disfigurement, as in His saying: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. It was also said: they are not asked with a question of rebuke and reproach. Abu Ja'far, in one transmission, read: "wa-la tas'al" with the ta' and jazm, and "al-mujrimin" in the accusative. Ibn Sirin and Abu al-ʿAliya read likewise "wa-la tas'al" as a prohibition addressed to the one addressed, and Ibn Abi Ishaq did not permit this unless "al-mujrimin" with the ya' is in the accusative position, the verb falling upon it. The author of al-Lawami' said: the apparent is what he said, and I have not received anything about the accusative of al-mujrimin. If they left it in its nominative, it has two aspects: the first: that the ha' and mim in ﴿ʿan dhunubihim﴾ refer to what preceded of the generations, and the nominative of "al-mujrimin" is by an implied subject, its estimate being: "they are the criminals," or "those are the criminals," and similar to it ﴿the repenting, the worshipping﴾ [al-Tawba: 112] in al-Tawba. The second: that it be a substitute for the original ha' and mim in (dhunubihim), for they, though in the genitive position by the annexation to them, their origin is the nominative, because the annexation to them is in the position of the annexation of the verbal noun to the active participle; so on that basis "al-mujrimun" is carried to the original, as we have previously mentioned that some of them read: ﴿that He should strike an example, a gnat﴾ [al-Baqara: 26] in the genitive, on the basis that it is a substitute for the original of "example," and "ma" is superfluous in it, its estimate being: "he is not ashamed to strike an example of a gnat," that is: to strike a gnat. Regarding this, it was explained that with the separation by the verbal noun, the governor reaches the object, then the gnat was substituted from it without my knowing any trace of a state in it. As for his saying "dhunub," it is a plural; if it is the plural of a verbal noun, there is a disagreement about its governing. As for his saying "as we have previously mentioned that some of them read," he mentioned in al-Baqara that he heard that, and we do not know any trace in it, so he should not make it a recitation.

When He mentioned Qarun, his description, what He gave him of treasures, and his exultation in that, the exultation of the exultant, and his claim that what he was given of that he was given on knowledge, He mentioned what arises from arrogance and joy in what he was given, and so He said: ﴿So he went out to his people in his adornment﴾, and it was a Saturday; that is: he displayed the most that he was able to of clothing, mounts, and the adornment of the world. Jabir and Mujahid said: in red garments. Ibn Zayd said: he and his retinue were in saffron-dyed garments. It was said: in garments of purple. It was said: on a white mule over which was purple, and over it a saddle of gold, and with him four thousand on his style. It was said: upon them and upon their horses was red brocade, and on his right were three hundred boys, and on his left three hundred white maidens upon whom were jewelry and brocade. It was said: in ninety thousand, upon them the saffron garments, and it was the first day in which saffron was seen. Other modes were said.

﴿Those who desired the life of this world said﴾: it was said: they were believers. Qatada said: they wished for it in order to draw near to God by it. It was said: out of desire for ease and wealth. It was said: they were disbelievers, and they wished ﴿the like of what Qarun was given﴾ and did not mention the end of his blessing, and this is from envy (al-ghibta).

﴿Indeed he is of great fortune﴾, that is: a great rank, said by al-Dahhak. It was said: a great portion of the world. The ḥaẓẓ (fortune) is luck and good fortune; it is said: "So-and-so is of fortune, lucky, and fortunate."

﴿And those who were given knowledge said﴾ among them: Yusha ʿ. Knowledge: the knowing of reward and punishment, or trust in God, or reporting, are sayings. (Woe to you) is a supplication with evil.

﴿The reward of God﴾, which is what He has prepared in the Hereafter for the believer, is ﴿better﴾ than what Qarun was given.

﴿And none receives it﴾, that is: this wisdom, which is the knowing of God's reward. It was said: Paradise and its bliss. It was said: this statement, which is their saying: ﴿The reward of God is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds﴾, with which He rebuked them.

﴿Except the patient﴾ in obedience and in restraining their souls from desires.

A portion of the account of Qarun and his envy of Moses has preceded (p-135). Among his envy was that he set a reward for a prostitute, on condition that she accuse Moses of seeking her and of fornication, and that she repented to God and confessed that Qarun was the one who had set for her a reward to accuse Moses of that. So God commanded the earth to obey him, and He said: "O earth, seize him and his followers," and they were swallowed up, in a long narrative of which God knows best. When Qarun and those with him were swallowed up, the Children of Israel said: Moses only prayed against Qarun so that he might seize his house and treasures, so he called upon God until He swallowed up his house and his wealth. And ﴿min﴾ is superfluous, that is: from a group which conveys the comprehensiveness of the categories. And when the sentence is negated and he was not able to help him, the negation of the one from his support is more emphatic.

﴿And he was not of those who were given victory﴾, that is: he was not, in himself, of those who could defend against the punishment of God.

﴿And those who had wished for his place yesterday morning﴾ is a substitute; and "asbaḥa" (became), if it is taken in its apparent sense, means that the swallowing up of him and his house was at night, and that is the most frightful of punishments, since night is the place of rest and tranquility. And "al-ams" (yesterday) may be intended as past time, and it may be intended as what was before the day of the swallowing, which is the day of wishing, and this is indicated by the conjunction with "fa" which implies sequence in His saying: ﴿So We caused to sink﴾; so the punishment followed his going out in his adornment, and in that is the hastening of punishment. "Makanahu" means his rank in the world, in wealth, retinue, and followers. "Wayka" according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh is a verb-name like "ṣah" and "mah," and its meaning is: "I am amazed." Al-Khalil said: that is because the people regretted and said, regretting what had passed from them: "wayka," and everyone who regrets and shows his regret says "wayka." "Ka'anna" is the particle of comparison entering upon "anna," and it was written joined to the comparison particle because of frequent use. Sibawayh recited:

"Wayka, as if he who has wealth is one who is given, and he who is poor lives the life of hardship."

The verse belongs to Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl. Al-Farra' related that a woman said to her husband: "Where is your son?" He said: "Wayka'annahu behind the house," and according to this view, the pause is on "wayka." Al-Akhfash said: it is "waykaʾ," and the kaf should be a particle of address, without any place in the grammar, and its pause is "wayk," and from it is the saying of ʿAntara:

"And indeed he has healed my soul and cured its sickness: the cry of the horsemen, 'Waykа, ʿAntar, advance!'"

Al-Akhfash said: "anna" after it is open by the estimate of knowledge, that is: "I know that God..." And the poet said:

"Alas, waykа, the harm does not last, and bliss does not leave misery."

Al-Kisa'i, Yunus, Abu Hatim and others held that its origin is "waylaka," so the lam and the kaf were deleted in a place of genitive by annexation. So according to the first view, it was said the kaf is free of the meaning of comparison, as it was said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. According to the second view, the meaning is: "I am amazed, because God..." And according to the third view, "waylaka" is an expression of grief, and the meaning likewise: "because God..." Abu Zayd and a group with him said: "wayka'anna" is one particle in its entirety, and it means: "Have you not seen?" Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Kisa'i and Abu ʿUbayd said with the meaning: "Have you not seen?" al-Farra' said: "wayka" in the speech of the Arabs is like the saying of a man: "Do you not see the handiwork of God?" Ibn Qutayba related from some scholars that he said: the meaning of "wayka" is: "mercy upon you," in the dialect of Himyar.

When there issued from them the wish for Qarun's condition, and they witnessed the swallowing up, that was a restraint for them from love of the world, and a summons to contentment with God's decree, so they awakened to their error and said: "Wayka," then they said: ﴿Indeed God extends provision to whom He wills of His servants﴾ according to His will and wisdom, not because of honor with Him, and He restricts it for whom He wills, not because of contempt, but for His wisdom and decree as a trial. Al-A'mash read: "lawla man Allahu" with the omission of "an," and it is superfluous. It is related from him: "manna Allahi" with the nun raised and the annexation. The majority read: "la-khusifa" in the passive voice. Hafs, ʿIsma, Aban from ʿAsim, and Ibn Abi Hammad from Abu Bakr: in the active voice. Ibn Mas'ud, Talha, and al-A'mash: "la-nkhasafa bina," as in your saying "inqata'a bina," as if it were a reflexive verb, and the position of the doer is held by "bina." It is permissible that it be the verbal noun, that is: "the sinking sank," and the reflexive of "fa'ala" is not transitive to a direct object, so for that reason it was built (p-136) either for the building or for the verbal noun. And also from Ibn Mas'ud: "latukhussifa," with a ta' and a doubled sin, in the passive voice.

(p-131) **[Verse 74]** ﴿On the Day He calls to them, He will say, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿And We will draw forth from every nation a witness, and We will say, "Bring your proof." Then they will know that the truth belongs to God, and what they used to fabricate will vanish from them.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa, but he oppressed them. We had given him treasures whose keys would weigh heavily upon a band of strong men, when his people said to him, "Do not exult. Indeed, God does not love the exultant."﴾ ﴿But seek, through what God has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world. Do good as God has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the land. Indeed, God does not love the corrupters."﴾ ﴿He said, "I was given it only on account of knowledge I possess." Did he not know that God had destroyed before him generations that were greater than him in strength and more abundant in wealth? The guilty will not be asked about their sins.﴾ ﴿So he went out before his people in his adornment. Those who desired the life of this world said, "Would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given. Indeed, he is possessed of great fortune."﴾ ﴿But those who had been given knowledge said, "Woe to you! The reward of God is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds, and it is granted only to the steadfast."﴾ ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. He had no group to help him against God, nor was he one of those who could defend himself.﴾ ﴿And by the morning, those who had coveted his position said, "Woe! It seems that God widens provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts it. Had God not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. Woe! It seems the disbelievers will not prosper."﴾.

The discussion of His saying: (Wa-yawma yunadihim) has already been addressed, and it is repeated here for emphasis and reinforcement. (Wa-naza'na) means: We separated and brought forth swiftly from every nation of the nations. (Shahidan), meaning the prophet of that nation, because he is the witness over it, as He said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness over these people?﴾ [An-Nisa': 41]. It is also said: (shahidan) means just and choice persons. According to this view, (al-shahid) is a generic noun (ism al-jins), and the witness testifies against that nation regarding what proceeded from it and how it responded when it was called to monotheism, and that its prophet had conveyed to them the message of their Lord. (Fa-qulna), meaning to the assembly: ﴿Bring your proof﴾, meaning your argument concerning what you were upon in the world of disbelief and opposition to this witness. ﴿Then they will know that the truth belongs to God﴾, not to their idols, nor to what they worshipped besides God. (Wa-dalla 'anhum), meaning: it vanished from them with the absence of a lost thing. ﴿What they used to fabricate﴾ of falsehood and vanity.

Qarun is non-Arabic (a'jami): it is not declined because of foreignness and being a proper name. It is also said that the meaning of "was of his people" is: he was among those who believed in him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He was an Israelite by consensus." End of quote. There has been disagreement about his kinship to Musa, peace be upon him, a disagreement that is confused and contradictory. The most plausible view is what Ibn 'Abbas said: that he was the son of Musa's paternal uncle, namely Qarun ibn Yashhur ibn Qahith, the grandfather of Musa, because genealogists recorded his lineage thus. He was called "al-Munawwar" because of the beauty of his appearance, and he was the most learned of the Children of Israel in the Torah and the best at reciting it. Then he became a hypocrite, just as the Samiri did.

﴿So he oppressed them﴾: they mentioned among the forms of his oppression: disbelief, arrogance, his envy of Musa regarding prophethood, and of Harun regarding the sacrificial offering and the sacrifice, his oppression of the Children of Israel when Pharaoh made him their ruler, and his scheming to bring a prostitute who would falsely accuse Musa of approaching her, thereby exposing him before an assembly of the Children of Israel. And among his arrogance was that he lengthened his garments by a span.

﴿We had given him treasures﴾: it is said that God caused him to find a treasure from the treasures of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It is also said that his wealth was called treasures because he withheld the payment of zakat, and because of this he became hostile to Musa, peace be upon him, at the very beginning of his enmity. The word (ma) is a relative pronoun whose relative clause is "inna" and its operands. Al-Nahhas said: "I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman, meaning al-Akhfash al-Saghir, say: 'How ugly is what the Kufans say about relative clauses, that the relative clause of (alladhi) cannot be "inna" and what it governs (p-132) within it, and in the Qur'an there is: ﴿what indeed its keys﴾.'" End of quote. The discussion of (mafatih) has already been addressed in Surat al-An'am. Here they said: it means the keys (maqalid) of his treasuries. Al-Suddi said: it means the treasuries themselves. Al-Dahhak said: its containers and receptacles. Al-A'mash read (mafatihahu) with a yāʾ, plural of (miftah), key. They also mentioned, concerning the great number of his keys, things that are false or close to falsehood, so I have not written them down. Abu Zayd said: "Nu'tu bil-'amal" means when you rise up with the work. The poet said:

*When we find a successor, a wretched successor, a servant who, when burdened with the load, gives way.*

He says: (na'a yanu'u) means he rose up under a weight. The poet said:

*Its hindquarters strain, so its standing is slow, and it walks at ease, yet soon it is breathless.*

Abu 'Ubayda said: it is inverted (maqlub), and its original form is: (la-tanu'u biha al-'usbatu), meaning, it rises up with it, the band. Inversion (al-qalb), according to our companions, belongs mainly to poetry. The correct view is that the (ba') is for transitivity (al-ta'diya), meaning: it makes the band give way, just as you say "dhahabtu bihi" and "adhhabtuhu," and "ji'tu bihi" and "aja'tuhu." This is reported from al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and al-Farra', and al-Nahhas chose it. Its meaning is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih, and al-Suddi. The Arabs say: "na'a al-himlu bil-ba'ir" when it made the camel heavy. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible to attribute (tanu'u) to the keys, because they rise with difficulty when the one who lifts them strains, and this is common in "na'a al-himlu bil-ba'ir" and similar expressions, so consider it. Budayl ibn Maysara read (la-yanu'u) with a yāʾ and masculine form, taking into account the omitted noun in the construction: the estimated meaning is: "Indeed, the weight of its keys," or "its amount," or something like that. Al-Zamakhshari said: its explanation is that (mafatih) is interpreted as treasuries, and it is given the ruling of what it is annexed to, through association and connection, like his saying: "dhahabat ahl al-Yamama" (the people of Yamama went). End of quote. He means that the keys acquired masculine gender from the pronoun referring to Qarun, just as the word (ahl) acquired feminine gender from its annexation to Yamama, so it was said: "dhahabat." Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that Budayl ibn Maysara read: "ma inna miftahahu" in the singular, so his reading (la-yanu'u) with a yāʾ does not require interpretation. The explanation of (al-'usbah) has already been given in Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him. And before the explanation of (al-mafatih) it was mentioned whether they are the keys, or the treasuries themselves, or the containers and receptacles. And from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan: the keys are wealth.

Ibn 'Abbas said: his treasuries were carried by forty strong men, and they were four hundred thousand, each man carrying ten thousand. Abu Muslim said: what is meant by the keys is knowledge and comprehension, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿With Him are the keys of the Unseen﴾ [Al-An'am: 59]. The meaning is: We gave him treasures whose preservation and knowledge of them would indeed burden a band, meaning these treasures, because of their abundance and the variety of their kinds, would exhaust those who are in charge of guarding them.

﴿When his people said to him, "Do not exult"﴾: they forbade him from the arrogant exultation, which is absorption, dissolution of the soul, insolence, and self-admiration. Only one who is at peace with the world and heedless of the matter of the Hereafter rejoices in the world's turning toward him, whereas one who considers himself about to part soon from the blossom of this world does not rejoice in it. Abu al-Tayyib said:

*The greatest grief to me, in joy, is one whose possessor is sure of departing from it.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: the position of (idh) is in the accusative, governed by (tanu'u). End of quote. This is very weak, because the weighing down of the band by the keys is not restricted to the time of his people's saying to him, "Do not exult." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is related to His saying: ﴿so he oppressed them﴾, and this is also weak, because his oppression of them was not restricted to that time. Al-Hawfi said: its governing verb is omitted, its estimate being: "Remember." Abu al-Baqa' said: "(idh qala lahu)" is an adverbial complement for "atayna-hu," and this is also weak, because the giving did not occur at the time of that saying. He also said: it is permissible that it be an adverbial complement for an omitted verb indicated by the context, meaning: he oppressed them ﴿when his people said to him﴾. End of quote. It seems that the estimate should be: he then displayed boasting and exultation over what he had been given of treasures ﴿when his people said to him, "Do not exult."﴾ And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not exult in what He has given you﴾ [Al-Hadid: 23], and the Arabs praise the abandonment of exultation when good comes. The poet said:

*I am not one who exults when fortune delights me, nor one who frets over its changing turns.*

Another said:

*If we meet a man who is generous, let us not be counted among those who rejoice in good, nor stumble from harm.*

It was also read: (al-farihin), with the active participle, reported by 'Isa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi. And (la yuhibbu) is a description of action, not a description of essence, meaning in the sense of will, because exultation is a matter that has already occurred. So the meaning is: He does not show His blessing upon them, nor does His mercy encompass them. And when they forbade him from insolent exultation, they commanded him to seek, in what God had given him of treasures and abundance of provision, the reward of the Hereafter, by doing acts of righteousness and making it provision for you toward the Hereafter.

﴿And do not forget your share of this world.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: its meaning is: do not waste your life by not doing righteous deeds in your world, since the Hereafter is only worked for in this world, so a person's share is his life and his righteous deeds in it. This interpretation contains admonition. Al-Hasan and Qatada said its meaning is: do not waste your portion of this world by enjoying the lawful and seeking it, meaning, by looking to the consequences of your worldly life. In this interpretation there is some gentleness. Al-Hasan also said: its meaning is: advance the surplus and hold back what you need to sustain you. Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. It was also said: they meant by his share the shroud, and this is a connected admonition, as if they said: you will leave all your wealth, and your share of it will be nothing but a shroud, as the poet said:

*Your share of all that you gather throughout the ages is two garments in which you will be lodged, and spices for embalming.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: that you take from it what suffices you and sets you right. This is close to the saying of al-Hasan. ﴿And do good﴾ to the servants of God, or through your thankfulness and obedience to God.

﴿As God has done good to you﴾ with those blessings with which He has entrusted you. The particle (ka) is for comparison, and it may apply to some attributes, because the resemblance of a servant's goodness to God's goodness in all attributes is impossible. So the comparison falls upon the absolute notion of goodness. Or (ka) may be for causation, meaning: do good for the sake of God's goodness to you.

﴿And do not seek corruption﴾, meaning: what you are upon of insolence and wrongdoing. (ʿalā ʿilm), where (ʿilm) is a verbal noun, may be read as annexed to what follows and as annexed to God. The majority said: he claimed that he possessed a knowledge that entitled him to be the owner of those treasures. It was said: the knowledge of the Torah and its memorization, and he was one of the seventy whom Musa chose for the appointed time, and this was a deception. Abu Sulayman al-Dani said: that is the knowledge of trade and the ways of gain, meaning: I was given it through my own understanding and effort. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the knowledge of alchemy (al-kimiya'), and Ibn al-Musayyab said: Musa, peace be upon him, knew alchemy, which is the transformation of lead and copper into gold. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "upon knowledge of making gold," but this is probably not authentically reported from him or from Ibn al-Musayyab. Al-Zajjaj denied the knowledge of alchemy and said: it is false and has no reality. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verse 74–82 (part 2 of 2):

The people of Egypt have often been fond of seeking things that are impossible and superstitious. Among these: drawing water underground (taghwir al-ma'), serving images depicted as lines on walls, and their claim that those lines move when they are served with various kinds of services for them and with alchemy (al-kimya'). Even their shaykhs of knowledge, who among them hold the appearance of sainthood (al-wilaya), demand this from the most ignorant of the newcomers from the Maghrib. Ibn Zayd and others said: he meant "I have been given it on knowledge" (﴿أوتيته على علم﴾) from God and a special grant from Him intended for me, that is, nothing of what you say binds me in it. Then he made his saying "with me" (ʿindi) like one who says: "in my belief and in what I see." Mujahid said: "on knowledge" means "on a good that God knew to be with me." The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Did he not know﴾ is an affirmation of his knowledge of that and a warning of his error in his self-deception, that is: he knew that God had destroyed before him generations who were stronger than him and richer, because he had read it in the Torah, and Moses informed him of it, and he heard it in the histories. As if it were said: did he not know, among what he has of knowledge? This is so that he not be deceived by the abundance of his wealth and his strength. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it be a description of his knowledge of that, because when he said ﴿I have been given it on knowledge with me﴾ he became puffed up with knowledge and magnified himself by it, it was said: does he have with him the like of that knowledge which he claims? He saw himself as deserving of every blessing, and he did not know this beneficial knowledge so as to protect himself from the fate of the ruined. End.

﴿And more abundant in number﴾ either refers to wealth, or to a group who surround and serve him. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: ﴿Did he not know﴾ with the preponderance that (p-134) Qarun had become intoxicated with knowledge of himself according to his own claim.

The majority read (wa-la yus'alu) in the passive voice, with al-mujrimun (the criminals) as its subject, and it is connected to what precedes it, as Muhammad ibn Ka'b said. The pronoun in (dhunubihim) refers to those of the generations who were destroyed, that is: those other than them of the guilty are not questioned, nor are those who did not commit crime questioned about those whom God destroyed; rather ﴿every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38]. It was also said: those of the generations whom He destroyed, He knew their sins, so He had no need to question them about them. It was also said: it is a new statement about the situation on the Day of Resurrection. Qatada said: they are not asked about their sins because they are manifest and numerous, for they enter the Fire without reckoning. Qatada and Mujahid also said: the angels do not ask them about their sins, because they recognize them by their marks of blackness and disfigurement, as in His saying: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. It was also said: they are not asked with a question of rebuke and reproach. Abu Ja'far, in one transmission, read: "wa-la tas'al" with the ta' and jazm, and "al-mujrimin" in the accusative. Ibn Sirin and Abu al-ʿAliya read likewise "wa-la tas'al" as a prohibition addressed to the one addressed, and Ibn Abi Ishaq did not permit this unless "al-mujrimin" with the ya' is in the accusative position, the verb falling upon it. The author of al-Lawami' said: the apparent is what he said, and I have not received anything about the accusative of al-mujrimin. If they left it in its nominative, it has two aspects: the first: that the ha' and mim in ﴿ʿan dhunubihim﴾ refer to what preceded of the generations, and the nominative of "al-mujrimin" is by an implied subject, its estimate being: "they are the criminals," or "those are the criminals," and similar to it ﴿the repenting, the worshipping﴾ [al-Tawba: 112] in al-Tawba. The second: that it be a substitute for the original ha' and mim in (dhunubihim), for they, though in the genitive position by the annexation to them, their origin is the nominative, because the annexation to them is in the position of the annexation of the verbal noun to the active participle; so on that basis "al-mujrimun" is carried to the original, as we have previously mentioned that some of them read: ﴿that He should strike an example, a gnat﴾ [al-Baqara: 26] in the genitive, on the basis that it is a substitute for the original of "example," and "ma" is superfluous in it, its estimate being: "he is not ashamed to strike an example of a gnat," that is: to strike a gnat. Regarding this, it was explained that with the separation by the verbal noun, the governor reaches the object, then the gnat was substituted from it without my knowing any trace of a state in it. As for his saying "dhunub," it is a plural; if it is the plural of a verbal noun, there is a disagreement about its governing. As for his saying "as we have previously mentioned that some of them read," he mentioned in al-Baqara that he heard that, and we do not know any trace in it, so he should not make it a recitation.

When He mentioned Qarun, his description, what He gave him of treasures, and his exultation in that, the exultation of the exultant, and his claim that what he was given of that he was given on knowledge, He mentioned what arises from arrogance and joy in what he was given, and so He said: ﴿So he went out to his people in his adornment﴾, and it was a Saturday; that is: he displayed the most that he was able to of clothing, mounts, and the adornment of the world. Jabir and Mujahid said: in red garments. Ibn Zayd said: he and his retinue were in saffron-dyed garments. It was said: in garments of purple. It was said: on a white mule over which was purple, and over it a saddle of gold, and with him four thousand on his style. It was said: upon them and upon their horses was red brocade, and on his right were three hundred boys, and on his left three hundred white maidens upon whom were jewelry and brocade. It was said: in ninety thousand, upon them the saffron garments, and it was the first day in which saffron was seen. Other modes were said.

﴿Those who desired the life of this world said﴾: it was said: they were believers. Qatada said: they wished for it in order to draw near to God by it. It was said: out of desire for ease and wealth. It was said: they were disbelievers, and they wished ﴿the like of what Qarun was given﴾ and did not mention the end of his blessing, and this is from envy (al-ghibta).

﴿Indeed he is of great fortune﴾, that is: a great rank, said by al-Dahhak. It was said: a great portion of the world. The ḥaẓẓ (fortune) is luck and good fortune; it is said: "So-and-so is of fortune, lucky, and fortunate."

﴿And those who were given knowledge said﴾ among them: Yusha ʿ. Knowledge: the knowing of reward and punishment, or trust in God, or reporting, are sayings. (Woe to you) is a supplication with evil.

﴿The reward of God﴾, which is what He has prepared in the Hereafter for the believer, is ﴿better﴾ than what Qarun was given.

﴿And none receives it﴾, that is: this wisdom, which is the knowing of God's reward. It was said: Paradise and its bliss. It was said: this statement, which is their saying: ﴿The reward of God is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds﴾, with which He rebuked them.

﴿Except the patient﴾ in obedience and in restraining their souls from desires.

A portion of the account of Qarun and his envy of Moses has preceded (p-135). Among his envy was that he set a reward for a prostitute, on condition that she accuse Moses of seeking her and of fornication, and that she repented to God and confessed that Qarun was the one who had set for her a reward to accuse Moses of that. So God commanded the earth to obey him, and He said: "O earth, seize him and his followers," and they were swallowed up, in a long narrative of which God knows best. When Qarun and those with him were swallowed up, the Children of Israel said: Moses only prayed against Qarun so that he might seize his house and treasures, so he called upon God until He swallowed up his house and his wealth. And ﴿min﴾ is superfluous, that is: from a group which conveys the comprehensiveness of the categories. And when the sentence is negated and he was not able to help him, the negation of the one from his support is more emphatic.

﴿And he was not of those who were given victory﴾, that is: he was not, in himself, of those who could defend against the punishment of God.

﴿And those who had wished for his place yesterday morning﴾ is a substitute; and "asbaḥa" (became), if it is taken in its apparent sense, means that the swallowing up of him and his house was at night, and that is the most frightful of punishments, since night is the place of rest and tranquility. And "al-ams" (yesterday) may be intended as past time, and it may be intended as what was before the day of the swallowing, which is the day of wishing, and this is indicated by the conjunction with "fa" which implies sequence in His saying: ﴿So We caused to sink﴾; so the punishment followed his going out in his adornment, and in that is the hastening of punishment. "Makanahu" means his rank in the world, in wealth, retinue, and followers. "Wayka" according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh is a verb-name like "ṣah" and "mah," and its meaning is: "I am amazed." Al-Khalil said: that is because the people regretted and said, regretting what had passed from them: "wayka," and everyone who regrets and shows his regret says "wayka." "Ka'anna" is the particle of comparison entering upon "anna," and it was written joined to the comparison particle because of frequent use. Sibawayh recited:

"Wayka, as if he who has wealth is one who is given, and he who is poor lives the life of hardship."

The verse belongs to Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl. Al-Farra' related that a woman said to her husband: "Where is your son?" He said: "Wayka'annahu behind the house," and according to this view, the pause is on "wayka." Al-Akhfash said: it is "waykaʾ," and the kaf should be a particle of address, without any place in the grammar, and its pause is "wayk," and from it is the saying of ʿAntara:

"And indeed he has healed my soul and cured its sickness: the cry of the horsemen, 'Waykа, ʿAntar, advance!'"

Al-Akhfash said: "anna" after it is open by the estimate of knowledge, that is: "I know that God..." And the poet said:

"Alas, waykа, the harm does not last, and bliss does not leave misery."

Al-Kisa'i, Yunus, Abu Hatim and others held that its origin is "waylaka," so the lam and the kaf were deleted in a place of genitive by annexation. So according to the first view, it was said the kaf is free of the meaning of comparison, as it was said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. According to the second view, the meaning is: "I am amazed, because God..." And according to the third view, "waylaka" is an expression of grief, and the meaning likewise: "because God..." Abu Zayd and a group with him said: "wayka'anna" is one particle in its entirety, and it means: "Have you not seen?" Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Kisa'i and Abu ʿUbayd said with the meaning: "Have you not seen?" al-Farra' said: "wayka" in the speech of the Arabs is like the saying of a man: "Do you not see the handiwork of God?" Ibn Qutayba related from some scholars that he said: the meaning of "wayka" is: "mercy upon you," in the dialect of Himyar.

When there issued from them the wish for Qarun's condition, and they witnessed the swallowing up, that was a restraint for them from love of the world, and a summons to contentment with God's decree, so they awakened to their error and said: "Wayka," then they said: ﴿Indeed God extends provision to whom He wills of His servants﴾ according to His will and wisdom, not because of honor with Him, and He restricts it for whom He wills, not because of contempt, but for His wisdom and decree as a trial. Al-A'mash read: "lawla man Allahu" with the omission of "an," and it is superfluous. It is related from him: "manna Allahi" with the nun raised and the annexation. The majority read: "la-khusifa" in the passive voice. Hafs, ʿIsma, Aban from ʿAsim, and Ibn Abi Hammad from Abu Bakr: in the active voice. Ibn Mas'ud, Talha, and al-A'mash: "la-nkhasafa bina," as in your saying "inqata'a bina," as if it were a reflexive verb, and the position of the doer is held by "bina." It is permissible that it be the verbal noun, that is: "the sinking sank," and the reflexive of "fa'ala" is not transitive to a direct object, so for that reason it was built (p-136) either for the building or for the verbal noun. And also from Ibn Mas'ud: "latukhussifa," with a ta' and a doubled sin, in the passive voice.

(p-131) **[Verse 74]** ﴿On the Day He calls to them, He will say, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿And We will draw forth from every nation a witness, and We will say, "Bring your proof." Then they will know that the truth belongs to God, and what they used to fabricate will vanish from them.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa, but he oppressed them. We had given him treasures whose keys would weigh heavily upon a band of strong men, when his people said to him, "Do not exult. Indeed, God does not love the exultant."﴾ ﴿But seek, through what God has given you, the Abode of the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of this world. Do good as God has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the land. Indeed, God does not love the corrupters."﴾ ﴿He said, "I was given it only on account of knowledge I possess." Did he not know that God had destroyed before him generations that were greater than him in strength and more abundant in wealth? The guilty will not be asked about their sins.﴾ ﴿So he went out before his people in his adornment. Those who desired the life of this world said, "Would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given. Indeed, he is possessed of great fortune."﴾ ﴿But those who had been given knowledge said, "Woe to you! The reward of God is better for those who believe and do righteous deeds, and it is granted only to the steadfast."﴾ ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. He had no group to help him against God, nor was he one of those who could defend himself.﴾ ﴿And by the morning, those who had coveted his position said, "Woe! It seems that God widens provision for whom He wills of His servants and restricts it. Had God not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. Woe! It seems the disbelievers will not prosper."﴾.

The discussion of His saying: (Wa-yawma yunadihim) has already been addressed, and it is repeated here for emphasis and reinforcement. (Wa-naza'na) means: We separated and brought forth swiftly from every nation of the nations. (Shahidan), meaning the prophet of that nation, because he is the witness over it, as He said: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you as a witness over these people?﴾ [An-Nisa': 41]. It is also said: (shahidan) means just and choice persons. According to this view, (al-shahid) is a generic noun (ism al-jins), and the witness testifies against that nation regarding what proceeded from it and how it responded when it was called to monotheism, and that its prophet had conveyed to them the message of their Lord. (Fa-qulna), meaning to the assembly: ﴿Bring your proof﴾, meaning your argument concerning what you were upon in the world of disbelief and opposition to this witness. ﴿Then they will know that the truth belongs to God﴾, not to their idols, nor to what they worshipped besides God. (Wa-dalla 'anhum), meaning: it vanished from them with the absence of a lost thing. ﴿What they used to fabricate﴾ of falsehood and vanity.

Qarun is non-Arabic (a'jami): it is not declined because of foreignness and being a proper name. It is also said that the meaning of "was of his people" is: he was among those who believed in him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He was an Israelite by consensus." End of quote. There has been disagreement about his kinship to Musa, peace be upon him, a disagreement that is confused and contradictory. The most plausible view is what Ibn 'Abbas said: that he was the son of Musa's paternal uncle, namely Qarun ibn Yashhur ibn Qahith, the grandfather of Musa, because genealogists recorded his lineage thus. He was called "al-Munawwar" because of the beauty of his appearance, and he was the most learned of the Children of Israel in the Torah and the best at reciting it. Then he became a hypocrite, just as the Samiri did.

﴿So he oppressed them﴾: they mentioned among the forms of his oppression: disbelief, arrogance, his envy of Musa regarding prophethood, and of Harun regarding the sacrificial offering and the sacrifice, his oppression of the Children of Israel when Pharaoh made him their ruler, and his scheming to bring a prostitute who would falsely accuse Musa of approaching her, thereby exposing him before an assembly of the Children of Israel. And among his arrogance was that he lengthened his garments by a span.

﴿We had given him treasures﴾: it is said that God caused him to find a treasure from the treasures of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It is also said that his wealth was called treasures because he withheld the payment of zakat, and because of this he became hostile to Musa, peace be upon him, at the very beginning of his enmity. The word (ma) is a relative pronoun whose relative clause is "inna" and its operands. Al-Nahhas said: "I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman, meaning al-Akhfash al-Saghir, say: 'How ugly is what the Kufans say about relative clauses, that the relative clause of (alladhi) cannot be "inna" and what it governs (p-132) within it, and in the Qur'an there is: ﴿what indeed its keys﴾.'" End of quote. The discussion of (mafatih) has already been addressed in Surat al-An'am. Here they said: it means the keys (maqalid) of his treasuries. Al-Suddi said: it means the treasuries themselves. Al-Dahhak said: its containers and receptacles. Al-A'mash read (mafatihahu) with a yāʾ, plural of (miftah), key. They also mentioned, concerning the great number of his keys, things that are false or close to falsehood, so I have not written them down. Abu Zayd said: "Nu'tu bil-'amal" means when you rise up with the work. The poet said:

*When we find a successor, a wretched successor, a servant who, when burdened with the load, gives way.*

He says: (na'a yanu'u) means he rose up under a weight. The poet said:

*Its hindquarters strain, so its standing is slow, and it walks at ease, yet soon it is breathless.*

Abu 'Ubayda said: it is inverted (maqlub), and its original form is: (la-tanu'u biha al-'usbatu), meaning, it rises up with it, the band. Inversion (al-qalb), according to our companions, belongs mainly to poetry. The correct view is that the (ba') is for transitivity (al-ta'diya), meaning: it makes the band give way, just as you say "dhahabtu bihi" and "adhhabtuhu," and "ji'tu bihi" and "aja'tuhu." This is reported from al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and al-Farra', and al-Nahhas chose it. Its meaning is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Salih, and al-Suddi. The Arabs say: "na'a al-himlu bil-ba'ir" when it made the camel heavy. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is possible to attribute (tanu'u) to the keys, because they rise with difficulty when the one who lifts them strains, and this is common in "na'a al-himlu bil-ba'ir" and similar expressions, so consider it. Budayl ibn Maysara read (la-yanu'u) with a yāʾ and masculine form, taking into account the omitted noun in the construction: the estimated meaning is: "Indeed, the weight of its keys," or "its amount," or something like that. Al-Zamakhshari said: its explanation is that (mafatih) is interpreted as treasuries, and it is given the ruling of what it is annexed to, through association and connection, like his saying: "dhahabat ahl al-Yamama" (the people of Yamama went). End of quote. He means that the keys acquired masculine gender from the pronoun referring to Qarun, just as the word (ahl) acquired feminine gender from its annexation to Yamama, so it was said: "dhahabat." Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned that Budayl ibn Maysara read: "ma inna miftahahu" in the singular, so his reading (la-yanu'u) with a yāʾ does not require interpretation. The explanation of (al-'usbah) has already been given in Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him. And before the explanation of (al-mafatih) it was mentioned whether they are the keys, or the treasuries themselves, or the containers and receptacles. And from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan: the keys are wealth.

Ibn 'Abbas said: his treasuries were carried by forty strong men, and they were four hundred thousand, each man carrying ten thousand. Abu Muslim said: what is meant by the keys is knowledge and comprehension, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿With Him are the keys of the Unseen﴾ [Al-An'am: 59]. The meaning is: We gave him treasures whose preservation and knowledge of them would indeed burden a band, meaning these treasures, because of their abundance and the variety of their kinds, would exhaust those who are in charge of guarding them.

﴿When his people said to him, "Do not exult"﴾: they forbade him from the arrogant exultation, which is absorption, dissolution of the soul, insolence, and self-admiration. Only one who is at peace with the world and heedless of the matter of the Hereafter rejoices in the world's turning toward him, whereas one who considers himself about to part soon from the blossom of this world does not rejoice in it. Abu al-Tayyib said:

*The greatest grief to me, in joy, is one whose possessor is sure of departing from it.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: the position of (idh) is in the accusative, governed by (tanu'u). End of quote. This is very weak, because the weighing down of the band by the keys is not restricted to the time of his people's saying to him, "Do not exult." Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is related to His saying: ﴿so he oppressed them﴾, and this is also weak, because his oppression of them was not restricted to that time. Al-Hawfi said: its governing verb is omitted, its estimate being: "Remember." Abu al-Baqa' said: "(idh qala lahu)" is an adverbial complement for "atayna-hu," and this is also weak, because the giving did not occur at the time of that saying. He also said: it is permissible that it be an adverbial complement for an omitted verb indicated by the context, meaning: he oppressed them ﴿when his people said to him﴾. End of quote. It seems that the estimate should be: he then displayed boasting and exultation over what he had been given of treasures ﴿when his people said to him, "Do not exult."﴾ And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not exult in what He has given you﴾ [Al-Hadid: 23], and the Arabs praise the abandonment of exultation when good comes. The poet said:

*I am not one who exults when fortune delights me, nor one who frets over its changing turns.*

Another said:

*If we meet a man who is generous, let us not be counted among those who rejoice in good, nor stumble from harm.*

It was also read: (al-farihin), with the active participle, reported by 'Isa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi. And (la yuhibbu) is a description of action, not a description of essence, meaning in the sense of will, because exultation is a matter that has already occurred. So the meaning is: He does not show His blessing upon them, nor does His mercy encompass them. And when they forbade him from insolent exultation, they commanded him to seek, in what God had given him of treasures and abundance of provision, the reward of the Hereafter, by doing acts of righteousness and making it provision for you toward the Hereafter.

﴿And do not forget your share of this world.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: its meaning is: do not waste your life by not doing righteous deeds in your world, since the Hereafter is only worked for in this world, so a person's share is his life and his righteous deeds in it. This interpretation contains admonition. Al-Hasan and Qatada said its meaning is: do not waste your portion of this world by enjoying the lawful and seeking it, meaning, by looking to the consequences of your worldly life. In this interpretation there is some gentleness. Al-Hasan also said: its meaning is: advance the surplus and hold back what you need to sustain you. Malik said: it is eating and drinking without extravagance. It was also said: they meant by his share the shroud, and this is a connected admonition, as if they said: you will leave all your wealth, and your share of it will be nothing but a shroud, as the poet said:

*Your share of all that you gather throughout the ages is two garments in which you will be lodged, and spices for embalming.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: that you take from it what suffices you and sets you right. This is close to the saying of al-Hasan. ﴿And do good﴾ to the servants of God, or through your thankfulness and obedience to God.

﴿As God has done good to you﴾ with those blessings with which He has entrusted you. The particle (ka) is for comparison, and it may apply to some attributes, because the resemblance of a servant's goodness to God's goodness in all attributes is impossible. So the comparison falls upon the absolute notion of goodness. Or (ka) may be for causation, meaning: do good for the sake of God's goodness to you.

﴿And do not seek corruption﴾, meaning: what you are upon of insolence and wrongdoing. (ʿalā ʿilm), where (ʿilm) is a verbal noun, may be read as annexed to what follows and as annexed to God. The majority said: he claimed that he possessed a knowledge that entitled him to be the owner of those treasures. It was said: the knowledge of the Torah and its memorization, and he was one of the seventy whom Musa chose for the appointed time, and this was a deception. Abu Sulayman al-Dani said: that is the knowledge of trade and the ways of gain, meaning: I was given it through my own understanding and effort. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the knowledge of alchemy (al-kimiya'), and Ibn al-Musayyab said: Musa, peace be upon him, knew alchemy, which is the transformation of lead and copper into gold. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "upon knowledge of making gold," but this is probably not authentically reported from him or from Ibn al-Musayyab. Al-Zajjaj denied the knowledge of alchemy and said: it is false and has no reality. End of quote.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 28, verse 74–82 (part 2 of 2):

The people of Egypt have often been fond of seeking things that are impossible and superstitious. Among these: drawing water underground (taghwir al-ma'), serving images depicted as lines on walls, and their claim that those lines move when they are served with various kinds of services for them and with alchemy (al-kimya'). Even their shaykhs of knowledge, who among them hold the appearance of sainthood (al-wilaya), demand this from the most ignorant of the newcomers from the Maghrib. Ibn Zayd and others said: he meant "I have been given it on knowledge" (﴿أوتيته على علم﴾) from God and a special grant from Him intended for me, that is, nothing of what you say binds me in it. Then he made his saying "with me" (ʿindi) like one who says: "in my belief and in what I see." Mujahid said: "on knowledge" means "on a good that God knew to be with me." The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿Did he not know﴾ is an affirmation of his knowledge of that and a warning of his error in his self-deception, that is: he knew that God had destroyed before him generations who were stronger than him and richer, because he had read it in the Torah, and Moses informed him of it, and he heard it in the histories. As if it were said: did he not know, among what he has of knowledge? This is so that he not be deceived by the abundance of his wealth and his strength. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that it be a description of his knowledge of that, because when he said ﴿I have been given it on knowledge with me﴾ he became puffed up with knowledge and magnified himself by it, it was said: does he have with him the like of that knowledge which he claims? He saw himself as deserving of every blessing, and he did not know this beneficial knowledge so as to protect himself from the fate of the ruined. End.

﴿And more abundant in number﴾ either refers to wealth, or to a group who surround and serve him. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: ﴿Did he not know﴾ with the preponderance that (p-134) Qarun had become intoxicated with knowledge of himself according to his own claim.

The majority read (wa-la yus'alu) in the passive voice, with al-mujrimun (the criminals) as its subject, and it is connected to what precedes it, as Muhammad ibn Ka'b said. The pronoun in (dhunubihim) refers to those of the generations who were destroyed, that is: those other than them of the guilty are not questioned, nor are those who did not commit crime questioned about those whom God destroyed; rather ﴿every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 38]. It was also said: those of the generations whom He destroyed, He knew their sins, so He had no need to question them about them. It was also said: it is a new statement about the situation on the Day of Resurrection. Qatada said: they are not asked about their sins because they are manifest and numerous, for they enter the Fire without reckoning. Qatada and Mujahid also said: the angels do not ask them about their sins, because they recognize them by their marks of blackness and disfigurement, as in His saying: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾ [al-Rahman: 41]. It was also said: they are not asked with a question of rebuke and reproach. Abu Ja'far, in one transmission, read: "wa-la tas'al" with the ta' and jazm, and "al-mujrimin" in the accusative. Ibn Sirin and Abu al-ʿAliya read likewise "wa-la tas'al" as a prohibition addressed to the one addressed, and Ibn Abi Ishaq did not permit this unless "al-mujrimin" with the ya' is in the accusative position, the verb falling upon it. The author of al-Lawami' said: the apparent is what he said, and I have not received anything about the accusative of al-mujrimin. If they left it in its nominative, it has two aspects: the first: that the ha' and mim in ﴿ʿan dhunubihim﴾ refer to what preceded of the generations, and the nominative of "al-mujrimin" is by an implied subject, its estimate being: "they are the criminals," or "those are the criminals," and similar to it ﴿the repenting, the worshipping﴾ [al-Tawba: 112] in al-Tawba. The second: that it be a substitute for the original ha' and mim in (dhunubihim), for they, though in the genitive position by the annexation to them, their origin is the nominative, because the annexation to them is in the position of the annexation of the verbal noun to the active participle; so on that basis "al-mujrimun" is carried to the original, as we have previously mentioned that some of them read: ﴿that He should strike an example, a gnat﴾ [al-Baqara: 26] in the genitive, on the basis that it is a substitute for the original of "example," and "ma" is superfluous in it, its estimate being: "he is not ashamed to strike an example of a gnat," that is: to strike a gnat. Regarding this, it was explained that with the separation by the verbal noun, the governor reaches the object, then the gnat was substituted from it without my knowing any trace of a state in it. As for his saying "dhunub," it is a plural; if it is the plural of a verbal noun, there is a disagreement about its governing. As for his saying "as we have previously mentioned that some of them read," he mentioned in al-Baqara that he heard that, and we do not know any trace in it, so he should not make it a recitation.

When He mentioned Qarun, his description, what He gave him of treasures, and his exultation in that, the exultation of the exultant, and his claim that what he was given of that he was given on knowledge, He mentioned what arises from arrogance and joy in what he was given, and so He said: ﴿So he went out to his people in his adornment﴾, and it was a Saturday; that is: he displayed the most that he was able to of clothing, mounts, and the adornment of the world. Jabir and Mujahid said: in red garments. Ibn Zayd said: he and his retinue were in saffron-dyed garments. It was said: in garments of purple. It was said: on a white mule over which was purple, and over it a saddle of gold, and with him four thousand on his style. It was said: upon them and upon their horses was red brocade, and on his right were three hundred boys, and on his left three hundred white maidens upon whom were jewelry and brocade. It was said: in ninety thousand, upon them the saffron garments, and it was the first day in which saffron was seen. Other modes were said.

﴿Those who desired the life of this world said﴾: it was said: they were believers. Qatada said: they wished for it in order to draw near to God by it. It was said: out of desire for ease and wealth. It was said: they were disbelievers, and they wished ﴿the like of what Qarun was given﴾ and did not mention the end of his blessing, and this is from envy (al-ghibta).

﴿Indeed he is of great fortune﴾, that is: a great rank, said by al-Dahhak. It was said: a great portion of the world. The ḥaẓẓ (fortune) is luck and good fortune; it is said: "So-and-so is of fortune, lucky, and fortunate."

﴿And those who were given knowledge said﴾ among them: Yusha ʿ. Knowledge: the knowing of reward and punishment, or trust in God, or reporting, are sayings. (Woe to you) is a supplication with evil.

﴿The reward of God﴾, which is what He has prepared in the Hereafter for the believer, is ﴿better﴾ than what Qarun was given.

﴿And none receives it﴾, that is: this wisdom, which is the knowing of God's reward. It was said: Paradise and its bliss. It was said: this statement, which is their saying: ﴿The reward of God is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds﴾, with which He rebuked them.

﴿Except the patient﴾ in obedience and in restraining their souls from desires.

A portion of the account of Qarun and his envy of Moses has preceded (p-135). Among his envy was that he set a reward for a prostitute, on condition that she accuse Moses of seeking her and of fornication, and that she repented to God and confessed that Qarun was the one who had set for her a reward to accuse Moses of that. So God commanded the earth to obey him, and He said: "O earth, seize him and his followers," and they were swallowed up, in a long narrative of which God knows best.
